Very often too, while we show too much sympathy to the flesh and spare it as though it were a fellow-citizen, we nourish an enemy for battle against ourselves. But when the vice of gluttony rules, people lose everything they have done bravely, because when the belly is not restrained, all the virtues are at once overwhelmed. For one does not rise up to the struggle of the spiritual contest unless the enemy placed within ourselves, namely the appetite of gluttony, is first subdued by us with God’s help; since unless we overcome the things that are nearer to us, we hasten in vain to fight against those set farther away. For war is waged uselessly in the field against foreign enemies while a citizen plotting within the city walls is present. We never conquer the assaults of demons unless we first overcome gluttony in ourselves.

Brothers, let no one deceive himself with empty persuasion, so as to believe that there is no sin among beans and vegetables if the mind, with excessive pleasure, loosens the appetite for receiving them. For guilt can be present everywhere in taking food, when appetite is extended beyond the rule of nature. See: we never eat meat, whether in the monastery or outside it; fish are very rarely seen here in this rural countryside; no one among us has ever seen richer foods; we neither can have delicacies, nor...

Our foods are barley, oats, beans, peas, and vegetables, also milk, cheese, and eggs. From these we receive the daily supports of our life; and lest disgust at them arise, hunger stirs up appetite. Outside the season of the Lenten fast, fish are so rare for us that scarcely once in a month are a few, and very tiny ones, brought from the river Nabe. In the whole Bursfeld reform there is no monastery less provided with fish in time of need. But can we therefore not fall into the vice of gluttony, because we cannot find more sumptuous foods? Indeed, since the vice lies not in the food, as has already been said, but in the appetite, the eater of peas or beans can sin no less in eating than one who is accustomed to eat the most sumptuous and choice dishes. Poverty does not make us wholly secure from gluttony, although it lessens the occasions of sinning in more delicate fare.

We do indeed have simple and rustic food, by which nature is somehow sustained. This, my brothers, I beg us to take care over: that by excess our conscience not be polluted by that which produces nausea in the delicate. Let us take with patience and thanksgiving from what the Lord has given as much as necessity itself requires; and let us not think that the snares of the devil cannot harm us, since he overthrew the first human beings in Paradise not with richer food, but with a small and common apple. For the vice is not in the food, but in the appetite, when either we desire what is forbidden to us, or, greedily gaping after what is permitted, we use it otherwise than we ought.

Abstinence befits no one more than a monk, who, since he has been specially called to the warfare of Christ, ought not by his profession to be free for any pleasures whatever. Our poverty imposes on us a certain necessity of abstinence, because we can restrain ourselves to temperance all the more easily, the less we can find delights into which to flow away. Let us therefore, I beg, turn the hardships of want into weapons of salvation, so that the less we are refreshed with richer foods, the more purely we may fast in holiness of soul. For temperance is more easily preserved in poverty, while in riches it is more quickly endangered.

What the food of monks ought to be, blessed Jerome makes clear, saying in a certain letter to Paulinus: Let your food be cheap and taken in the evening, namely vegetables and legumes, and sometimes count it the highest delicacy to eat a few little fish. He who desires Christ and feeds on that heavenly bread does not greatly seek from what precious foods he may make dung. The lover of Christ loves abstinence, honors fasting as the one remedy of soul and body, and with the greatest care guards against his heart being weighed down with excess; nor does he take more food than nature, content with little, demands.

But the monk who casts aside fasting, who hates abstinence, the nurse of virtues, who gulps down food greedily, who drinks wine or strong drink, and whatever can intoxicate, to satiety, is unworthy of the very name of monk, and cannot be Christ’s [unclear].

to be a disciple. Woe to our times, in which many clerics and monks have now shamefully cast aside the virtue of abstinence; and those who ought to have shown the people of God the way of salvation no less by example than by word, given to feasting and continual drinking, and sunk in pleasures contrary to all clerical honor, hasten to go before them into the perdition of eternal death.

Scripture says: “The beginning of man’s life is bread and water.” But now our monks and cloistered men buy for themselves, at great expense, whatever is sold most dearly and whatever is found most luxurious; they bury it by gorging it into their bellies, and through intemperance corrupt both soul and body. Amid banquets they debate fasting, and when they are drunk they praise temperance. There each man boasts that he is the conqueror of vices, although he has already been overcome by gluttony and drunkenness.

“Take heed,” says our Lord Jesus Christ in the holy Gospel according to Luke, “lest your hearts be weighed down in gluttonous excess.” It does not befit a man dedicated to God to eat or drink to satiety, nor is it lawful for a monk to eat more than nature requires. Let eating calm hunger, not bring on fullness. Let belches, which satiety is accustomed to produce in banqueters, be far away; let vomiting and indigestions never be heard of among monks. It is fitting that all we cloistered men use a great moderation of discretion, so that the body is nourished with foods and drinks in such a way that, serving the spirit, it can live, but not so that, fattened, it begins to grow wanton against the command of the mind. Let satiety always be far away, since nothing so inflames the body and stirs the generative members as undigested food and a belly heated with wine or beer.

Hence blessed Jerome, admonishing Eustochium to temperance, the guardian of all virtues, says in a certain letter: “Let the bride of Christ flee wine as poison,” since wine and youth itself are weapons against adolescence, which is more inclined to gluttony. Avarice does not so shake youth, nor does pride puff it up, nor ambition delight it, as do those vices of the flesh which seem to us bound together with pleasure. We shall easily lack other vices if we keep watch even moderately in the fear of the Lord. But this enemy of ours is always shut up within; wherever we go, we carry this adversary with us. Wine and youth are a double fire of pleasure. Why do we add oil to the flame, or why do we supply fiery fuel to a little body already burning? Gluttony has overthrown many who were walking chastely in the middle of the road, and those whom the devil could not conquer by his own incitements, excessive drinking of wine has cast down into the depth of lust.

Therefore Benedict, the most holy founder of our way of life, when listing the instruments of good works, set among the chief ones: “to chastise the body, to embrace vigils, to love fasting.” For no one truly follows Christ who, nourishing his flesh delicately, lives in a monastery without daily abstinence. For moderate abstinence, pleasing to God, does many things in us.

Homily XV.

It works good things, if it continues with a religious intention until the end of life. For above all it increases merit, and nourishes in us every kind of virtue.

What was the reason that almighty God forbade our first parents to eat the fruit, under threat of death, except to show them the occasion of merit through the good of obedience? For, as Scripture bears witness, he created two intellects from the beginning, namely the angelic and the human, to whom, through grace, he might communicate himself for the enjoyment of eternal happiness. Yet although he created both by the gift of his grace, he most rightly ordained that they should become forever blessed also by their own merit, so that in them both mercy might have its place, and conversion might obtain the merit necessary for salvation.

But the angelic intellect was immediately divided in two: some, falling of their own accord through pride, while others, humble and subject through love of their Principle, cleaved to him. Those who apostatized from their Principle departed in misery; but these, for the merit of their cleaving to him, were endowed with everlasting blessedness.

The human intellect, however, was sent down into flesh; and soon, at the devil’s persuasion, it transgressed the command of God and feasted on the food forbidden to it. From this followed the ruin of the whole human race, which no one could take away except the Son of God, made man from the Virgin for our sake. For what condemned our first parents except the transgression of the command? God was not concerned about the food, but about obedience. For if man had abstained, as almighty God had commanded him, surely by this obedience he would have merited, in his innocence, the enjoyment of eternal happiness.

For it is established by the tradition of the Scriptures that man cannot be saved without the merit of free will, since, even if the grace of God works all things in all, nevertheless he will save no one without the cooperation of his own will, except only infants baptized in the name of the Trinity, and those who cannot have the free use of reason. For just as free will does nothing toward salvation without the grace of the Savior, so the grace of God will not save an adult without the merit of a good will.

But the first man, placed in Paradise, transgressed the command of God through intemperance, and did not have the merit of obedience in a good will; therefore he was cast out, wretched and unhappy. Yet the mercy of almighty God determined from eternity to restore the one who had fallen through weakness, knowing that he had been deceived rather by the suggestion of the envious serpent than by his own malice. He pardoned this guilt through the passion and death of his only-begotten Son, born in time of the Virgin, so that the one who perished by his own rashness might be restored to salvation by the obedience of the mediator.

For it was impossible for the human race, lost through disobedience, to come to the mercy of the Creator except through the obedience of such a mediator, who would be God and man, in whom there would be both the power of divinity and the innocence of nature. For we were blind through ignorance, and mute through silence. The mediator of God came, and

Christ Jesus, appointed to enlighten every man coming into this world, gave mortals knowledge of God; and, dying for the lost, he sealed for the redeemed the greatest cause for love. He instructed the intellect through faith, by which we know God; he stirred the affection through his passion, so that we may deservedly love him above all things.

Therefore, if we love our Lord and Redeemer with unbroken sincerity, it is altogether fitting that for love of him we should discipline our body. For our abstinence will lead us to merit in a twofold way: namely, when by fasting we satisfy the statutes of the fathers through obedience, and when by abstaining out of charity toward God we show ourselves grateful to our Redeemer, who endured death for our sake.

Abstinence increases merit, commends obedience, bestows wisdom and learning, purifies affection, enlightens the intellect, grants victory against demons, perfects religion, obtains pardon for sins, subdues the unlawful motions of the flesh, wins efficacy for prayers, and displays to one’s neighbor an example of virtue. Abstinence purifies the mind, adorns the soul with virtues, and heals the weak little body. Whoever loves abstinence is wise; whoever loves fasting is a strong ruler. A sober mind is the dwelling place of wisdom; but whoever pursues banquets will die in poverty of spirit. It is hard for a man to become wise who lives a life of pleasures.

Nature is content with few things, and the health of life is preserved in moderation. Long-continued voracity has harmed many, and more have perished by drunken excess than by the sword. For habit seems to alter nature, and the longer it has grown strong, the stronger it will then be in any undertaking.

There is among the Swiss a man named Nicholas, whose abstinence has turned the people of all Germany to admiration; and today, as you have heard, he is named by everyone with the title of holiness. He was once a peasant in a certain Swiss village, and according to the custom of the pagans he used to pronounce judgment among fourteen for quarrelling villagers. It happened at one time that he could not revoke a sentence of his associates which he thought unjust; and fearing danger to the salvation of his soul, he left house, wife, children, and all the business and possessions of the world, and withdrew alone into a neighboring wood for love of God, where he lives a solitary life.

And behold, today it is the twentieth year since, entering solitude, he has taken no human food. I am saying things very well known to all; nor do I think there is any man living in Germany who has not heard the fame of this miracle. And lest anyone perhaps in the future believe that we have been deceived by simulation, we call as witnesses the Swiss, together with the bishop of the church of Constance, who observe his habits and life with the utmost care. He is a man of very keen intelligence, and though he is utterly ignorant of letters, nevertheless, like another Antony the hermit of old, he understands the sense of the Scriptures extremely well. We saw the things which he most eloquently debated with a certain master concerning the sacrament of the altar, things at which he who [unclear] heavenly matters by [unclear] will not be able to marvel enough.

Homily XV.

He has by no means tasted the zeal for contemplation. I have introduced these things, brothers, so that you may understand that nothing is so difficult that habit, continued over a long time, does not make it easy. This holy man, as he himself confesses, did not suddenly arrive at the height of this abstinence, but gradually over time, by degrees, little by little subtracting a little from his food, until at last he was able to abstain altogether. For, as we have said, he had abstained from every perishable food for almost twenty years.

By the example of this man, my brothers, let each of you learn daily to subtract something from his food and drink for the love of God, and accustom himself to give his body not as much as it can take, but as much as is sufficient to sustain nature. For nature, as Boethius testifies, is content with few and very small things. Many dishes produce many illnesses, and gluttony of the belly dulls the mind and torments life. For the wise man says: “The sleep of the laboring man is sweet, whether he eats little or much; but the fullness of the rich man does not allow him to sleep.”

The belly should be filled without satiety, and one should rise from table without disgust, so that we eat not as much as we can, but as much as, at nature’s demand, we ought. Monks especially must avoid variety of foods; for whoever uses varied dishes, trying to put into his stomach more than nature requires, feasts not without the vice of gluttony. The strength of our body must be restored by moderate and simple food, not shamefully oppressed by varied and many foods, because the body was not created for food, but food for the body. That variety of foods brings diseases upon the body we prove from the temperance of the ancients, whom a uniform simplicity of foods preserved for a very long time in this life.

Our most holy founder, Benedict, the most modest sacred teacher of all the leaders of monks, prescribed for us a rule adorned with the highest discretion; in it, wishing to show monks the measure of foods, he says: “We believe that for the daily meal, whether at the sixth or at the ninth hour, two cooked dishes are sufficient for all tables, on account of the different infirmities, so that anyone who perhaps cannot eat from one may be refreshed from the other. Therefore two cooked dishes should suffice for all the brothers. And if there are fruits there, or fresh vegetables, let a third be added.”

If I understand our lawgiver’s mind soundly, he allowed monks two cooked dishes where the necessity of infirmity requires it, not for the filling of the appetite of the healthy. For a monk who is healthy is rightly excepted from this indulgence, so that he is refreshed by only one cooked dish. But in my judgment the sick man is rightly permitted to be refreshed from both, since no excess is to be feared in him. Yet since we cannot all do all things equally, and one person needs more food while others need less, it is impossible to prescribe one form of abstinence for all, but [unclear].

It is left to the judgment of each person’s discretion, that he should take only as much as necessity demands, not as much as the pleasure of appetite commands. This above all must be guarded against: that immoderate fullness of food not creep in, which defiles the soul when either disgust follows refreshment, or heavy acedia follows the mind. Vomiting that proceeds from fullness is for dogs rather than for monks. The Christian religion especially detests a man who is a glutton, since the delights of the servants of God are not food and drink, but piety and justice, because God is worshiped by purity of faith, and to each person what is his own is justly administered.

Therefore, whoever you are who desire to please God with your whole heart, whoever you are who hasten to arrive at the joys of eternal happiness, appoint for yourself a measure of fasting according to the measure of your strength, and apply the greatest care that, while fasting, you be constant in prayer, just in judgments, outstanding in brotherly love, patient under injuries, humble under rebukes, circumspect in speech, clean in conscience, fervent in the love of God, and in all your actions, with prudence accompanying you, filled with fear. Flee useless and idle words, and be persevering in good works at all times, having constancy in adversities, watchfulness in temptations, continence in refreshment, and simple purity in heart.

Let fasts be moderate and holy in all humility of mind, so that they weaken the body in such a way that they do not lift the mind into pride, lest the exercise of humility become material for vices. Fasting detests idleness, does not love wordiness, loves solitude, and applies itself to prayers and tears. Fasting, as holy Ambrose bears witness, is the death of guilt, the destruction of offenses, the remedy of salvation, the root of grace, the foundation of chastity. By this step the righteous Moses came to God; by this gift Elijah ascended into heaven in a chariot before he died.

Those who walk in the spirit love fasting; and those who profess chastity necessarily flee an abundance of delights. For hunger is a friend to virginity, an enemy to wantonness. Fullness, however, betrays chastity and nourishes wantonness. For fasting extinguishes the burning arrows of the devil, the urgency of prayer restrains them, and the continuance of vigils in the love of Christ repels all the snares of demons.

Hence holy Pope Leo says in a certain sermon: What can be more effective than fasting, by whose observance we draw near to God, and, resisting the devil, overcome a flattering life? For fasting has always been food for virtue, and abstinence the nourishment of holy chastity. From abstinence, indeed, chaste thoughts proceed; it begets reasonable desires, modest counsels too; and through voluntary afflictions the flesh dies to concupiscences, while the spirit is renewed in virtues.

Therefore, my brothers, let us love fasting with the love of virtue, for the sake of him who did not refuse to undergo death for us; and let us abstain not only from illicit things, but also, as far as possible, from permitted things, so that we who have offended in many ways against the commandments of salvation may, in compensation of satisfaction, henceforth keep ourselves from every pleasure.

Homily XV

Let us restrain ourselves. Let us fast from every sin; let us take no food of malice; let us devour no feasts of pleasure; nor let us be drunk with the wine of luxury. Let us fast from all depravity; let us abstain from evil works. Let us not speak useless, vain, idle, buffoonish, and harmful words; and let us always beware of harmful and perverse thoughts, which separate us from God. Let us keep most diligent watch in prayers to God, knowing that he whom we call upon with our prayers is everywhere most present to us. Let his praise be always in our mouth, and, since we cannot praise his magnificence in speech, let us adore him in our heart with the desires of a most chaste love. For then our fasts are pleasing to him, when they have been adorned with holy works and continual prayers. For the prayer of the righteous person, as sacred Scripture bears witness, pierces the heavens; and it becomes the more efficacious, the more it is found adorned with charity and fasting. Let us join to it, as it were, two wings, fasting and charity, and it will obtain for us from the Lord whatever we ask that is conducive to salvation.

On the Lenten fast of monks. Homily XVI.

Since, by the bounty of our Lord Jesus Christ, dearest brothers, we have begun the Lenten fast, reason demands that we say something briefly about its observance. For although you have many writings of the holy fathers concerning this most sacred exercise of fasting, nevertheless, because I find that my sermons among you are not wholly fruitless, I gladly share for your edification what the Lord has granted.

For, as blessed Jerome bears witness, the act of a living voice has a certain hidden operation within, which in the adorned Greek language he called energy, and a discourse spoken by the mouth of one who goes before is stronger for persuasion. But I, set apart in your midst by the name of shepherd alone, confess myself to be a young man, unlearned, and lacking at once the experience and discretion necessary for the governance of souls. Hence it comes about that I speak with a certain blush and modesty: a young man among elders, an ignorant man among the learned, a disciple among masters. Therefore I beg that none of you despise the simplicity of my speech, that none take it hard that I speak, since even if I am not fit for speaking, nevertheless by reason of the office of pastoral care committed to me I acknowledge myself bound before God to admonish you.

Your charity gives me boldness to speak, and the more ready you show yourselves to listen, the more you stir me to speak. Nor will any labor be burdensome to me, however great it may seem, by which the salvation of your souls is brought to completion. Help me with your prayers, that the Lord Jesus may speak in my mouth and grant strength to my small talent to bring forth into the midst whatever can produce in you an increase of holy fervor. For, as much as I desire, to profit your charity by sermons

I cannot [serve you], because I am too much compelled to be occupied with secular affairs. Hence only on feast days, and in that part of the night which after the night lauds I am accustomed to spend sleepless, do I serve you by exhorting you, setting down in little pages what occurs to me to say.

And so I wished to introduce today’s discourse from the Rule of our most holy father Benedict, who speaks thus about the Lenten observance: “Although at every time the life of a monk ought to have the observance of Lent, nevertheless, because this virtue belongs to few, we therefore advise that in these days of Lent they guard their life with all purity, and together wash away in these holy days all the stains and negligences of other times. This is then done worthily if we restrain ourselves from all vices and devote ourselves to prayer with tears, to reading, and to compunction of heart.”

If this virtue belongs to few, that they should at every time lead lives of Lenten observance, it is now plainly clear that few monks live in religion according to the purity of the Gospel, since all who profess the warfare of Christ are bound to direct their effort toward the height of perfection. For a monk, according to the interpretation of his name, is solitary; and he is believed then to live rightly in the monastery according to the Gospel and the Rule which he has professed, when, having despised worldly things and honors for the love of God, he lives before God and men in all purity of heart, vigorous in work, clean in thought, sparing and peaceable in speech.

This is the life of a monk that has Lenten observance at every time: to chastise the body for the love of God through abstinence, and to nourish the mind through inward compunction. He lives rightly who lives justly, who loves God above all things, who with the highest zeal and the highest diligence observes his commandments in words and holy works. For he is a true monk of Christ who imitates Christ with all his strength.

But if you wish to imitate Christ, O monk, observe most diligently what I am about to say. Flee the world and all comforts of the flesh, so that you may deserve truly to be solitary. Never allow vain, useless, foul, and harmful thoughts to remain in your heart, but always think on something good, and let the memory of the Lord’s passion never withdraw from your mind, so that each day with thanksgiving you may contemplate the Lord hanging on the cross. Consider God as present to you everywhere, who sees, knows, and understands whatever you have either thought or done, since nothing is hidden from him.

Keep your heart clean from every stain of sin, and always have a pure conscience burning with the true love of Christ. Let no idle time fly away from you, but let thought always find you engaged in good works. Do not grow sluggish with much sleep, and make yourself far removed from every acedia of lukewarmness. Embrace moderation in food and drink, and live as sparingly as is permitted, so that the body, moderately sustained, may always serve the spirit in humility, and by no means against the command of reason [unclear].

Homily XVI.

Let him rise. As soon as you sense any sluggishness arising in you, flee to the remembrance of the most bitter Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, and call back to mind whatever can most quickly drive away acedia. Break off all delays, I beg you, because sluggishness of mind, if ignored, suddenly increases, and acedia, if it is not at once extinguished by a renewed fervor of mind, is immediately strengthened into grave ruin of the soul.

For among all evils in a monk this is the worst: if through sluggishness and acedia he gives place in his heart to a seedbed of vices. And you, monks, must keep watch against this beast not only every day, but every hour and every moment, because once it has been admitted into the heart, it never enters alone; rather, the whole heap and spring of all vices accompanies it. There is no more destructive plague for a monk than bodily acedia, by which every fervor of devotion is extinguished, and, in place of faithful service, the mind, through the interruption brought by idleness and leisure, is driven headlong into the pit of despair. Whoever allows acedia to linger quickly falls away from the purpose of holiness.

Against this Solomon admonishes you in the book of Proverbs, saying: “Go to the ant, sluggard, and consider her ways, and learn wisdom: though she has no guide, nor teacher, nor ruler, she prepares her food in summer and gathers at harvest what she may eat.” And again he says: “Desires kill the sluggard, because his hands refused to work at anything.”

Nothing is worse for those who have professed the purpose of holiness than idleness, because it not only accumulates nothing good, but also consumes and scatters everything previously accumulated. For the fervor of holy devotion rejoices in progress and advances; but through cessation it grows sluggish and little by little, not to say suddenly, vanishes. For sloth is the root of despair, and the mother and nurse of all vices. For just as a garment both produces and nourishes the moth, so the most destructive plague of acedia both gives birth to and fosters despair.

This beast is accustomed to trouble no one more than monks, and especially those who lead a withdrawn life in solitude. Therefore you must take the greatest care, monks, against this enemy of the salvation of souls, and you must fight it bravely not by fleeing but by resisting. You must diligently consider that no one has attained the honor of holiness by sluggishness and sloth, nor has anyone merited the kingdom of eternal happiness without great and continual labor.

Therefore the mind must always be renewed by daily and fresh increases of virtues, and this dangerous journey of life must be measured not by what has passed, but rather by what remains. Let no one promise himself security in this life, which is entirely called temptation, full of as many dangers as there are affections in the soul; but let each person take care that one who could become better from worse does not become worse from better.

And especially in these holy days let us all take care, as much as we can, to become better, adding for ourselves, according to the counsel of our holy forerunner, something to the fixed measure of our service: namely special prayers, and abstinences from food and drink.

abstinence, so that each one, beyond the measure enjoined on him, may of his own will, with the joy of the Holy Spirit, offer something to God, that is, withhold from his body food, drink, sleep, talkativeness, and buffoonery, and await holy Easter with the joy of spiritual longing. For he is shown to be but little religious as a monk at other times, who on these holy days is not found more religious, more fervent in the love of God, and more devout.

Hence the holy Pope Gregory says in a certain homily: “Lent must be observed with the utmost care, so that during it the fast, apart from Sundays, which are withdrawn from abstinence, is in no way broken, unless illness prevents someone; for these days are the tithe of the year, which we are commanded to offer to the Lord.” Saint Ambrose likewise says: “He keeps Lent who by fasting and watching ascends to Easter. For just as at the remaining time of the year fasting is a reward, so in Lent not to fast is a sin. Those fasts are voluntary, but these are necessary; those come from choice, these from law. To those we are invited; to these we are compelled. And therefore whoever passes beyond the appointed number by eating on one day is accused not as a violator of one day, but is charged as a transgressor of the whole of Lent.”

In these sacred days all desires of the flesh must be restrained; the body must be chastised through abstinence, so that if perhaps at other times we have lived less temperately, we may in some way make amends for it by this Lenten fast. Therefore, dearest brothers, let us follow the admonitions of our most holy father Benedict, and with as much diligence as we can let us exercise ourselves in holy works, withholding something each day from our body, for the love of God, in food and drink, so that we may prove ourselves true servants of God.

Then our holy founder adds, saying: “Yet this very thing which each one offers he should suggest to his abbot, and it should be done with his prayer and consent, because what is done without the permission of the spiritual father will be reckoned to presumption and vainglory, not to reward. Therefore all things must be done with the abbot’s consent.”

The words of our holy lawgiver are clear, brothers, so that no one can have recourse to the veil of ignorance. For if all things must be done with the abbot’s consent, then without his permission absolutely nothing is to be done. Indeed, the more some good work is adorned by many virtues, the more it must not be doubted that it is of greater merit before God. Therefore, when a monk, by the leave and blessing of his abbot, withholds from his body some food or drink for the love of God, he will receive from the Lord not only the promised reward of eternal fullness for that abstinence itself, but also the kingdom for humility, and for the merit of holy obedience he will obtain without end the fellowship of all the saints in heaven.

For the monk who, once professed, has submitted his head to monastic institutions has resigned his will to Christ in the hands of the abbot; and if afterwards he again usurps it for his own judgment, he has now shamefully [unclear] Christ.

denied. For what else is a monk who usurps his own will, if not an unjust possessor of another’s property? Let the monk, therefore, be always humbly subject to his abbot in all things for the love of Christ; let him presume to do nothing at all against his command, and let him omit nothing, or neglect nothing, that has been enjoined upon him by him. Let him take the greatest care lest by restless conduct he either grieve or disturb his pastor; let him not murmur against him, nor disparage him, nor say any evil whatever against him. Rather, let him revere him with the sincere affection of charity as the vicar of Christ, and not grieve his spirit by troublesome or disorderly words or deeds. Let him also assist him, as far as he can, in his labors, and intercede for him continually before God with prayers. Monks sin greatly against God when they are not afraid to grieve their abbot by their troublesome disparagements and corrupt ways.

Therefore, whatever monk desires to be good, whatever monk truly wishes to be devout in the Lord, let him always and everywhere venerate his abbot with pure love as the vicar of Jesus Christ in the monastery; let him humbly obey his commands in all things, and in no way depart from his direction.

The abbot, for his part, should strive to show himself in all things a worthy shepherd to his monks, one who feeds the sheep of Christ entrusted to him both by word and by example, in all gentleness of charity. Let him not trouble the brothers without just and reasonable necessity. Let him not be a despiser of the holy community. Let him recognize himself as steward of the monastery’s goods, not lord. Let him not be a mocker of his subjects, not turbulent, not troublesome, not a tyrant, but their sincere lover: gentle in speech, mild and upright in conduct, holy in his way of life, clean in conscience, always devout in mind toward God.

Let him at all times bear solicitous care for the souls entrusted to him, and neglect nothing that seems able to conduce to their salvation. Let him not on that account exalt himself on high because he has been set as ruler of others, but let him remember that he must fear so much the more, as he is most certainly bound to render an account for all in the dread judgment of God. Let him correct the proud, rebellious, and contumacious as a lord; but let him kindly cherish the humble, obedient, and tractable as a most gentle father, and wisely distribute to each his due without respect of persons. Let him always consider himself the mother and nurse of the monks; and therefore he ought not to embitter with troublesome words and harsh invectives those whom he can bring back to better things by gentleness.

Let him always bear solicitous care for the sick, and make provision for all in such a way that they have no just cause for murmuring. In his own weaknesses let him learn how he ought to have compassion on his subjects. For he cannot be a good shepherd of souls who disdains from the heart to suffer with the needs of his sickly subjects. But he can become a good abbot among monks who knows how to adapt himself to the persons of the weak, so that whenever a brother asks something of him, [he considers] the condition of the person...

On the Lenten fast of monks.

Taking upon himself in his own heart the position of the petitioner, let him say: “What would I wish to be done for me in this matter, according to the right judgment of reason, if I were in the position of the petitioner?” Indeed, if the abbot imagines himself a subject, he will not send anyone away from him saddened.

We have already said, brothers, what sort of men you ought to be toward us for the love of God, so that, being good monks, you may truly please the Lord Jesus. Nevertheless you have heard what kind of shepherd I ought to show myself to you; whether I do so or not, you yourselves will judge better than I. For we shall fast in vain, and shall find no fruit of Lenten observance, unless we all remain in true brotherly charity, with purity of heart, in the love of God.

What does it profit eternal salvation to afflict the body by abstinence and fasting, and not to be of one accord before God in the true charity of ecclesiastical unity? Or what good will it do to abstain from richer foods and defile the conscience with evil works or thoughts? For, if the fasts we have begun are to be pleasing to God, they must not only be alien and far removed from vices and sins, but also adorned with the fullness of all virtues.

For holy Ambrose says: “What does it profit to fast with the belly and to indulge in hunting? to abstain from foods and to wander in sins? Do you think, brothers, that he fasts who at first dawn does not keep vigil in the church, does not seek out the holy places of the blessed martyrs, but rises in the morning, gathers his servants, sets out nets, brings out dogs, searches through groves and woods, and, I say, drags his servants along with him, who perhaps are more eager to hasten to church? To his own pleasures he adds the sins of others, not knowing that he will be guilty both of his own fault and of the ruin of his servants.”

And Saint Leo the Pope says: “The whole substance of our fast does not stand in abstinence from food alone. For food is not fruitfully withdrawn from the body unless the mind is called back from every iniquity.”

The blessed Jerome also says: “What does it profit for the body to be made thin by abstinence, if the soul swells with pride? What virtue is there in not drinking wine, and being drunk with anger, hatred, and the other poisonous cups of the soul?”

Therefore let none of you promise himself holiness from abstinence from foods alone, since whatever is required for true repentance is judged necessary also for fasting. For fasts profit unto salvation for those who are contrite for their sins in a true purpose of amendment, who fervently devote themselves to good and holy works. Therefore those who fast from food and drink must also abstain from all vices, so that the mind, adorned with the beauty of virtues, may sweetly burn in the love of Christ and by no means grow lukewarm in the progress of inward conduct.

For abstinence is no virtue if it has not been adorned with works of charity. Therefore hear my counsel, O monk, if you wish to make your fast fruitful before God: first cleanse your conscience from every stain of sin, so that no desire for evil may remain in you, so that your mind may become fervent in the exercise of divine love and be laudably adorned with all virtues.

By the remedy of contrition and confession wash away your past sins, and by persevering in prayers with tears strengthen your mind, with God’s help, against all temptations. Toward God, as much as you can, be fervent in the exercise of love; toward yourself, be well at peace in a pure conscience; toward your brother, be rightly ordered in true charity. Always be foremost in humility, firm in constancy and obedience, shining in chastity of mind and body, gentle in meekness, a monk in deed, and continually kindled with desire for perfection. If you commend your abstinence by this kind of cleanness and purity, you will fast rightly.

Diligently exercise your mind in meditation on the Passion of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, so that no day may pass on which, with thanksgiving, you do not at least once run through his life and death in meditation with tears. For crude and exceedingly undevout, not to say ungrateful, is the Christian who is so immersed in temporal affairs, or so occupied with the pleasures of the flesh, that he does not daily, at least once, remember with thanksgiving the most bitter Passion of his Redeemer. But the monk who forgets the benefits of our Lord Jesus Christ, who does not once each day recall his Passion with thanksgiving, who does not every day meditate on the evangelical law of the Lord, is rightly judged the most ungrateful of all men.

For nothing is more powerful than that prayer which is offered to God the Father in union with, and in the power of, the Lord’s Passion. Most justly is that spirit to be condemned which, redeemed by the most precious blood of Christ, is led astray by the pleasures of its flesh so as not to remember such great benefits of God toward it. For there was no cause for the Son of God to become man except that he willed to justify us sinners: born in the world for us, suffering in the world for us, and cruelly dying on the wood for our crimes. He, the just one, came into the world to justify us who were sinners; the merciful one came to the impious, so that we might learn mercy, humility, and patience from him. The physician came to the sick, life to the dead, compassion to the despairing; it was not our merits that drew him down from heaven into the world, but our sins.

It is fitting, therefore, my brothers, that with all devotion we celebrate this Lenten fast dedicated to his most sacred Passion, since he first deigned to do such great things for our salvation and, in order to rescue us from the destruction of death, did not hesitate to give himself over to death for us. Let us do, for love of Christ, whatever good we can; let us endure, in view of his Passion and death, every adversity that befalls us in this world, since the Lord Jesus, who out of charity willed to suffer for us, has truly shown himself most worthy that we should love him with all our heart. For if, brother, you acknowledge yourself a sinner, Christ saved you by his death. Contemplate him hanging on the Cross as you ought, and you will be healed from every bite of sin. For nothing is found in this world more effective for healing the wounds of conscience, nothing more

[unclear] for cleansing the sight of a frightened mind than diligent meditation on Christ’s wounds. For the most precious blood of the Lord, poured out, has been made a sufficient medicine for sin. Hence the holy bishop Augustine says: “Brothers, that we, wounded by sin, may be healed, let us look upon Christ crucified. For just as those who looked upon the bronze serpent in the desert did not perish from the bites of serpents, so those who with faith and devotion look upon the death of Jesus Christ are healed from the bites of sins.”

But if you trust that you have been justified from sin, then all the more, and more fervently, must you look upon Christ hanging on the cross, without the merit of whose passion no one lives righteous on earth. For outside faith in Christ there is no righteousness; and however religiously a man may live, if he does not believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, he will in no way attain eternal salvation, but the wrath of God remains upon him, and he will necessarily perish forever. Christ’s death opened the gate of salvation, through which no one else can enter except one who faithfully believes in Christ. For this reason Christ humbly submitted himself to the condemnation of death, that he might free believers from the yoke of perpetual damnation.

O infinite charity, O mercy without measure, who among those who believe in you, eternal Majesty, would not marvel at such astounding benefits granted to us? For your Passion, Lord Jesus, is the price of our salvation, the final refuge of sinners, the singular remedy of infirm minds, the fountain, origin, and end of all good things. Therefore now, dearest brothers, let us recall and diligently bring back to memory the bitterness of the Lord’s Passion, so that, since we necessarily recognize ourselves to be sinners, we may at last be justified through the merit of that same Savior of ours.

For meditation on the Lord’s Passion surpasses all exercises of this world, if it is continued for a long time with the fervor of inward devotion. The mind of that monk which, kindled by zeal for divine love, has been accustomed daily, with tears, to keep the memory of the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ for at least a short hour, does not easily lie open to the suggestions of demons. For the heart which the love of Jesus possesses always remains inaccessible and closed to all evil thoughts.

Happy indeed is that monk, and never to be named except with honor, who meditates day and night with loving zeal on the teaching and Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ; who never forgets his Savior; who, whether he eats or drinks or does anything else, always beholds with the eyes of the mind the Lord Jesus hanging on the cross. No destructive thoughts move about in his heart; no evil or idle word proceeds from his mouth; he thinks of nothing but Jesus crucified for us; and whatever he says sounds of Jesus or of righteousness. As soon as he sees a painted image of Jesus crucified, he dissolves into tears, and, made as it were senseless by the exceeding desire of his mind, he is filled with sweetest bitterness. He cannot admit any consolations of the present life, because, when his Lord in heaven

Homily XVI.

When he thinks of dwelling there, he weeps over his exile prolonged on earth. He loves nothing in this world except Jesus; he seeks nothing other than him crucified. If riches are present, he utterly refuses to set his heart on them; but if they are lacking, he does not seek to find them. For since he knows himself to be a disciple of the poor Jesus, he understands very well that the riches of this world are a great obstacle to Christian perfection. Having scant food and a poor covering for his body, he is content with his Lord, who became poor for us and foretold that those who hunger for righteousness are blessed.

Happy, I say, is that monk who can truly say with the holy martyr of Christ, Theophorus: “My love is crucified, and therefore my heart receives no consolation of this world.” And that saying of the Christ-loving Paul: “The world is crucified to me, and I to the world.”

Now therefore, my dearest brothers, hear my counsel, and sanctify the fast you have begun by continual remembrance of the Lord’s Passion. For I tell you that, among all the exercises of monks, none can be holier, none more acceptable to God, none more wholesome for you, than that which is practiced in meditation on the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ with daily diligence and with the compunction of inward love. For this exercise of the saving Passion suddenly makes a penitent out of a sinner, a devout man by wondrous compunction out of one who is lukewarm and dry, and a just man out of an impious one. It covers a multitude of sins; it gives strength to the spirit against demons; it sets an end to all vices; and it gives strong increase to the holy virtues of the soul.

Devout and continual remembrance of the Lord’s Passion purifies the conscience of the one who meditates, enlightens the understanding in every knowledge of truth, and sweetly inflames the affection in the love of God. Devout meditation on Christ’s Passion makes one despise all the delights of this world and fear nothing, however hard or contrary. It destroys lust; subdues luxury of both mind and body; drives away envy; restrains gluttony; calms avarice; sets sloth aflame; softens anger; and roots out pride. Moreover, no passion for any carnal thing wearies the mind of the man whom the Passion of Christ truly occupies.

O how sweetly he burns whom the memory of Jesus’ Passion gently inflames; and how happily that mind grows fervent which embraces continual meditation on Christ’s death. O good Jesus, my crucified love, who are the salvation and savior of faithful souls, grant us to keep continual remembrance of your Passion; grant your servants always to commend the fasts they have begun with good works, because then our abstinence will be most pleasing to your uncircumscribable majesty, when it has been adorned by meditation on your precious blood; you who live and reign with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever.

On the sleep and waking of monks.

On the sleep and waking of monks. Homily XVII.

The monk who always thinks he will die permits no idle time to pass. For Scripture says: “Remember your last things, and you will not sin forever.” On the contrary, concerning the forgetful and the sluggish it is written: “They are a nation without counsel and without prudence. Would that they were wise and understood, and would foresee their last things.” The memory of death brings watchfulness into the soul and extinguishes every disordered thought of the mind. Whoever rightly fears death is never sluggish in good work.

For the wise man says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it earnestly, because neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge will be among the dead, where you are hastening.” For the monk who is a true worshiper of God spends no moment of time uselessly, but by night and by day, in the exercise of good work, he continually practices watchfulness of mind with the greatest devotion; and, though sleeping in body, in his soul he says constantly to God’s messengers: “I sleep, and my heart keeps watch.” Sleep is the image of death and the binding of the bodily senses; but one who is a true lover of Christ keeps watch in mind even while sleeping in body, and, praying without ceasing, cries to the Lord with the affection of charity: “Before you is all my desire; dreaming of you, I think of you, Jesus crucified, my love.”

I blush, my brothers, and am deeply ashamed to bring forward a discourse on the watchfulness of monks, because when I recall to mind the practice of keeping vigil among the holy Fathers who went before us, I recognize with sorrow how far our weakness stands from their perfection. They, kindled with divine love, often passed whole nights without sleep in the praises of God; but to us even a span of eight hours for sleeping sometimes scarcely seems enough, of which we do not cease complaining that the five before Matins and the three afterward are too short.

For the true abstinence of monks consists not only in sparing use of food and drink, but also in the continuation of vigils for the praise of God, because that mortification of the flesh is foolish in which the belly is restrained from foods and the whole body is fattened through sleepiness. For the body is refreshed for its subsistence not only by food and drink, but is also restored by the quiet of sleep. What sort of fasting by monks is it to be sparing by abstaining from foods and drinks, and to indulge in sleep to satiety? It makes little difference whether you refresh the body with food or with sleep, since in both satiety is a vice.

Therefore the ancient men and the first leaders of the monks, observing temperance in sleeping no less than in eating and drinking, remained most continent in both. Some of them, standing on their feet, and others lying on the bare ground, granted nature only the scantiest sleep. We know that one of these, not least in the merit of holiness, said: “One hour is enough for a monk to sleep,”

Homily XVII.

if he is a fighter and an adversary of vices. For sleep nourishes sensuality no less than food and drink. A certain other of the saints wished two or three hours to suffice a monk for sleeping, so that he might commend sparingness in food also by moderation in rest. But the more recent reformers of our order, who under the name of the Bursfeld Union handed down to us throughout Germany a manner of living according to the purity of the Rule, considering the weakness of the human condition, arranged the measure of vigils very moderately. For they mercifully allowed the monks in community a space of five hours before the nocturnal praises, and likewise added two, or two and a half, after matins for sleep. Whoever does not find this time, namely seven hours, sufficient for rest shows himself to be an excessively sluggish and slothful monk. Hence we are admonished to keep watch not only in mind but also in body, because he who disdains to keep bodily vigil in the service of God can scarcely preserve his heart in true purity.

Let us therefore keep watch, most beloved brothers, especially in these holy days of Lent, in which we have declared war on vices and are strongly prepared to conquer and overcome the ancient enemy, the devil. For you hear the holy Prince of the Apostles admonishing us in these words: “Brothers, be sober and keep watch.” Why did he warn us of this? “Because,” he says, “your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in faith.” And so, my brothers, let us keep watch as long as we are set in battle, lest at some time, weighed down by sleepiness or idleness, we be overcome by the adversary of our salvation. For as long as we live in the flesh, we must fight bravely against the enemy by vigilance and by chastising our body.

Do not let the labor of the struggle frighten you; for although our adversary is troublesome, yet he is so weak and feeble that he can overcome no one except one who is willing, and one who has utterly cast aside all guard over himself. But the Lord Jesus Christ, our helper and protector, is strong: he grants strength to those who fight eagerly, and will bestow on the victors an unfading crown with all his saints in heaven. As dust is scattered by the wind, so our adversary the devil, confounded and terrified by the voice of those singing psalms with humble devotion, is driven to flight.

Therefore let none of you, most beloved brothers, act negligently; let no one grow dull at the time of prayer through sluggishness of mind and sleepiness; let no one fear the devil’s contest with disordered dread. Stand manfully for the salvation of your souls, fighting continually against a weak adversary; and regard your own flesh with no less suspicion than the demons. For you know, as not only Scripture bears witness but long experience also teaches, that the flesh lusts against the spirit; and therefore the monk who is not harmed by the wantonness of his own flesh is rarely overcome by demons in the struggle. Walk, then, in the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh. He who keeps watch,

and is a strong fighter should stir up a weaker brother who is sluggish in devotion, and by words as well as by examples should, as far as he can, restore him to the holy fervor of the spirit. Let the one among you who is spiritual not despise his disorderly brother, but rather bring him back, by humble admonition, to the pursuit of piety. For Scripture says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.”

Indeed, if, agreeing together in brotherly love, you have always been of one mind with one another through faith in Jesus Christ, without doubt you will easily overcome your adversary the devil. For where the true charity of Christ makes the monks dwelling in a monastery of one mind, there God is worshiped in all holiness; there the invisible presence of the holy angels is believed to be, through whom the rashness of evil spirits is restrained. In such a congregation of holy men God dwells, whom the army of the heavenly kingdom praises together with the voices of the monks singing psalms. A multitude of monks burning in the love of God is a paradise of heavenly delights. A congregation of monks who are of the same mind in the Lord is a city adorned with a multitude of towers.

Watch, my brothers, I beg you, watch in holy prayers, and shake off drowsiness and sluggishness of mind especially at that time when you stand in church before the Lord to sing psalms. For if, standing before God in psalmody, you are fervent in prayer, you will without doubt feel his grace present with you. For he is very far removed from the purpose of a monk who, while praying, thinks of something else, and lets his mind be stirred not by divine things but by fleeting matters or occupations.

For you know what our holy founder Benedict says in the Rule: “If we wish to suggest anything to powerful men,” he says, “we do not presume to do so except with humility and reverence; how much more must we supplicate the Lord God of all things with all humility and devotion of purity? And let us know that we are heard not in much speaking, but in purity of heart and compunction of tears.” Since, then, when we sing psalms we believe that God is present everywhere, great reverence is needed in prayer, so that our mind may agree in all things with our voice.

Let us therefore consider, brothers, whom we attend upon, and to whom, in the sight of the angels, we recite the psalms in prayer. For the monk who, at the time of prayer, occupies his heart with vain thoughts is like a man who, standing before a king or emperor and speaking with him about matters very necessary for the safety of his body, when called by his servant leaves the king and turns himself to the servant’s vain and useless conversations. Truly, whoever did this would be judged foolish by all, and would rightly seem deserving of the severest punishments. But what does the monk deserve who, standing before the supreme King of all things and speaking with him about the salvation of his soul, suddenly turns his inner eyes to useless occupations and, neglecting the presence of the eternal King, admits vain or even harmful thoughts into his mind?

Homily XVII.

If one who mocks and despises an earthly king is punished by beheading, what does one deserve who despises the heavenly emperor? Therefore I warn you, brothers, and with all the sincerity I can I beg you, to purify your hearts, especially in the time of prayer, from the stain of wicked thought, so that you may turn over in your mind only what you chant with your mouth. As the angels always stand before God with fear and the greatest reverence, chanting an everlasting hymn of praise, so let us also take care, my brothers, to stand before him with a pure heart, a clean conscience, and most fervent devotion, so that we may chant his praises much more in spirit than in body.

Let us therefore separate our minds from all troublesome earthly affairs; let us cleanse our consciences from all enticements of the flesh; let us put on the fervor of the Holy Spirit, and drive far from us all laziness and cowardice. For just as a heavy burden weighs down the back of a slothful man, so drowsiness during psalmody is accustomed to oppress the minds of monks. Nothing harms monks more than acedia, or sloth, which little by little weakens all the powers of the mind and extinguishes the whole fervor of the spirit. For as soon as a monk begins to fall away from the fervor of holy devotion, countless evil thoughts creep into his mind; and he is now able to repel them so much the less, the farther he is shown to have withdrawn from his former fervor.

From this arises drowsiness in the performance of the divine offices; the mind is weighed down excessively by sadness and melancholy, and the monk, growing lukewarm in spirit, strives with all his effort to relieve it not by spiritual consolations, but by earthly and carnal little comforts. And when he goes on longer in this estrangement of mind, he is hardened, as though insensible, against the exercise of compunction; and the more he pants after the consolations of the flesh, the farther he wanders from the inward fervor of the spirit. For what makes you drowsy during psalmody except acedia? For the mind that falls into sluggishness soon makes the body doze.

But again I warn you, brothers, as I have been accustomed to do very often: above all, flee laziness and drowsiness in the time of prayer, because just as drunkenness brings forgetfulness upon the soul, so too drowsiness makes the mind senseless and foolish before God. Beware this vice of drowsiness, O you young men, with which we sorrow to see some of the older men already infected by long habit; for in choir dozing is familiar to them, and compunction of mind toward God is very rare. Beware, I say, this evil habit of sleeping, which, once it has led a monk away captive, rarely lets him go free. Therefore at the very beginning of conversion, young men especially must fight against this most destructive enemy of religion, as someone said in verse:

Resist at the beginnings: medicine is prepared too late, When evils have grown strong through long delays. But make haste, and do not put yourself off to the coming hours; He who is not ready today will be less ready tomorrow.

On the sleep and wakefulness of monks.

For it is difficult to cure an illness that is long and has become inveterate through length of time. Let us consider with how great diligence and attentiveness servants stand before earthly kings and princes, so that we may not be ignorant of how it befits us to stand in prayer before God, who alone is King of all and Lord of the universe. The eyes of all look to the Lord, and all together and each one singly depend most carefully upon his nod, lest, when he commands, anything escape those who attend him through negligence. From this, therefore, let us consider with how great purity we ought to stand before the Lord God, day and night, in the assembly of prayer, from whom we desire to obtain the kingdom of eternal blessedness.

Not voice, not shouting, but an intention fervent in the love of God merits being heard. Therefore flee drowsiness and sluggishness of mind as a deadly poison, because sleep and the [unclear] of the eyes are the source of all vices. But the watchful eye is the servant of inward devotion, and the monk who truly loves Jesus Christ guards himself from every excess. He who is watchful sharpens his mind with understanding; but the monk who sleeps much shamefully blinds his own soul. A monk watchful in prayer and fasting is formidable to the devil; but one who is sated with food and sleep is not permitted to rest by the spirit of fornication.

For a vigil dedicated to prayers breaks the heat of lust, powerfully extinguishes the fire of desire, purifies the inward parts of the heart, enlightens the mind, and inflames the affection toward love of heavenly things. Vigil is the parent, nurse, and guardian of good thoughts, the sure victory over the temptations of the ancient enemy, the flight of phantasms, the death of vices, the life and fountain of all virtues. But much sleep is the companion and fosterer of lust, the robber of a man’s life, the image of death, the bringer of forgetfulness, the spouse of sloth. Immoderate sleep corrupts the stomach, harms the brain, and weakens both body and soul. A monk often given over to sleep despises wisdom, prostitutes chastity, neglects the salvation of his soul, loses precious time, kills the mind, and nourishes vices.

Therefore, whoever among you, most beloved brothers, desires to reach the rest of heavenly blessedness, let him vigorously drive away from himself all sluggishness and cowardice of mind. Let him learn first of all to conquer himself, so that thereafter he may be able to overcome the devil, the enemy of his salvation. For truly, unless you first root out the evil that is in you, when will you overcome that which comes from outside? Learn to rule your passions, and with the Lord’s help you will easily overcome everything that happens outwardly. Cleanse your mind from every disordered desire, so that in truth you may love Jesus alone above all things, with whom you hope to rejoice forever.

But no one will reign with Christ in heaven who does not imitate him on earth by holy conduct, as holy Scripture says: “He who says that he remains in Christ ought himself also to walk just as he walked.” For the Lord Jesus, who by his death freed us from the destruction of eternal damnation, himself willingly became mediator between God and men; he himself is the way by which the path of life must be continued for us; he himself is the powerful guide of the journey; he himself is the pattern and rule of saving conduct for Christians. No one comes to God the Father except through Christ; no one will see the Father except through the Son.

Therefore, if you wish to come to salvation, you must pass through the Savior. For he himself said in the holy Gospel: “No one comes to the Father except through me.” And also: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will find the pasture of eternal life.” And again: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” By this way, living with pious and holy conduct, I beg you, my brothers, always walk; love this truth fervently with a pure heart; hasten ardently toward this life, which alone is lasting.

Let the teaching of Christ never depart from your hearts, but remain in memory at all times, since he refuses to become a true imitator of him who has not been exercised day and night in meditation on his words. Therefore, always watchful in prayers, live with such purity of mind that at the hour of death you may deserve to hear with joy our Lord Jesus Christ calling you, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God almighty, one, forever and ever. Amen.

Among all professors of the Christian faith today, there is no class of men to whom the virtue of patience seems more necessary than to the company of monks. For, as the charity of many grows cold in these our days, to use Paul’s expression, we have become a spectacle to mortals, so that wherever a monk comes among worldly people, he is marked out to be mocked and derided by the fingers of almost all who see him.

You know why I have said this; you are not unaware of what recently happened in the town of Bingen. A drunken crowd of youths and boys accosted a certain monk passing along the public road, and, as though he, by traveling, had caused the rain, threw him into the mud; and by treating the man outrageously, it made him a pitiable spectacle of its own shamelessness. No one was there to restrain the insolent men. Yet the monk’s patience overcame their frenzy, and, full of the love of Christ, when he was being badly handled, he answered nothing else but “Thanks be to God.”

Therefore, the more he showed himself tranquil in mind and spirit, the more those worthless men dragged him into the fountain, thinking that he was heated with wine, when the love of Christ had made him glad and joyful. He left to all monks a great lesson in patience: although he could have avenged himself when wronged, he would not.

Would that we, my brothers, were as patient for the love of God and for our sins in the smallest things as that good man was in the greatest. There are some among you, I say it unwillingly, too insolent and impatient, who are moved to anger by a word, even one that is not insulting; and while they are justly corrected for their negligences, they murmur unjustly, adding sin to sin through impatience. But to what end patience...

I set before them the example of the man already mentioned, who do not heed Jesus Christ, the most patient of all men. For indeed, whoever does not embrace patience and humility after the example of the King of heaven will not be recalled to gentleness by the imitation of any man. For the Son of God is the highest and supreme model of patience and humility; whoever is not bent toward endurance by the remembrance of his passion is rightly judged hardened and a companion of demons.

No good Christian doubts that the words of our Lord Jesus Christ are true. Now Christ says in the holy Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.” If the meek are to be called blessed, what prevents the rancorous, the wrathful, and the unmeek from being called accursed? Certainly nothing. And if, as our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ himself bears witness, we possess our souls in patience, there is no doubt that through impatience we lose them.

It is therefore especially fitting that monks be meek, gentle, and patient, since they have solemnly devoted themselves to the imitation of Christ and the apostles. But Christ, the meekest of all, commands his disciples and imitators in the Gospel, saying: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls.”

Hence the holy bishop Augustine says: If you wish to reign with Christ in heaven, first learn from him to be meek, patient, humble, and gentle, since unless you have lived in this world in imitation of his life, you will by no means reign with him forever.

Saint Ambrose also says: When I have laid aside every sin, stripped off every malice, and, content with simplicity, have been poor in evils, it remains that I temper my conduct. For what does it profit me to be free of crimes, unless I am meek and gentle? But he is meek who yields to wickedness and does not resist in evil, but overcomes evil with good.

And, as Chrysostom bears witness, he is gentle who, when provoked by injuries, neither thinks of doing evil nor does it.

Cassiodorus, moreover, says: We call the gentle “accustomed to the hand,” that is, patient and meek, those who bear the wrongs of others and do not presume to burden anyone. Of them it is said in the psalm: “My soul shall be praised in the Lord; let the gentle hear and rejoice.” He did not say, “let those skilled in the law rejoice,” nor “those who fast,” nor “those who sing psalms,” but “let the gentle rejoice,” those who, together with charity, have especially been accustomed to possess temperance in all things.

But those are truly meek, gentle, and patient who harm no one, wrong no one, offend no one at all, but, standing firm in their simple humility, always bear with evenness of mind all injuries, insults, and mockeries for the love of Christ, and are moved by no grief of heart against those who harm them, just as we have already said that monk was, whom the raging boys at Bingen treated with great insult.

It is easy, however, to be meek, patient, and gentle so long as nothing is said or done except according to the will and judgment of the one who is patient. But it will become clear how far he is from true gentleness

[unclear], if even a slight occasion arises. Great is the virtue if you do not harm the one by whom you were harmed; great is the courage of soul if, for the love of God, you forgive the one inflicting injury; great is the glory if you observe Christ’s command and pour out prayers for those who wrong you. No one has known the strength of his own soul whom no notable insult has yet burned. Let no one boast that he is meek or patient who has not been sated with reproaches. There is no patience without adversity, nor meekness without insult, because if you wish to keep the proper bounds of endurance, an insult-inflicter must first be present.

“If I had lived,” says the lazy and fleshly monk, “in the days of the martyrs, I would have feared to undergo no kind of torment for the love of Christ; I would willingly have exposed my body to tortures, so that I might have gained the crown of martyrdom.” Great rashness of folly. You have never been able patiently to endure a word for the love of God, and you promise the constancy of the holy martyrs? You fear a slight correction, you who promise that you will give your body for Christ. If martyrdom delights you, hear what the most blessed Pope Gregory says: “If, with Christ helping us, we strive to preserve the virtue of patience, then we live in the peace of the Church and hold the palm of martyrdom. For we can be martyrs without sword and flame, if we truly preserve patience in the soul. To die at the hands of a persecutor is martyrdom in open deed; but to bear insults and love one who hates you is martyrdom in hidden thought.”

True patience is to endure another’s evils with equanimity, and not to be gnawed by any grief against the one who has inflicted the evil. What will you say now, O lazy monk, who, unable to endure the very light martyrdom of words, boast so insolently of constancy in shedding blood? Learn, miserable man, to have patience in small things, and consider that, as Scripture says, “He who is unfaithful in little, who will trust him with what is greater?”

You murmur at everything done in the monastery; when rebuked, however gently, for your grave faults and negligences, you bear it most impatiently. No one in the monastery walks rightly in your eyes; no one besides you, in your estimation, lives religiously. You alone, as it seems to you, are holy in the monastery; you, the most learned of all, allow no one to know what you alone do not know. You judge yourself worthy of all honors above everyone, because you not only lack patience, but possess neither true humility nor obedience.

This is not the road by which one goes to the kingdom of heaven, when a monk is proud in the school of humility and a Christian lives in conduct contrary to Christ. But the monk, the solemnly sworn servant of Jesus Christ, so that he may imitate his Lord, must not be proud, but humble; obedient, not rebellious; gentle, not cruel; not insolent, but meek. But a monk who is proud, wrathful, contentious, and a lover of his own will, such as, alas, those placed in charge of temporal affairs often are, whom among us according to the Rule we call cellarers, whose arrogance to many

made a path to destruction. Grief compels me to speak, shame restrains me, although you all know the misfortune by which the devil lately confounded us in our brother. Who was higher than he in our whole congregation? Who went about filled with greater insolence? Because he seemed to have greater experience than we in temporal affairs, he therefore judged himself superior to all. The Almighty permitted him to fall, so that the man who, through self-regard, refused to acknowledge his own weakness might at last, confounded and not without the scandal of many, understand that God is the adversary of the proud. I grieve deeply, more than can be said, and the fault of the one who fell seems heavier to me because, when he falls, we are all confounded. May God grant him true repentance, so that those who had been scandalized by his fall may be built up by his satisfaction before God and men.

Pride has always been destructive to monks, and once it has invaded a man’s mind, it plunges him into the pit of every vice. Beware pride, my brothers, for it is the beginning of every sin; it is pride which, through the devil’s envy, brings death into the whole world. Pride is the death of all virtues, and the fountain and source of all vices. But humility, the nurse of the virtues, most befits monks, because it makes them gentle and meek. For every proud man is impatient, and every arrogant man is an enemy of meekness. He who is humble of heart has patience in adversity for the love of God; and he who remains calm in spirit under insults deserves a double crown. A patient man in adversity is near to God; but one who is proud and harsh gladdens his enemies. For Scripture says: “A patient man is better than a strong man, and he who rules his own spirit than a conqueror of cities.” The holy bishop Augustine also says: “A just and devout man must be ready to endure patiently the malice of those whom he wishes to become good, so that the number of the good may rather increase, and no one by equal malice add himself to the number of the wicked.”

Patience is greatly necessary for us, brothers, so that, doing the will of God, we may receive the holy promise in Christ. Each day adversities are present to us by which we may be exercised; therefore, just as a cause for endurance is never lacking, so, I pray, may necessary patience always be present. We are oppressed by want and poverty in necessary things; we are burdened by the commerce of the flesh’s weakness; besides this the world tempts us, to allure us, and the devil tempts us, to seduce us. Among so many adversaries of our salvation it is necessary, brothers, that we keep watch in all patience and humility, because in this pilgrimage, as long as we live, we are placed, so to speak, in the midst of evils. Our poverty ought to be enough for us, because it does not belong to monastic religion to be exalted in temporal things, but rather to be brought low, so that poor monks, imitating Christ, who was made poor for us, may deserve to glory with him forever in heaven. What if we see certain wicked men and sinners in the world abounding in riches? If good and just men are rich in this world, it is granted through [unclear] to their weakness, not to their strength.

God’s providence is consulted, so that by benefits they may be stirred toward better things. “I was young,” says the prophet, “and now am old, and I have not seen the just man forsaken, nor his seed begging bread.” “Cast,” he says, “your thought upon the Lord, and he will nourish you; he will not allow the just man to waver forever.”

The Lord Jesus knows what is fitting for the salvation of each one of his little servants, and therefore he distributes the gifts of the present life unequally, according to the capacity of each individual. For not everything is suitable for everyone; therefore among the just in this world some are poor in temporal goods, while others are wealthy. Concerning the poor the Lord Jesus says in the holy Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” And through the prophet he speaks, saying: “Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty.”

For it is not conducive to eternal salvation for everyone to possess the riches of this world; rather, it is expedient for some to be poor and for others to be wealthy, according as the Lord of all has provided what is more useful for each. Concerning just and good rich men Solomon says in the book of Proverbs: “The blessing of the Lord makes men rich, and affliction will not be joined to it.” But if evil and reprobate rich men have abundance in this age, good men ought not be moved to indignation, but should rather fear him who leaves no good unrewarded and no evil unpunished.

For the evil, whom because of their iniquity he cannot reward in heaven, he rewards in this life for their good deeds; and for the good, whom he nourishes here in poverty, he preserves eternal rewards in heaven for the merit of their justice. Yet just as not all the poor in this world are just and good, so not all who are rich in temporal things in this life are evil. The reward of the evil on earth is rightly to be borne without indignation, since not the love of God but his justice willed it to be present.

Therefore, just as the evil have nothing in heaven, so you, who have professed monastic poverty, ought to have nothing on earth; but in hope of that good toward which you are hastening, you ought to bear most patiently whatever adversity befalls you on the way.
