Let us consider those who have fallen into this most foul pit and afterward, by the authority of their superiors, have been compelled to do penance: how do they live among the brothers? They do not have the signs of true compunction, but pass an unquiet life in dryness of heart. No devotion of mind is seen in them, but everywhere they follow the accustomed ways of the flesh. How rarely is anyone converted to the sweetness of inward love who has once plunged into the pit of fornication. For unless, before he comes into this misery, he has been grounded in the fear of the Lord, once fallen he returns with the greatest difficulty to true compunction.

Therefore live soberly, dearest brothers, and always keep watch in holy prayers, because unless you walk most cautiously in all things, you will by no means be able to escape the snares of demons. Love abstinence; guard humility above all things. For no one can suppress the impulses of his flesh who has neglected to tame gluttony and pride.

The insolent demon of fornication is never better conquered than when true humility of heart is preserved in the fullness of all virtues. For just as almighty God, resisting the proud, gives grace to the humble, so the devil, fleeing the humble, hurls the proud down into fornication. Therefore anyone who is gluttonous, eating and drinking to satiety, and desires to conquer the spirit of fornication, is carrying oil to the fire. And anyone who strives to extinguish the impulses of lust by abstinence alone is like a man seen swimming with one hand in the midst of the waves. Let continual prayer to God be joined to abstinence, and he will sail securely in the ship of holy humility.

Let prayer always be in the monk’s mouth, and let the memory of the passion and death of the Lord Jesus never depart from his meditation. For nothing so strengthens the mind against the demon of fornication, and the soul, as devout meditation on the passion of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Therefore, as often as you feel a disordered movement of the flesh, as often as you perceive that the invisible enemy is present to do harm, at once flee to the Son of God hanging on the cross, and, with your knees bent to the ground, let such a prayer be formed to him:

O Jesus crucified, my love, through the pain of your wounds have mercy on me; through the shedding of your most holy blood help me in this struggle; and through the power of your most innocent death free me from every defilement of mind and body.

Nothing is more wholesome than this manner of prayer, in which the memory of Christ’s passion is honored and all petitions are strengthened in the power of the Savior. Nothing more weakens the snares of the ancient enemy, nothing more quickly enfeebles the forces of his malice, than if the devoted servant of Christ humbly perseveres in meditation on the most bitter passion of the Lord. Just as some thief flees before the face of the pursuing judge, so the devil swiftly vanishes from the sight of a monk meditating attentively on the passion and death of the Savior. The movement of wicked thought is quickly extinguished where the bitterness of Christ’s passion is recalled to mind. Just as snow melts when the sun grows warm, so the devil is put to flight by meditation on the Lord’s passion.

The greatest safeguard of chastity is always to invoke divine aid. And unless you run back to the Lord at once from the beginning of temptation, you will gradually feel the harm caused by delay. For if you allow delay amid pernicious thoughts, the demons soon introduce an imperceptible blindness of mind. For unless the mind has first been blinded, the will does not succumb to the demon. But the spirit of fornication first heavily darkens the mind; afterward, until it has hurled it down into sin, it fights against the blinded one. And after it has hurled the monk into the mire of unspeakable crime, lest he rise again to repentance, it sets itself in the way in two ways. For either it subtly tries to lessen the gravity of the sin, so that he may not fear a great punishment; or it brings back to the fallen man’s memory the strictness of judgment, so that he may fall into the pit of despair. By these snares the sinful soul is caught, and the longer it has lain in the deep...

Homily XXI.

of misery, the more hardened it becomes. Flee idleness, O cloistered ones, and shun gluttony and fullness of the belly with all your strength, because the monk who fills his belly with food and drink gives the demon of fornication material for doing harm. Take on true contrition of heart, and restrain the unlawful motions of the flesh through the tears of prayer. For no one is able rightly to conquer his body unless he has first taken up the goad of contrition. But he cannot attain the grace of holy contrition who has not perfectly despised and denied himself. Yet whoever has perfectly denied himself for the love of Christ, already overcoming the assault of the flesh, will more easily obtain the grace of contrition. For one who has been mortified in will desires nothing carnal, nothing shameful. But which of us, brother, is there who would dare to say that he has reached this grace of mortification? Which of us does not know himself to be weak? We run in the arena of spiritual warfare, and in daily struggle we fight against vices. We have received no assurance of peace, even if at times we have peace. The more familiar to us the weakness of the flesh is, the harder are the battles of chastity. Therefore we must be especially watchful, since we carry about with us a familiar enemy and endure an evil impulse as though it were domestic. Therefore, as long as we live in this mortality, let us always fear the corrupter of chastity. Let us beware of everything that stirs up lust, and as much as we can, let us flee sloth and idleness. For the strongest enemies of true chastity are fullness of bread and idleness; unless they are driven far away by abstinence and by the work of salutary exercise, they threaten chastity with imminent shipwreck. Guard your hearts with every care, my dearly beloved brothers, and always keep watch in mind against your adversary, who never sleeps. Arm yourselves with the breastplate of perfect faith in Jesus Christ, so that in deed and in belief you may be true Christians. Always be of one mind in brotherly charity, and without pretense be united in the true observance of regular discipline. Love fasting and continence; always pray without ceasing. Flee idleness as a deadly plague of the soul, and continually exercise yourselves in holy works. Love silence, and do not flee monastic solitude, if you desire to obtain true purity of mind and body. Keep continual guard over your eyes, ears, and speech, lest death enter the soul through the windows. Flee conversations with women, and avoid even the touch of holy women as a blazing fire. No one safely looks willingly at what, when desired, brings the sting of death. Always behold with the faithful eyes of the mind, through love, our Lord Jesus Christ dying for you on the cross; occupy yourselves each day for your salvation in his evangelical teaching; humbly give thanks for his passion and death alike. If with continued perseverance and in true simplicity of heart you do these things until death, we trust that you will be rewarded with the fellowship of the saints.

On the Fraternal Charity of Monks.

On the Fraternal Charity of Monks. Homily XXII.

We have heard, my dearest brothers, our Lord Jesus Christ commanding in the holy Gospel: “Whatever you wish that men should do to you, do likewise to them.” It is indeed a brief, but solid commendation of brotherly charity, without which no one can ascend to the love of God. For no one can love God who is proved not to love his fellow Christian. Hence the blessed apostle John says: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.” Therefore, if anyone says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar.

For this reason holy Paul, the lover of Christ, exhorts us, saying: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.” And Peter, the prince of the apostles, admonished us in this way: “Before all things,” he says, “have constant mutual charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins.”

How necessary brotherly charity is for salvation, Jesus Christ, the Lord of all, made clear when he said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the first and greatest commandment. The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets.” For whatever is commanded anywhere in the whole sequence of the Scriptures is without doubt referred to these two commandments.

Here we understand “neighbor” not as someone joined by kinship of blood, but as every human being joined by the fellowship of reason, and especially a Christian, whom each person is commanded to love as himself, since he is seen to await eternal salvation together with him.

But it especially befits you, brothers, to love one another in the true charity of Jesus Christ the Savior, since the monastic profession enjoins you to strive with all your strength toward the summit of perfection. For just as covetousness is the root of all evils, so charity is the root of all goods. First you must love God for his own sake, because he is the highest good, above all things with a pure heart; and then you must love your neighbor with sincere charity for the Lord’s sake.

These two precepts of charity have been joined together by Christ’s authority, so that neither can in any way be fulfilled without the other. For one who truly loves God cannot hate his neighbor. If he hates his neighbor, he does not truly love God. For the love of God brings forth love of neighbor, and through love of neighbor the love of God is nourished. If one of the two loves is lacking, the other does not grow strong. For one who does not perfectly love his neighbor shows himself empty of the love of God. Therefore we truly love God when we love our neighbor, that is, every Christian human being, more earnestly with sincere intention.

For brotherly charity is the bond of peace, which alone nourishes in the dwelling of

mercy, and preserves Christian unity among the brothers. Charity is the begetter of meekness and the noble mother of catholic piety. Brotherly charity is formidable to demons, since it makes victorious all whose courtyard of the heart it surrounds. Charity extinguishes the fire of lust and covers the whole multitude of sins. Charity makes a man most dear to God and makes him a companion of the holy angels. Charity preserves the Church in the unity of the saints; outside it no one obtains eternal salvation. Brotherly charity orders the conduct of cloistered men and causes God to dwell in the midst of monks. Charity does injury to no one, but ministers help to all through compassion. Charity drives out every vice, because it is the one nurse of all virtues. Charity keeps the reform of brotherhood in vigor among cloistered men and works great salvation for souls. Mutual charity strengthens obedience and makes brotherly correction fruitful. Charity nourishes true concord among the brothers, and preserves a sweet-smelling chastity of both minds and bodies. Charity makes monks of one mind in the house of God and praiseworthily harmonious in every good work. Mutual charity lightens the rigor of the order, and all things that seem hard and rough to carnal people it changes through habit into nature, as though they were very light. Charity is the most beautiful beauty of monks, adorned with all virtues. Charity utterly drives hatred and envy from the monasteries of God’s servants, and by its presence drives far away the other crimes of death. The charity of the brothers is a fitting dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit and a fortress of serene conscience. Charity is the servant of justice and the sole preserver of regular discipline in the monastery. Charity keeps the mind harmless from cruelty and supplies to all a peaceful gentleness of spirit. Brotherly charity seeks the salvation of all and does not allow the one who possesses it to grow sluggish [unclear]. Charity does not loathe want, but is ready, for love of the brothers, to endure every poverty. Charity is the water of heavenly sweetness; if anyone drinks it in the fervor of the Holy Spirit, he does not fear the everlasting thirst of hell. Brotherly charity does not seek the enticements of the flesh, but directs pure, holy, and undefiled affections toward one’s neighbor. Charity bears the name of chaste beauty, which cannot be shared with the things or actions of most impure pleasure. Charity loves purity and cleanness, and admits no impurity. In the work of love, charity does not consider the flesh of one’s neighbor, but the soul, which it does not doubt was created in the image of God. Brotherly charity raises up a sinning neighbor with pious admonitions, and keeps all its actions pure and harmless from every malice. Charity walks in peace and tranquility of mind, and saddens one’s neighbor neither by word, nor by deed, nor by sign. Charity humbles itself in all things as far as it can, and most diligently [unclear] for a neighboring brother who is weak, as for a son of God.

serves. Charity judges no one rashly, but humbly corrects a sinning neighbor with the gentlest admonitions. Charity is terrible and fearsome to the reprobate, but kind and gracious to the meek. Charity counts others’ troubles as its own, and weeps for brothers in tribulation as though it itself were suffering. Charity has compassion for all who are in need, and is saddened no less by the misfortunes of others than by its own. Charity reproaches a neighbor with nothing, but for the love of God always bears the weaknesses of all with equanimity. Charity is constant in good works, and so long as it remains in the heart, it is never idle. Charity neglects none of the things to which it is bound, but keeps all things as diligently as possible.

Fraternal charity is the fulfillment of the law, since whatever is commanded after the worship of God is referred to love of neighbor. Hence the holy lover of Christ says: “He who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. For, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not kill, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness, You shall not covet your neighbor’s property, and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Love of neighbor works no evil. Therefore love is the fullness of the law.”

And so, my dearest brothers, we beseech you through our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead, that you always preserve fraternal charity unharmed; without it you can neither truly love God nor fulfill any commandment of his. For the preservation of fraternal charity is as necessary for your salvation as the nourishment of food and drink is for bodies to preserve life. For the body dies without necessary nourishment, and all the virtues of the soul are scattered without fraternal charity.

Indeed, fraternal charity preserves a multitude of monks in unity of spirit, because without the bond of mutual love no cloistered man perseveres without disturbance of the community. The monk who pursues his brother with hatred is driven far away from the charity of God. For the holy Evangelist John says: “He who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.”

But the chaste and prudent lover of his neighbor walks securely in the light of the Holy Spirit, and is neither disturbed by anyone himself nor disturbs anyone else. For true love of neighbor is gentle, sweet, and most dutiful, and in all its common life meek, peaceable, and tranquil. Yet among rulers the vigor of discipline guides meekness, and the clemency of fraternal consideration beautifully tempers vigor. For one must be so tempered by the other that vigor is not harsh, nor love lax. The lover of fraternal charity does not abandon the way of justice; and he who rightly loves his neighbor admits no corruption.

For true love of neighbor covets no gold, nor seeks the services of attendants, but, despising all things that can overthrow the state of the soul,

Homily 22.

pursues only the soul’s growth. For it is not sincere charity toward one’s neighbors to seek gifts of corruption, or, in the manner of boys, to love with an affection of likeness someone who comes running because of distributions of little dainties. The friendship of monks, among good men who are zealous for the same purpose, ought to be common, and far removed from every carnal attachment. Let it be pure, simple, upright, lasting without injury to anyone, and let it have in itself nothing of suspicious conspiracy. This is not the rule of brotherly charity: to seek private forbidden meetings for consolation and, without the prior’s blessing, to spend time in furtive, indeed prohibited, conversations. You bestow your love upon your neighbor not rightly, but rather ruinously, whenever you come together, contrary to the rule of regular observance, for the comforts of the flesh. The monk’s love ought to be solid and most remote from every transgression of regular discipline, since unless charity is mute with regard to carnal conversations, it does not have in itself the fire of divine love.

Now examine your conversations, brothers, and see whether your hearts are also radiant with true charity. For charity that either gives to a neighbor, or receives from him, consolations harmful to the spirit was never sincere. Therefore take care to direct the eye of the mind not toward the beauty of the flesh, but rather toward contemplation of the soul, if you wish to love your neighbor rightly and praiseworthily. For when the flesh is loved without regard for the soul, a love is generated that is not sincere, but carnal and impure. Consider that your brother has a soul like your own, and always remember that you both await an equal happiness. By mind we mean soul; by soul, not by body, we are immortal. What is immortal is what each is commanded to love in the other, and to order the regard of charity toward the soul rather than toward the body. For just as we are distinguished from brute animals by reason and understanding, so the gaze of our love should be referred to the mind by which we understand, not to the body, which we have in common with beasts.

Let all carnal attachments be far from holy monks, who are not ignorant of the mutual and sincere rule of charity. Let love for one another be pure, upright, and conceived from fear of God alone, so that no advantage of any corruptible thing may intervene, but the simple intention of charity may remain. But simple and pure charity does not seek the byways of evil conspiracy, nor does it arm itself with the murmur of contention for the contrivances of iniquity. Whoever possesses true brotherly charity in his heart preserves peace in all things, and stirs up no matter or cause of ruinous dissension. Charity, giving each one his due, does injury to no one, and whatever it does not wish done to itself, it never transfers onto the person of another. Do not think that you have true brotherly charity when you love one another with regard to the flesh, or for the advantage of any temporal thing whatever, since where the cause of love is not the Lord, the affection of the one who loves is always faulty either in part or in whole. But he rightly loves his brother who

...binds with love of God, and because of the common participation in the kingdom which we await. Therefore, as the holy bishop John says, we have been baptized into one body of the Church, so that we may not be dissolved, but may preserve forever, in that harmony which exists toward one another and in the friendship of one body, charity and mutual concord. Just as no one outside the unity of the catholic Church can obtain salvation, so no one is believed able to be saved without brotherly charity.

Charity, therefore, is necessary for you before all things for salvation; without it the remaining works of the virtues are utterly fruitless. For there can be nothing good, no saving merit for life, which has not taken its origin from it. Charity is a certain short path to virtue; if anyone enters upon it by the right track of the journey, he will need no direction from a guide. Charity, pure, simple, and upright, is not accustomed to harm one’s neighbor, nor to inflict evil on anyone. Charity is accustomed to bestow on all the affection which it gives to its own advantages; and whatever it hopes will conduce to its own salvation, it desires this to be common to all people in Christ Jesus. Charity exercises the office of love without any disturbance, and although it loves all people greatly, nevertheless for no one is it provoked to a zeal of bitterness. It is always solid, always constant, always stable and firm, because it is neither touched by passions nor shaken by movements of unrest. It shows itself common to all, and so bestows its love on each one that nevertheless it seems nearest to all. Charity does not neglect itself in those things which pertain to the reason of the mind and soul; but in those things which regard the advantage of the body, it often places the causes of others before its own benefits. Great is the command of true charity, which compels a person to make another’s disadvantage his own.

You, therefore, my brothers, who have solemnly girded yourselves for the warfare of Christ, who through the arduous way of obedience pant after eternal life, if you do not wish to run in vain in the arena of so laborious a contest, take care, we exhort you, before all things always to keep brotherly charity inviolate among you. For unless you have sincere and perfect charity toward one another, you labor without fruit in regular observance. Abstinence from eating meat will contribute nothing to the salvation of your souls; the renunciation of all private property will profit nothing toward the adoption of eternal happiness, if brotherly love does not hold a place in your hearts. Therefore, desiring to be saved with Christ, love one another in truth, and, as Christ loved you, so we beg you, love one another. Whatever each one of you desires to be done to himself, let him bestow that very thing on his brother without envy, for the love of God, at all times. Let divine love overcome in you all quarrels of the flesh and every kind of contention; and let no pernicious dissension of the flesh find a place where the fullness of brotherly charity ought continually to dwell. For if all of you in the monastery live according to the law of Christian instruction, you necessarily always abstain from injuring one another. But if through contentions and wrongs you injure one another, you are certainly neither monks nor true Christians.

For it befits cloistered men and all monks to be outstanding in the observance of charity, and to be far removed from the rancor of envy and hatred. Therefore let the monk be stable in his purpose of holiness even to death; let him be faithful in the service of God, so that he may both sweetly burn in love of the Creator and never depart from purity of conscience. For whoever perfectly loves the Lord God with his whole heart both preserves his conscience clean from every pollution of sin and always shows pure and sincere charity to his neighbor. But the one whom either envy burns or hatred stirs up against his brother, it is clear that he neither truly loves God nor has a conscience pure from sin. Therefore everyone who pursues his brother with hatred and indignation is neither a true monk nor worthy of the name of Christian, but by merit and conduct a servant and companion of demons.

Therefore let hatreds depart far from this holy congregation of yours; let there be no contests of pernicious contention among you; let no zeal of bitterness be found here; let no speech of displeasing pride be heard. Let the concord of brotherly unity flourish here continually; let the innocence of Christian purity adorn the consciences of each one, so that we may live in this brief time in such a way that after death we may be glorified with Christ in eternity.

On the Charity of Man toward God. Homily XXIII.

Nothing can be so just, nothing so holy, nothing in human actions so honorable, as always to love God above all things with the whole heart, with the whole mind, and with the whole strength, and for love of him to fear neither death nor any kinds of punishments. There is no greater cause for any action in us than divine love, because, since God is the author of all things, nothing is more justly loved than he; and since he is the greatest of all goods, nothing is loved more fruitfully than he. God first loved us: the highest loved the lowest, the greatest loved the little, the almighty loved the weak.

Therefore, my brothers, let us love the Lord God with our whole heart, our whole soul, and our whole strength, by whom we are most sweetly loved, who not only created us in his image and likeness, but, as a proof of the greatest love, mercifully called us to the kingdom of eternal happiness through the teaching and death of his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. No fleshly mother ever loved her only son so tenderly, sweetly, and strongly as almighty God loved us, who not only willed to become man for our instruction, but also deigned to undergo death in the flesh he had assumed for our salvation.

No love has ever been greater, if we weigh rightly who it was who endured such things for us. For out of love for us, he who was free from the debt of death voluntarily dies; and he who was always immune from every sin is willingly condemned, innocent and just, for our sins. Therefore with the most just reason we are commanded to love the Lord our God with our whole heart, who, when we did not exist, created us from his goodness alone, and when we had perished, mercifully delivered us.

The love of God is the greatest of all virtues, since whatever good, whatever virtue is done in this world, if it is not done from charity toward God, is deprived of reward. Charity toward God purifies the conscience from every fault, because he who truly loves the Lord his God with his whole soul, with his whole heart, and with all his strength undoubtedly grants no place in his conscience to vices. For no uncleanness of vices enters a heart occupied by the love of God.

The love of God is an unfailing treasure: whoever possesses it is richer than all the wealthy of the world; whoever lacks it is more wretched than all the poor. Hence the holy Apostle of Christ says: “For those who love God, all things work together for good,” because nothing is lacking to those who fear him. Happy is the man in whose heart no bond of earthly affection dwells besides the love of Christ, who sighs after the remembrance of no human being, in whose conscience purity resides, and divine love always burns most ardently.

Love him, my brothers, who for love of you descended into the Virgin’s womb. Always carry in your hearts him who by his death opened heaven to you. Let the love of Christ be in you at all times, brothers, strong as death, so that your life may be conformed to Christ’s teaching, and, if it should ever be necessary to die for love of him, you may not fear, just as he himself first deigned calmly and kindly to undergo death for us.

For the love of Christ makes a monk near to God, and whoever is always fervent in the charity of the Lord will obtain the fellowship of angels. The love of Christ makes a man most strong against all assaults of demons, and no less patient and tranquil in adversity than in prosperity. The love of Christ teaches one truly to despise the world and all its delights, and to count all comforts of the flesh as nothing. The love of Christ quickly suppresses the unlawful movements of the flesh and brings the purest chastity into the mind. The love of Christ sweetly raises the mind with desire to heavenly things, and preserves it, separated from earthly things, in spiritual exercise.

The love of God smooths all hard and rough things, because where Christ is truly loved, tribulations and any adversities are reckoned as delights. The love of God is always constant in good works and is never idle. The love of God despises present things and strongly raises the mind to eternal things. The love of God neither seeks honors nor looks for riches, but, joined to Christ through desire, covets absolutely nothing except him. The love of God covers a multitude of sins and forgives all offenses to those who repent. The love of God suddenly justifies the impious, and the more love has grown,

By so much the more swiftly and strongly does the perfection of the soul rise up. The love of God is a tower of strength, which all the ministers of diabolical depravity cannot approach. The love of God is the consummation of all justice and the end of monastic discipline. The love of God perfects the monk and makes him complete in all good works. The love of God is the sweet yoke of inward sweetness, through which every filth of earthly corruption is driven out from the mind. The love of God honors souls and makes them pure and immaculate from all stains. The love of God perfectly enlightens the mind in every knowledge of heavenly goods, and purges the very affection from all unclean vanities. The love of God makes the one who truly possesses it most learned and wonderfully instructed in every Scripture. The love of God renders the monk formidable to all enemies and grants angelic power to those who persevere. The love of God defends a man in dangers, because whoever truly loves God fears no adversities. The love of God makes the one who possesses it secure in the hour of death and safe from demons, and joins the soul to the heavenly companies. The love of God brings its possessor back to the heavenly fatherland and grants eternal glory to those who love God. The love of God is the greatest of all good works and the single foundation of all virtues in the faith of Christ. The love of God is the best ointment, in which all the wounds of languishing souls are healed. The love of God is an abundant remedy for poverty and want, and a consolation more effective than every possession of riches. The love of Christ far surpasses all the learning of this world, and most perfectly instructs those who possess it in all knowledge necessary for salvation. The love of God prepares a delightful dwelling for the Holy Spirit in the heart of man, and preserves him, if he perseveres, in all purity. The love of God is the swiftest of all teachers, because what fleshly people learn over time and with much study, the Holy Spirit hands on in a moment to those who love God. The love of God gives knowledge to little ones and makes rustics more learned than the educated. The love of God is stronger than all things, and by its virtue rules over all. The love of God commands demons by a single word, and by the sign of the cross drives them from the bodies of possessed men. The love of God has bestowed eternal blessedness on the holy spirits in heaven, whom the grace of the Creator confirmed in love. The love of God beatifies, in eternal happiness, men baptized in the faith of Jesus Christ, because no one has ever been able to reach the fellowship of the angels unless he was proved to have been inflamed by persevering love of God. For the love of God alone is what makes works good and meritorious, since God accepts from us as an offered gift of good work only that which the flame of charity has made worthy in his sight. Whatever is done outside charity is judged unworthy in God's sight. Attend now, my brothers, to our admonitions, and consider diligently how necessary it is for you to love God above all things, if you desire to come to his kingdom.

On the charity of man toward God.

And happily to triumph with him forever. Let none of you seduce his own soul with empty words, so that he believes he truly loves God while neglecting to keep his commandments. You hear the Lord Jesus saying in the holy Gospel: “Whoever loves me will keep my words.” And, as the blessed Pope Gregory says, “the carrying out of the commanded work is the proof of the love that has been declared.” For then we truly love the Lord our God with our whole heart, when, having despised worldly pleasures, we keep all his commandments perfectly even unto death. Likewise, then we love him above all things when, for love of him, we walk innocently, not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit.

He truly loves God who, always intent upon good works, keeps himself pure and unstained from this world. But he rightly loves the Lord God who desires absolutely nothing in this world. He truly loves God with his whole heart who, for love of him, bravely despises the honors, riches, pleasures, and all comforts of the flesh belonging to the world. He loves God with his whole soul who, always solicitous in observing his commandments, omits to do none of the things that are pleasing to him. For the love of God neglects nothing, but is accustomed most diligently to keep and fulfill everything that he has commanded. He who loves God in true charity has fulfilled the law, the prophets, and the Gospel. Therefore by your works you will give testimony whether you truly love God. For everyone who has deserved to receive a ray of divine love always shows great and manifest signs of that love.

Indeed, the fire of divine love makes the one who possesses it pious, chaste, meek, and most humble in all things, and always tranquil in the same constancy of mind, without disturbance, both in adversity and in prosperity. The monk who truly loves the Lord God, according to the Rule of our most holy father Benedict, cheerfully obeys the elders’ commands in all things, embraces patience in hard and contrary matters, and preserves true humility everywhere. The love of God makes its possessor exceedingly rich in every good work, and renders him wholly alien to every kind of vice. The lover of God does not murmur at the command of obedience; in rebukes he does not rashly excuse himself; he is not touched by the bitter gall against his neighbor, nor is he disturbed even when injured.

He who is a true lover of God preserves his life blameless in all purity of mind and body, and shows within himself a charity fervent not only in word, but also in deed and in truth. Whatever is seen in the world as beautiful, whatever as pleasant or delightful, whatever flatters the insolence of wanton flesh, the true lover of God most steadfastly despises it all, and desires nothing other than to please Christ and to live with him as soon as possible. Great and incredible to those who do not know it is the power of divine love, which always impels a man to work well and never allows him to live idly. For what else is the inward love of God than a sweet

intoxication of the soul? Through it a man is carried away from all the consolations of the world and, as though he felt nothing of what mortals are doing, feasts at the banquet of the Holy Spirit alone. The monk who is a true lover of God has laid aside, for Christ’s sake, all curiosity about the world and anxiety over worldly things, and, as though he did not feel them, has risen above all the functions of the soul’s cares. With the Apostle he cries out to me, “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

O wine of divine love, how sweetly you intoxicate, how you satisfy the innocent, how wisely you make them foolish, how chastely you inflame them. For everyone who has been intoxicated with your taste, separated from every tumult of carnal pleasures, rests sweetly in the shadow of the Holy Spirit. Because of the excessive intoxication of the spirit, he speaks things foreign to the flesh and to the world, and nothing contrary to God is heard from his mouth. This is the immaculate satiety of spiritual wine, which is enlarged by desire the more it is continued.

O holy and venerable simplicity of the lover of Christ: although to many who savor earthly things it seems to be foolishness, before God and all his saints it is nevertheless the greatest and truly the highest wisdom. Let the world have its prudence, let it have honors, dignities, and riches; but I would choose the merit of one simple monk who truly loves God rather than the rule of the whole world. The love of God is both the highest delight of the soul and always the most chaste; its fire illuminates the mind and also sweetly inflames its affection. The love of God is a heavenly fountain of grace, because the grace of the Holy Spirit makes fruitful with the fruits of all virtues the mind which the charity of Christ purifies by plowing. The love of Christ wins for human beings the friendship of almighty God and reveals to mortals the will of the supreme majesty. The love of God makes a monk acceptable to God, because he does not require from us knowledge, learning, or eloquence, but charity.

Therefore the monk who has publicly offered himself to the Lord God ought to care for nothing except God, lest he seem to have a divided heart; for just as God is one, so love for God ought not to be divided. Hence the holy bishop Augustine says: “He loves you less, Lord, who loves anything with you that he does not love for your sake.” Just as God is perfect, so also he must be loved by us with all our strength, because he is not rightly loved whenever anything besides him is loved together with him. Love of God advances rightly when nothing is mixed with it that could weaken it. Let each one of you, as much as he can, strive to love the Lord his God above all things with the whole strength of his mind, because love for God alone is what will open for you the gate of paradise. For the more ardently you now love God, the greater glory you will receive in the heavenly fatherland. Blessed is that monk in whose conscience, apart from the love of Christ, no imagining of any occupation resides; who, awake, thinks of nothing but Christ; asleep, dreams of Christ; living and dying, sighs most constantly for Christ. O how well and securely

He dies who has always been solicitous in the exercise of divine love and at all times zealous in the observance of God’s commandments. For only the love of God is admitted into the kingdom of heaven; and the more fervent the mind has been in loving, the greater will be its reward in the kingdom of heaven. He who loves much receives much; and he who now loves less will then also receive less in glory. Therefore, as much as each one can, with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his strength, so much let him love, because our God is not to be loved lukewarmly or sluggishly, but fervently, wisely, and sweetly.

The love of God gathers strength and grows through spiritual exercises, just as a burning fire is enlarged by a supply of wood. Indeed, if the wood is taken away, the fire is extinguished; and if spiritual exercises are interrupted, charity is soon shipwrecked. True love of God is never idle, but at all times is delightfully occupied in those things that nourish and preserve charity. For the lover of God never forgets his beloved, but always meditates on his presence and beauty; now in most devout prayers he speaks to Jesus, now in the holy Scriptures he marvels at him speaking to him. The true lover of Christ meditates day and night on the law of the Lord, and with the greatest diligence does everything that he understands to be pleasing to God.

O how sweetly he burns whom the love of God truly inflames! How pleasantly he glows whose mind the flame of the Holy Spirit sets on fire! Blessed is that monk who, full of divine love, withdraws himself wholly from earthly vanities and rests in the shade of heavenly desire. O if only we had love for God as strong, whole, and vehement as mad and foolish lovers have for their corruptible mistresses, with desire for whom they often burn, shamefully go mad, and fear no scandal of this world. But the love of God is stronger than all things, if it has been truly rooted in us.

Whoever truly loves the Lord God always keeps in his memory his most bitter Passion, because nothing so perfectly causes love of God in the human heart, nothing so induces true compunction, as the never-interrupted remembrance of God’s benefits. Therefore let the written sequence of Christ’s Passion always be in your memory, and let this word never depart from your mouth: O crucified Jesus, my love, by the power of your most innocent death have mercy on me, and make me your faithful servant.

On serenity of conscience. Homily XXIV.

With great solicitude we must watch, dearly beloved brothers, and with continual meditation take care that we always keep our conscience, whose testimony we cannot escape, clean and immaculate from every contagion of worldly sin. For nothing more beautiful...

Homily XXIV.

Nothing is more pleasant, nothing, finally, more precious than a good conscience; for where the mind has within itself the manifest testimony of its own uprightness, it suffers no remorse of destructive unrest. An upright and good conscience is an incredible exultation of the mind and a sure comfort in every adversity. The monk who has obtained the testimony of a good conscience neither refuses to live nor fears the coming arrival of death. A good conscience is always glad, always pleasant, always fearless, and truly tranquil in the peace of Jesus Christ. In a good conscience there is always peace, piety, goodness, light, virtue, honor, joy, gladness, sweetness, and delight without dissipation. Conscience is the treasury of the soul, because whatever is placed in it is kept as provision for the future life. A good conscience is the best treasure; if anyone has neglected to possess it, he must be judged the most wretched and unhappy of all men. A good conscience is the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit and the earthly paradise of all graces.

A good conscience does not fear the slanders of the wicked, and a mind conscious of what is right despises the lies of reputation. A good conscience is always cheerful, and he who works the justice of God is not uselessly sad. A good conscience always advances in the love of the Lord, and he who lives innocently will not dread danger. A good conscience has peace and concord with all in God, and in humble simplicity takes care for its salvation. A good conscience strengthens the soul; but he who is constant in evil will fall into despair. A good conscience confidently rebukes the foolish; but he who is evil keeps bitter silence. A good conscience gladdens the soul; but he who is conscious of evil in himself suffers continual desolation of mind. A good conscience safely reproves the impious; but he who has lost the testimony of uprightness always fears being accused. A good conscience is the most beautiful adornment of the soul; and he who does not care for wisdom in this life will die in poverty.

A good conscience is the dwelling place of virtues and the true abode of heavenly mysteries. A good conscience is the consummation of all philosophy and the fullness of all sciences. A good conscience is the best teacher of virtues and the completed discipline of all studies. A good conscience bears the best fruit of holiness, and, standing founded in the fear of the Lord, admits no sin. A good conscience is more precious than all the riches of the world, and far sweeter than all desirable things that can be possessed in this life. A good conscience is the merit of Christian perfection and the humbly presumable beginning of future happiness. A good conscience is the fertile field of virtues and the sweet and pleasant fragrance of the Paradise of God. A good conscience is the sweetest companion of this life and a glorious mediator between God and man. A good conscience is very fearful to demons, but a pleasing friend to the holy angels. A good conscience makes the dying man secure against the envy of demons, and deserves to have the escort of angels. Conscience

A good conscience does not fear to appear in the sight of the judge, nor does it dread the accusing judgment of synderesis. A good conscience has hope in God and, without the unrest of hesitation, the best confidence, because one who remembers having committed no evil comes confidently to the judge’s examination.

A good conscience is richly rewarded by the Lord God and is changed into everlasting joy. A good conscience is not one that commits no evil, but one that, preserving purity for the love of God from every sin, also adorns itself most fittingly with the practice of all good works. For a good conscience, according to the prophet’s admonition, turns completely away from evil and always and continually does good with the most zealous intention.

A good conscience especially adorns a monk and makes him utterly alien to worldly actions. A good conscience follows the Lord Jesus in simple purity and is stained by no spots of error. For a conscience that is good, and as long as it is good, cannot be erroneous, but always remains grounded in the truth of the Holy Spirit. But a conscience that has been erroneous is not good. For error is opposed to truth and has no share at all in goodness. When the conscience is in error, however, the danger is near, and the descent into hell very steep.

There are many among cloistered people who are weak and far too feeble in spirit, who are not always directed by the right judgment of their consciences, being preoccupied by various causes. And often, indeed, either a small or a great error of conscience arises from ignorance, namely whenever one who is less experienced in spiritual practice doubts whether the way he is considering in his mind is good or evil. For who, walking uprightly in his simplicity, understands everything? In doubtful matters the counsels of elders must be sought; and what they have decided, the monk should not doubt must be embraced as the judgment of truth.

Sometimes the conscience errs from negligence, when a monk neglects to examine himself by the scrutiny of reason and does not labor to search out the truth in doubtful matters. From this a pernicious error arises in the conscience, through which reason is gradually darkened. Pride also frequently makes the conscience erroneous and far removed from the knowledge of truth. For the proud man, although he understands that he does not know, nevertheless desires to seem wise and learned to everyone; for this reason he is ashamed to confess his ignorance.

Sometimes, however, error of conscience arises from singularity, to which presumption is always said to be joined. And this plague is frequently troublesome to monks and to those who profess holiness without the necessary foundation of humility. For the sheep that walks singular paths is more quickly seized and strangled by wolves.

Sometimes too an excessively disordered affection hurls the conscience into error, namely when a person loves his own will more than is expedient. For whoever is led by the affection of his own sensuality is frequently blinded in the judgment of truth. From this there is no doubt that it happens that many have erroneous consciences, because they love the pleasures of their own flesh too much. Every

But the proud, luxurious, impure man, entangled in great or public crimes, darkens his conscience by deliberate perversity, and often shows, both by words and by deeds, how wrongly he thinks about the future repayment of merits. A malicious disposition perverts the judgment of uprightness, and the disordered desire of the flesh darkens the understanding. Sometimes, moreover, excessive and immoderate faintheartedness makes the conscience err; this evil is born partly from ignorance, and partly generated from one’s own sensuality.

In this scrupulosity, however, a monk should follow the counsel either of the abbot or of some other more experienced elder, and should not rashly defend the opinion of his own head. Excessive scrupulosity is dangerous, because it hurls the conscience into error and unhappily overthrows many. For everything that is done against conscience is said to build toward hell. Excessive perplexity of mind has also harmed many and cast them headlong into various errors. But he who is truly a humble monk submits himself to his superior’s examination. For whoever makes use of his superior’s counsel in doubts that arise is not easily overthrown by the snares of demons. For the more the consciences of monks have been exposed to the inquiry of a wise prelate, the more secure and the brighter they will shine.

Therefore, dearest brothers, you must take care first of all to have consciences free from every error, then pure from all vices, and finally adorned with the holy fragrances of all the virtues. Therefore let the monk who truly desires to make progress guard his heart with every watchfulness, and, as far as possible, set a cloister over his senses, and not allow anything deadly to enter. But if by any occasion he recognizes that he has fallen into some sin, let him at once strive to wipe it away by true repentance, and not grant time to the wicked seed, by which it may grow strong into something worse. While the wound is small, let the remedy be applied; for if it is neglected, it grows beyond measure.

Therefore, my brothers, resist bravely the first movements of demonic suggestion, and overcome the enemy when he is small and weak. But if the sensuality of the body has become altogether wanton, let it be brought back to obedience by harsh mortification, just as we know our holy father Benedict did when he rooted out the slippery insolence of the flesh by the stings of nettles and brambles. Finally, if you diligently recall to mind the dreadful punishments that await the wicked, you will easily overcome the illicit movements of the flesh. For there is no one who does not fear pain more than he loves pleasure.

Also often bring back to mind the joys of heavenly happiness, to which you desire to come, because if you faithfully consider them, you will strongly lessen the fire of the flesh. Whatever delights in the world is corruptible and momentary, but the joys of eternal delight remain forever without end. It is therefore foolish, and a mark of extreme madness, to choose a passing advantage and to despise that good which remains forever. Foolish in the eyes of

On Continual Preparation for Death.

A man is judged foolish among men who prefers dross to gold; but he is considered most foolish before God who places temporal pleasure before everlasting goods. Ecclesiasticus 33.

He who loves a serene conscience should flee idleness; for, as Scripture says, every idle man is in desires, and idleness has taught much evil. The mind must be occupied with good exercises, and the fire of holy conduct, which burns with charity, must be nourished by continual practice. For an idle man lives neither for himself nor for his neighbor, but is always given over to his belly or to sleep: he opens his mind to vices, and keeps it closed and empty of virtues. Idleness, the kindler of lust, quickly extinguishes the fervor of spiritual devotion.

Abstinence also is especially very necessary for a monk, so that his conscience may remain clean. For, as Saint Jerome says, a full belly readily foams over into lust; and he who feeds his servant delicately will find him rebellious. The lover of serenity of conscience should be constant in holy prayers; for as dogs flee a stone, so demons flee devout and continual prayer. He should also carefully beware of sloth, and likewise sadness of mind; and as soon as he feels some temptation creeping in, he should have recourse to the consolation of the Scriptures. Indeed, a foul thought will not enter a mind which the word of God has filled. Whatever we do, whatever we think, whatever we undertake, let us always know that God’s presence is at hand, and we shall easily overcome disordered delight. A good conscience never forgets the presence of God, but always meditates that its judge is present. Act now, my brothers, so that you may have consciences pure from every crime; and if anyone feels himself burdened by some fault, let him return without delay, through true repentance, to necessary purity. For unless you have clean and good consciences at all times, you live as apostates, not as monks.

On Continual Preparation for Death. Homily 25.

The highest philosophy of cloistered men, my dearest brothers, is continual meditation on death. Hence a certain wise man, considering the usefulness of this philosophy, admonished every mortal, saying: Remember your last things, and you will not sin forever. Meditation on death draws a man back from the pleasures of the flesh and brings in contempt for all corruptible things. Meditation on death despises present things through voluntary poverty, and drives the mind toward desire for future things. Meditation on death removes pride far away and plants true humility in the heart of the one meditating. Meditation on death makes a monk attentive to the observance of regular discipline and never allows him to be idle. Meditation on death cuts off all the vanities of the world and preserves the mind in the highest temperance. Meditation on death makes one despise the vain and passing honors of the world, and think of nothing other than the future judgment of God. Meditation on death

Homily XXV.

He does not fear the poverty of this life, because with his whole desire he longs for eternal riches. Meditation on death endures all the adversities of this world most patiently for love of Christ, because it hopes for nothing other than the recompense from above. Meditation on death makes the monk humble and obedient in all the commandments of righteousness. Meditation on death makes the monk quiet, stable in the congregation, and in good concord with everyone in Christ. Meditation on death makes the monk calm and peaceable, and tranquil without any disturbance of mind. Meditation on death exterminates all dissoluteness and levity, and preserves the monk mature and healthfully sorrowful in all things. Meditation on death makes the monk solitary and continually devoted to holy prayers.

Meditation on death hastens penitence and brings in true compunction. Meditation on death withdraws desire from every vanity, and keeps the conscience serene and most pure. Meditation on death makes a man despise all the comforts of this world, and prepare himself daily for his departure. Meditation on death teaches him to flee idleness, and makes a man keep continual watch in the fear of the Lord. Meditation on death does injury to no one, because it always fears the strict accounting of judgment. Meditation on death mitigates anger and all disordered impulses, because, while a man considers that he will soon die, nothing external disturbs his mind. Meditation on death makes the heart contrite and humble, because attentive remembrance of things to come permits no one to be proud.

Continual meditation on death makes one’s departure safe at the end, because it has made the meditator prepared over a long period of time. Meditation on death is especially fitting for cloistered men and monks, whom the renunciation of all earthly things and the very profession of the rule have already made dead and buried to the world. Meditation on death makes the monk run prudently in the course of spiritual warfare, and renew daily the purpose of holy fervor. Continual meditation on death is very useful for cloistered men, because it both powerfully restrains the vices of the flesh and grants no entrance of the mind to perverse thoughts.

For the holy bishop Augustine says: Fear of future death necessarily shakes the mind, and, like a nail of the flesh, fastens all the motions of pride to the wood of the cross. And the holy champion of the Church, Jerome, says: Nothing will help you as much toward temperance in all things as frequent thought of this brief life, whose end is certain, while nothing is more uncertain than its hour. Therefore meditation on death corrects all intemperance, and arranges the habits of the one who meditates in stable order with beautiful variety. Meditation on death gives a man true wisdom, and perfects the highest philosophy among cloistered men. For Plato too held the opinion that the whole life of the wise is meditation on death, because we are all born on this condition: that from here we must depart again through death.

For Scripture says: We all die, and like waters we flow down into the earth, which do not return again. And the holy Apostle of Christ

Paul says: “It is appointed for human beings to die once.” Continual meditation on necessary death makes a person never trust in earthly things, but await his departure in every place and time with foresight. Meditation on death always expects the end of life in every place, because it is wholly ignorant of the moment of dying. Whoever meditates daily on the coming of future death prepares himself for dying at every time with all the diligence he can. For nothing is more certain for us than death, although we all are ignorant of the hour of dying.

Therefore, brothers, with all the urgency we can, we admonish your charity always to think that you are going to die, and with such foresight diligently to prepare yourselves for dying that, when the hour comes, you may not fear to depart. Let no one promise himself a long life in this world, because nothing deceives mortals as much as the hope of a longer span. For what does a longer age produce in human beings except that it makes them liable to more sins and always less prepared for dying? The longer we live in this world, the more we fear death. A longer age piles up greater debts of spiritual obligation; and an old man fears all the more to come before the sight of the strict judge, the more he recognizes that he is bound before the Lord in many matters to render an account. For the soul departs unwillingly from its body when it is tormented by the heavier stings of its conscience.

But whoever is pure from every evil of iniquity and adorned for salvation with the beauty of the necessary virtues does not fear to die, because through death he goes to everlasting life. Therefore, O monk, live now as you wish to die; for the death which has been preceded by the integrity of a good life cannot be evil. O how securely he dies, whoever loves the Lord Jesus above all things and, despising all the goods of this world for love of him, faithfully keeps his words. He departs securely from this life who always lives in the love of God without stain of conscience. He dies securely whose life is defiled by no pleasures of this world. For the death of the saints is a most sweet sleep and a peaceful entrance into eternal life. But the death of sinners is worst, whose evil life has gone before it, contrary to the divine ordinances. For one who lives in sins, opposed to God, death becomes for him a dreadful entrance into hell.

He does not die badly who has lived well; and rarely does he die well who is shown always to have lived badly. He dies securely who loves God above all things with a pure mind and at all times keeps himself from this wicked world. Death is desirable for the good and upright in heart, because it sets an end to exile and restores life in heaven. Death is the leaving of the body, the overthrow of the dark prison, and the laying down of a heavy burden. Death is the end of present evils, the finish of sadness, and the grave of every earthly pleasure. A good life in the faith and charity of Jesus Christ makes death precious and especially desirable to the servant of God. Therefore now, brothers, take care to anticipate death with holy works, and make for yourselves

pleasant through the pursuit of virtues, which nature willed to be necessary for all. Remember that we are all necessarily mortal, and when we do not expect it, we shall pass from this world. For, as a certain venerable prelate said:

We are all taken from the midst as the fates press on, and we are drawn where life, once completed, calls us.

Therefore, wherever we can do good, my brothers, let us do it while we have time, lest, when death’s command forestalls us, we grieve too late that we have been negligent. Time alone is ours; all other things are another’s. The labor of our spiritual warfare, even if it seems somewhat hard to lukewarm minds, is nevertheless very brief, and will soon be ended with life; but the reward of good works, which will be given to us, remains forever.

Let meditation on death soon to come never leave you; but by consideration of the strict judgment, which no one can escape, let it continually pierce your minds with love of God. Behold how many monks in this monastery of Sponheim have gone before us, living and dying, through almost four hundred years from its first foundation; of them no memory at all remains among us today. What we are, they were; what they are, we shall soon be. They were mortal men, as we are; they died and returned to the dust of the earth, as we shall.

I am the twenty-fifth abbot of this monastery of Sponheim; unless twenty-four had gone before me to death, I certainly would not have come as the twenty-fifth to this abbacy. I too shall shortly give place to another, so that the number of the twenty-sixth abbot may be fulfilled. After him another again will be appointed; and the death of one becomes the institution of another; and while one succeeds another, all are subjected to the command of death.

Where, then, brothers, are those who went before us in this monastery? Just as there is no memory among us of those who went before, so we too shall be in everlasting oblivion among those who follow. Let us think on these things beforehand, dearly beloved brothers, while we live, lest we fall upon death unprepared. As daily we hasten toward death, so daily let us prepare ourselves according to our strength; for he dies secure who in life is adorned with good and holy works.

Do not let the hope of a longer life deceive you; for the longer you live in this world, the shorter is the time you will still live. Behold, daily tending toward death, we die; daily one part of our life is cut away from us; and the longer our life is drawn out, the more the remaining time for living is shortened. All the time that we have lived we have wholly lost, because it has passed away; the present moment in which we live today we share with death; how much time for living remains to us in the future, we do not know. Why, then, do we trust in the vanity of this life, we who are soon to die? And so, brothers, let us constantly consider that we shall soon come to that place where all our forefathers long ago went before us. All by this law

We are born so that we may shortly die. Let death seem terrible to those whose whole life is defiled in the pleasure of the flesh, and for whom no good things are reserved in heaven. But we, who have placed our hope in the Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior of all, and for love of him have despised the pleasures of the world, why should we fear death?

Nevertheless, since death is the most terrible of all terrible things, we shall be able to drive away an indiscreet fear of dying if each day we prepare ourselves as though we were already about to die. Yet it is one thing to have dread of death, another to have trembling fear. For the Lord Jesus too felt the dread of death in advance, but not trembling fear, so that he might show the properties of the two natures. Therefore continual meditation on death is altogether necessary for us who are weak, so that the mind, not yet perfected in the charity of Christ, may be stirred, as though by a certain violent impulse, to the grace of compunction.

For by the remembrance of future death the mind is pierced with a useful dread, like a nail driven into wood. The remembrance of death introduces arduous repentance and true sobriety of mind. The remembrance of death is necessary for the unwise, whose conversion begins from servile fear, so that through filial fear it may be raised by degrees into charity. The remembrance of death, and of the strict examination of God, the judge to come, is especially necessary for those who by evil habit and daily practice are drawn into sin.

And there are among you some who are too lukewarm and negligent in the spiritual warfare; admonishing them, we exhort them paternally to remember that they are mortal, and to live henceforth in such a way that they do not fear to die. For it is very dangerous to live in that state in which a man would dread to die. We must live so that we await death securely; and this can be done only if, preserving ourselves in all purity of mind and body, we continually burn with the exercises of divine charity. Let us live, as far as possible, innocently, according to the rule of the holy Father Benedict, which we have professed, and we shall have good hope, because almighty God, who does not allow a man of good will to perish, will have mercy on us. Let us always think of God as present with us everywhere: he sees all things, knows all things, understands all things, rewards all things. And let us live in that purity in which we have promised to serve his most holy Majesty.

THE END.

Here ends the first book of exhortations to monks, written by my own hand, Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, on the ninth day of the month of June, in the year of Christians 1486, in the fourth indiction, in the twenty-fourth year of my age. I dedicated this work to my predecessor, now abbot of Seligenstadt, most dear to me.

LETTER

Johannes Trithemius, though unworthy, abbot of the monastery of Sponheim, to the reverend father and lord Johannes de Colenhausen, abbot of Seligenstadt, formerly of Sponheim, my most dear predecessor: with prayers, ready and prepared to please him in spirit.

Recently, venerable predecessor, I sent you my first book of exhortations to monks, containing twenty-five homilies. After I learned that it had been approved by your examination, I judged that this second book also, which I now send, should confidently be inscribed with your name. Into the former I gathered twenty-five homilies for the instruction of the brothers, which I had delivered before them; in this one I have arranged seven sermons, according to the order in which they were spoken in their presence.

I do not fear to undergo the examination of your paternity, because I always had you as a gentle predecessor, and long ago found you to be a sincere lover of truth. For you flourish with a keen, gentle, and deep intellect, which can easily discern between true and false, and necessity requires you to correct all things sufficiently. Therefore I pray that, according to the gentleness innate in you, you patiently bear the rudeness of my talent, since I am both a little child in the knowledge of the Scriptures and a novice in the order of prelates.

Practice in the Scriptures, as I trust, will give me experience, and continued diligence in writing will give me progress. The occupation of household affairs and the poverty of the place often draw me back from salutary study, and turn my mind elsewhere against the purpose of my will. Only on feast days and Sundays is leisure granted me for writing, on which, out of reverence for God, I am not accustomed to admit any business of the peasants. Sometimes also, after the customary singing of matins and lauds, I am accustomed to spend what remains of the night on the study of letters, and, as far as I can, to compose something by lamplight for the instruction of my brothers. I desire in all things to follow in your footsteps, and, if I can, to observe forever the praiseworthy custom of teaching subjects which you introduced. I know that I am bound to this.

by duty; and, although I am unskilled and unlearned, I nevertheless gladly wish, according to my powers, to be diligent both in learning and in teaching. I submit these sermons to your examination, and with humble supplication I earnestly ask that the file of your mastery may correct them. I have arranged a few out of many in order, since I neither committed them all to writing, nor did an excessive length of the book seem to me either necessary or useful. For on feast days, when we are free from the turmoil of worldly business, we devote ourselves to reading according to the rule of the Scriptures. And lest I seem to occupy the place of shepherd in vain, what I have labored over by night I am accustomed, after None, in place of the regular study, to speak and to recite from a little sheet before the brothers in chapter. For I find that this care of mine not only profits the brothers for edification, but also helps me toward skill in composition. Farewell, venerable teacher, and pray for us.

From Spanheim, on the twelfth day of the month of September, in the year of the Christians one thousand four hundred eighty-six.

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the second book of exhortations to monks by Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Spanheim, afterward of [unclear].

That monks must live cautiously. Sermon I.

Many things indeed, most beloved brothers, are necessary for your consideration in this life, if you desire to attain the glory of eternal salvation. For you know, as Scripture bears witness, that your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour; and we know that he must be resisted with great watchfulness in the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ through works of charity. Therefore let no one presume on his own strength, lest he trust in vanity; for unless you humbly keep yourselves in the fear of the Lord, you will quickly fall into the snare of the devil. “The greater you are,” Scripture commands, “humble yourself in all things,” for God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble.

For it befits a monk to be humble and a true despiser of this world. A monk ought always to be diligent in the observance of regular discipline and continually zealous in the fear of the Lord. A monk ought to be chaste and modest in mind and body alike, so that he may serve God, as he promised, in all purity. A monk must not live according to his own will, but according to the rule and according to the direction of his shepherd, conforming to the norm of cenobitic instruction. A monk [unclear] ought also to love holy silence and to occupy his mind usefully in the reading of the Scriptures. A monk ought at all times, even until death, to be diligent, so that he may be perfect in the observance of the commandments of God and of the rule.

But so that you may know what things are necessary for you, who live in holy religion, for perfection, I shall describe for you a certain path of virtues, by which you must direct your way to the kingdom of heaven. All the virtues, however, cling together by the bond of mutual connection, so that whoever perfectly possesses one seems to have them all; and whoever lacks even one is said to possess none at all.

The first of all the virtues necessary for salvation is the most holy catholic faith, separated from every pollution of errors and heresies, and rooted originally in the teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ. For, as Scripture bears witness, without faith it is impossible to please God; and whoever does not believe in the only-begotten Son of God is already judged, and the wrath of God remains.

Hebrews 1: concerning him. Therefore faith is the origin of all virtues, from which all pursuits of salvation arise. True and right faith in God begets fear of the Lord, since if we believe God to be just, we shall rightly confess that he is to be feared. Right faith produces hope and confidence, because, when we believe God to be merciful, we at once hope that we can obtain salvation from his goodness. Faith begets charity, because if we believe God to be the supreme good, we undoubtedly love him. For who would not love what he does not doubt to be supremely good?

Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen, and the one foundation of our salvation. Faith joins the soul to God and, in the midst of charity, makes it the friend of the eternal King. For the most holy bishop Augustine says: There are no greater riches, no treasures, no honors, no greater substance of this world, than the catholic faith, which saves sinful men, enlightens the blind, heals the sick, baptizes catechumens, justifies the faithful, restores penitents, increases the just, crowns martyrs, preserves virgins, widows, and married people in chaste modesty, ordains clerics, consecrates priests, and places believers with the holy angels in the eternal inheritance of heaven.

But where sound faith is not present, there can be no justice, because the just man lives by faith; and whoever lacks the merit of justice will have no share with Christ. Faith is the beginning of human salvation; without it no one can reach the number of the children of God or possess any part in the kingdom of God. Faith is the foundation of all virtues: whatever is done outside faith is without doubt built for Gehenna. Christian faith is a most beautiful lamp, enlightening the soul and, through observance of the commandments, leading it to eternal happiness.

Faith first brings the mind back to the knowledge of God; afterward it gives the precepts of living for obedience. And when a person has kept God’s commandments, hope of obtaining salvation is raised up; then charity is strengthened in the heart. Faith gives knowledge to the soul; knowledge brings forth action in charity; and to these two blessedness is promised in eternity. One must take the greatest care that there be no error in knowledge, because when right faith is corrupted by the falsehood of heresies, no action brings one to the harbor of salvation. Therefore let there be rectitude and truth in faith, justice and sincerity in action, and no iniquity will have dominion.

For faith without works is dead and merits nothing toward the salvation of eternal happiness. To have faith without the works of charity is to imitate the demons, who, though they are wholly estranged from all charity, nevertheless both believe that God is just and tremble. Hence the Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah, and afterward through himself in the holy Gospel, concerning believers who do not show the works of charity, saying: This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. Whoever praises Christ with his mouth without works is like a man who doubts in faith. For if he truly believed, he would surely fear God. Faith

without works, like a body dead without the spirit, which is removed from the sight of the living and hidden in the tomb. If you believe rightly and live badly, you destroy yourself with your own sword, because for one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin.

Take care, my brothers, not to admit any error in faith, and strive with the utmost care that there be no wickedness in your conduct. Follow the faith which holy Church commends to us; live as the Gospel commands, and as the monastic rule commands. Then have at all times a most certain hope in the mercy of God, yet never one estranged from the fear of the Lord.

Hope is the certain expectation, through the grace of the merciful God, of future goods, and a solicitude to merit, through the exercise of charity, the crown of righteousness. Hope is the certain expectation of future blessedness, which the grace of God works in us, accompanied by the uprightness of a good will. Hope is that by which a person hopes to come to the life of eternal happiness, which he desires, and, through the mediation of God’s grace, also arranges and adapts his own will to meet it. Hope is of good things, difficult, future, and possible, for no one hopes for the contrary. For no one hopes for evil, nor for what is slight, nor for what is present or past; nor are we unaware that hope is not concerned with impossibilities.

Hope is the moderator of all labors and the sole consoler in the midst of tribulations. For hope of future goods brings rest to those who labor for Christ in this life, just as, for those contending in the arena, the expectation of the crown through continual victory lessens the pain of wounds. Hope strengthened the martyrs amid torments and made them, in the power of Christ, stronger than all their persecutors. Hope of eternal blessedness preserves the Church, and gave to the holy confessors and virgins true charity in Christ. Hope powerfully raises up a spirit cast down by grief; and the higher it lifts itself through love, the less it feels the adversities of this world. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, because hope does not confound, as the holy Apostle promised, by which we have been saved.

But so that hope may not break out into presumption, the fear of the Lord is necessary for our salvation, so that, while we believe him to be kind and merciful, we may not doubt that he is also just and upright. For the most blessed Pope Gregory says: Nothing is safer for us than to fear under hope, lest an unwary mind either cast itself down into the depth of vices by despairing, or fall presumptuously by exalting itself over gifts received. For the more it trembles humbly under hope before the eyes of the strict judge, the more firmly it stands in him.

The fear of God corrects the mind and keeps it pure from all malice. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, because in the way of God one begins from fear, so that little by little one may come to the strength of charity. The fear of the Lord orders the monk and makes him zealous in the observance of regular discipline. The fear of the Lord guards the rule and preserves true purity of mind and body. The fear of the Lord neglects none of the things that have been prescribed, but guards them all with care. The fear of the Lord admits no idleness, but is continually occupied.

about the good, so as to exclude sin. The monk who has cast off fear of the Lord is like a city that has come into the midst of enemies, all of whose walls have been destroyed. A city without the protection of walls is quickly captured by enemies; and a monk who does not have fear of God is easily overcome by demons.

For fear of God alone corrects minds, drives away crimes, preserves innocence, and makes a monk persevering in his purpose of holiness. From fear charity gradually arises; and when, with God’s help, it has been truly rooted in the mind, overcoming servile fear, it now casts it out. Charity is the root of all good things, because whatever good is done in this life in order to please God is governed by charity alone. Charity is the greatest of all virtues; without it all mortal deeds are nothing.

For the most holy Apostle of Christ says: If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity, I have become like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I could move mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my goods as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I burn, but have not charity, it profits me nothing.
