The second thing that persuades one to flee sin is fear of the future judgment, at which all human beings must necessarily be presented. No one can escape this terrible judgment; rather, we must all appear at it. Two things must be feared by us.

Two judgments are impending, neither of which we shall be able to escape; rather, necessity compels us to appear at both. One is called the particular judgment, in which, immediately after death, the soul is judged according to its merits, either to grace or to punishment. The other is named the general judgment, which will be at the end of the age, where we shall all be judged publicly by the only-begotten Son of God.

Both judgments are exceedingly terrible and greatly to be feared by all mortals. Hence the prophet Joel says: “Great is the day of the Lord, and very terrible; and who shall endure it?” Likewise in Ecclesiastes King Solomon says: “All things that are done under the sun God will bring into judgment, judging every error, whether it be good or evil.” In Isaiah also it is read thus: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people and its princes.” And in the book of the prophet Amos it is written: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord. What is it to you? For that day of the Lord is darkness and not light.” Zephaniah also, the prophet of the Lord, foretelling the bitterness of the future judgment, said: “The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; the strong man will be troubled there. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind. In the fire of the Lord’s zeal the whole earth will be devoured, because he will make a consummation with haste upon all who dwell on the earth.”

This day, exceedingly terrible and fearful to all mortals, which you believe will certainly come, dearest brothers, you should always keep in memory. For the most holy bishop Ambrose says: “There is nothing that profits more toward an honorable life than that we believe there will be a judge whom neither the hidden things of minds deceive nor shameful things delight.” For all of us, as holy Christophilus says, must be made manifest before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive the things proper to the body, according as he has done, whether good or evil.

How much that future day of terrible judgment is to be feared, the holy priest Jerome indicates, saying: “Whether I eat, or drink, or do anything else, that voice always seems to sound in my ears: Rise, you dead, come to judgment. Whenever I think of the day of judgment, I tremble in my whole heart and body.” Therefore, if there is any joy in the present life, it must be carried on in such a way that the bitterness of the future judgment never withdraws from memory.

What shall we wretches say on that day, or how shall we stand before the strict judge, if, as the divine apostle Peter says, scarcely will the just man be saved? If Jerome, a just and most holy man, feared the future judgment, O good God, how will Trithemius, an unhappy sinner, appear? If the just man fears, how will the sinner stand? For what shall we say, or what shall we answer, accused heavily on every side? All the elements will stand against us as witnesses; earth and heaven together will accuse us. But even if all things were silent, each one’s own conscience will be a heavy accuser. He who knows all things is ignorant of nothing, for there all things will be manifest to the judge. The evil things we have done will be there, accusing us heavily; they will be present all around as witnesses [unclear].

Sermon V.

We shall see countless demons around us as witnesses against us; below us we shall see the horrible open chaos; above us we shall behold the judge, angry; and on every side the utmost danger will be hanging over us. My brothers, always turn over in the memory of your heart these dangers of the examination to come, and diligently consider how dreadful it is to fall under the future sentence of the judge. In that terrible hour pure hearts will have more power than the crafty words of rhetoricians; a clean conscience will help a man more than the money of the whole world, because he who is to judge all things is not deceived, indeed is changed neither by price nor by prayers.

O what incredible horror will seize all the wicked, what fearful sentence they will hear: “Depart, accursed, into eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.” O worst of all evils; O deepest sorrow of all sorrows, to be separated from the fellowship of the saints and to be tormented with demons forever. Truly the day of judgment is horrible and to be feared by all, because it is exceedingly bitter: there the worm of conscience does not die; there one once damned to punishment is never set free.

Therefore the monk who desires to attain eternal salvation should always keep himself, as far as he can, clean from every sin, and that voice, “Depart, accursed, into eternal fire,” should never depart from his memory. Hence the third thing which we judge to be of great help in turning away from sin is to think diligently on the bitterness of the punishments of eternal damnation. For no temptation of fleshly pleasure is so violent that it will not at once fail, overcome, if the person tempted recalls in earnest meditation what the damned are now suffering in hell.

What profit now to the damned are the riches they once possessed? What do past pleasures bring to the lustful who have been placed in hell? What do the emptiest honors bring to the proud? What does the power once so broad bring to the arrogant? Think, brothers, what the damned are now suffering in the lower world, and lest similar things befall you, persevere continually in good and holy works. If you fear hell, flee sin. For hell will do no harm if a man has remained in the faith of Christ, free from sins; nor will he burn in punishment who has not first burned here in guilt.

The place of hell must be feared, where there is no redemption; but whoever, once damned, has entered there will no longer go out to salvation. They cry out in torments, wretched in anguish, placed in everlasting horror, saying: “What does our pride profit us now, our riches, honors, dignities, luxury, gluttony, and all past fleshly pleasures? What do they profit us now, damned forever? Behold, all things have passed like a shadow, and everything has vanished like the brief dream of a single night. But we have been assigned to eternal torments, in which we know most certainly that there is no redemption.”

In hell, as Augustine bears witness, even if there will be the sting of repentance, nevertheless there will be no correction of the will in the damned; by them iniquity will be blamed in such a way that justice [unclear] can in no way be loved or desired by them. There then the devouring [unclear] of hell...

208

How sin is to be fled.

The flame burns those whom carnal pleasure now defiles; and each person is burned all the more in torments, the more he takes delight here in the flesh against God. In hell, as Gregory bears witness, there will be intolerable cold, inextinguishable fire, the immortal worm of conscience, unbearable stench, palpable darkness, immeasurable pains, scourges of those who strike without intermission, the dreadful sight of demons, confusion over crimes committed, and despair of all good things. But of all the punishments in hell, by far the gravest must be judged to be this: that those damned ones are forever deprived of the vision of eternal light.

Hence the most blessed bishop John Chrysostom says: “Gehenna is an intolerable thing, and all men shrink from it. For who does not know that the punishment of hell is very dreadful? Yet if someone should set down a thousand, indeed ten thousand gehennas, all that he says is nothing in comparison with this: for a soul hated by Christ to be driven away from the glory of the saints, and to hear that terrible voice from the mouth of the Judge of all: ‘Depart from me, you workers of iniquity, for I do not know you’; and: ‘Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for you and for the devil.’”

O voice by far the most terrible of all terrible things; O sentence to be feared, and exceedingly dreadful to all mortals: to be hated by Christ for one’s deserts, to be reproached by the Judge, to be separated from the fellowship of glory, and to retain no further hope of recovery. Think now, brothers, on the punishments of the wicked that most certainly will come; and compare all the torments of this passing age, and every imaginable torture of this world, with those everlasting punishments of the damned, and they will be as nothing compared with something else, imagination compared with truth, a dream compared with waking. You will easily overcome the temptations of the flesh and the law of sin if you continually keep the thought of these things in memory.

O eternity, what an inconceivable span of time; an age without end, a world without time. Blessed is he who now foresees in time how he may fare well in eternity after this very brief life.

The fourth thing that can draw a person back from sin is to keep continual remembrance in the heart of future and everlasting happiness. Truly, the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which will be revealed in the saints, where there will be no discord, no disharmony at all, but the highest peace of all and the everlasting concord of the rejoicing saints. In the heavenly blessedness of the saints there is true joy without sadness, peace without discord, goodness without malice, gladness without end, light without darkness, everlasting life without pain. There is sweetness without bitterness, rest without labor, praise without blame, love without fault, brightness without cloud, satiety without disgust. Eternity remains without weariness; goodness abounds without defect; happiness continues without misery. For where God is all in all, perfect and full joy will be present to everyone. There the soul, or holy mind, is joined to its beginning through love; the intellect is perfectly enlightened for the knowledge of the highest good;

and from these two there is poured into the exultant the enjoyment of eternal happiness.

To know God in the kingdom of eternity and to love him is to possess, by enjoyment, the very glory of happiness. For man was created for this: that he should understand God his creator as the supreme good; that, understanding him, he should love him above all things; and that, loving him, he should enjoy and possess him forever. This is the end of the monastic institution; this is the destination of the Christian faith: that God, whom we now know through faith and love with all our heart through works of charity, we may, in the blessed life, understand perfectly and have as the everlasting object of our enjoyment.

For the attainment of this eternal happiness, most beloved brothers, all good things must be done even with the greatest labor, and all adversities must be endured with the greatest patience, since the very brief exercise of virtue brings forth for us an eternal reward. Hear what holy Bishop John says on these matters: If every day, he says, it were necessary for us to endure torments, indeed if we had to tolerate even gehenna itself for a short time, so that we might see Christ reigning in eternal glory and be joined forever to the number of his saints, would it not, by equal reasoning, be fitting to endure everything sorrowful that can befall us, so that we may deserve to possess the glory of so great a good? But one does not arrive at the supreme good except through the greatest labors; for, as the Lord says in the holy Gospel, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.

The fifth thing that ought to draw a man back from sin is to consider the dignity of the human condition, which, by the natural guidance of reason, detests vice and loves the good of virtue. Every man who lives according to the command of reason is a lover of virtue; but he who, becoming filthy in the dung of vices, rolls about in it, conducts himself as a beast, not as a man. But for you, my brothers, vices must especially be detested and virtues loved, since you have despised the world for this reason: that in the monastery you might lead a life estranged from sins and adorned with holy virtues.

Virtues, therefore, are to be cultivated by you. I say virtues are to be cultivated, not images of virtues; not with incense, not with sacrifice, but with love and with the purpose of a wholly upright will. For to cultivate virtues is nothing other than to embrace them in the soul and, for the love of God, to keep them inviolate even to death. For, as Lactantius says, the whole duty of virtue is not to sin; and therefore there is no true virtue except that which, through faith in Christ, tends toward that end where the supreme good of man is, than which nothing better can exist. But he is not virtuous who does not love God, since charity is the sum of all virtues. Therefore, if you love God with all your heart above all things, you are truly virtuous. Thus there is one virtue and one way of the good, by which, through faith and love of Jesus Christ, one arrives at the kingdom. He who truly loves God does not sin, because of his love of virtue.

Consider your dignity, my brothers, and flee sin; for everyone who is swollen with pride, who is defiled by lust, who is infected by the other plagues of the soul, does not live as a man, but ...

How sin is to be fled.

He is confounded in himself and goes forward into the destruction of eternal death. For the more one falls into sin, the farther he withdraws from God, and the nearer he approaches hell. Since, however, all men naturally desire the good, it is most shameful to love sin, because every sinner abandons the good and turns himself to evil.

Sixth, it strongly draws the mind back from sin if it remains always occupied, by habit, in meditation on the Lord’s Passion. For who will be able to devote himself to the pleasures of the flesh, if he has thought of Jesus Christ, the ruler of the world, hanging for him on the cross? The death of Christ freed the world from perpetual death; whoever carries this benefit with him in memory will easily abstain from every crime of vice.

Finally, if anyone considers with the whole attention of his mind that God is present to him in every place, and knows and understands all things, he will without doubt always abhor every sin. For God is everywhere with us: not only present, but truly inward and most present. No secret is hidden from him; nothing remains concealed from him, but everything lies open and manifest to him. He searches the hearts of all; he knows the most secret thoughts, he who alone has true knowledge of all things. For what mortal dares to sin in the presence of such majesty, which he believes sees all things, without the greatest shame, if he considers who and how great he is who sees?

Therefore, whenever an evil thought troubles the mind, whenever the disordered movements of the flesh disturb the soul, think of the Lord God, the avenger of evils, as present; recall to memory the bitterness of the Passion of Jesus Christ; devoutly implore the help of heavenly grace. Harder than stone is the man whom these things, if carefully considered, cannot call back from the intention of sinning.

Seventh, what recalls the mind of a studious monk from the desire of sinning is that by continual reading he should go through the accounts of the martyrs’ sufferings. Indeed, whoever often recalls to memory the invincible constancy of the holy martyrs of Christ cannot fail to become stronger and more robust in resisting sins. For this reason the brave deeds of the saints were committed to writing: so that, whenever we who are weak read such things, we may rise up to imitate those who have gone before.

Do not pay regard, brothers, to those who, with proud rashness, deny faith to the histories of the saints, and think that the glorious things narrated about the most blessed friends of Christ are fables. For the virtues and good things which they do not find in themselves, they disdain to believe that the saints of God possessed. For there are many, and especially among those who think themselves great because of their learning, who too rashly reject the histories of the holy fathers; and since they themselves cannot enter upon the arduous path of virtue, with windy loquacity they invent that no one, or only a rare few, could have done so. Whatever is read before them from the lives of the saints, whether arduous or great, they cry out that it is invented and fabulous; and, being placed as they themselves are in the darkness of vices, they suppose that those whose histories they mock lived in the same way before them. A monk

But the prudent and devout man is not moved by the sloth of the proud, since he proves and understands that a certain effective power of exhortation lies in the histories of the saints. For, to confess meanwhile what is true about myself, I am stirred more to devotion of inward fervor by the life of one saint than by many curious sermons, because, as the most holy Pope Leo says, examples are stronger than words, and it is more to teach by deed than by voice.

But just as not all things please everyone, so not all things are suited to everyone. We advise each person to read more often and more eagerly that by whose reading his mind is stirred to greater progress.

The eighth thing that restrains a man from sin is charity, concerning which the holy Apostle says: Charity is patient, is kind; it does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek the things that are its own, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices together with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails.

He who loves God flees sin; but he who is the slave of crimes certainly does not love God. The lover of God does not commit sin, and he who truly loves his Lord and always beholds him as present does not work iniquity. God is the highest and unchangeable good; out of love for him sin must both be fled and detested, because he who fears to sin only from fear of punishments does not rise to the rewards of charity. For a slave does not sin from fear of blows; but a son withdraws from evil out of love for his parent, lest he offend his father’s heart.

Let us beware of sin, my brothers, and with as much purity of soul as we can let us live in the sight of the Lord, because just as deadly poison, when taken, kills the body, so sin kills the soul of the offender. Hence the wise man admonishes us in Ecclesiasticus, saying: Flee sins as from the face of a serpent, because if you approach them, they will take hold of you. The teeth of a lion are the teeth of sin, killing the souls of men. Like a two-edged sword is the iniquity of man; for its wounds there is no healing. In Ezekiel too it is said: The soul that has sinned, that soul shall die.

With all care we must always keep watch, so that we may not, through the mediation of sin, be separated from the Lord. Nothing is stronger than perfect charity toward God for overcoming every sin, because, as the most holy evangelist John says, everyone who is born of God does not commit sin; but he who sins does not imitate God, but the devil, the reward of sin. Let us love God, and sin will not rule in us; let us love Christ, and we shall do nothing contrary to our salvation. Nothing is better, nothing stronger against sin, nothing safer, than to love God, who first loved us and washed us from all sins in the blood of his only-begotten Son.

God is to be loved by us with our whole soul for many reasons. For we are bound to God, and we are obliged to love him with all the powers of our heart for many reasons. First, indeed, God must be loved by us above all, for no other reason than for his own sake, who is the highest and [unclear].

How Sin Is to Be Fled.

Since he is good, in him alone are the soul’s rest and salvation; without him there is no salvation, no rest, no blessedness, no happiness, neither in heaven nor on earth. For since God is the cause, maker, and beginning of all things, he alone is the object of the soul’s blessedness; to his everlasting enjoyment the soul comes only through charity, and to the love of him it comes only through purity of mind.

Therefore, since God is the soul’s one and highest good, he is to be loved by us for his own sake with all our strength. Outside God there is nothing good, nothing holy, nothing that can gladden the soul forever. For God alone is the center of the soul’s blessedness.

Second, we are commanded to love the Lord our God because he deigns to show himself our most loving father. For thus he taught us to pray: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Truly God is the father of us all: he created us, nourishes all, feeds all, and preserves us in being, lest we perish. There has never been any father on earth so indulgent that he loved his only-begotten son with so great a charity as God almighty, our father, loves, cherishes, guides, and follows us with loving affection. And therefore we are bound to love him with a pure heart above all things, for he gives us both being and life. He indeed is our father; and Adam, who was created first of all men, did not know us.

Third, we ought to love God above all things because of likeness, since man was made in God’s image, following his creator by a certain likeness in his intellect. But God is perfect, infinite, and everlasting intellect; and our intellect, sharing in his goodness through grace, is made blessed in him who created all things. For although there is no comparison between God and man, nevertheless there is, from the nobility of its condition, a likeness of dignity not to be despised between the rational soul itself and its principle. For the Prophet says: I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High. The Lord God also said in the beginning: Let us make man to our image and likeness. Great is the condescension of divine loving-kindness toward our race, which it befits us at all times to remember with a pure mind of charitable reverence.

Fourth, we ought to love our God above all things because of his inestimable generosity, for we acknowledge that he has bestowed such great benefits on us though we did not deserve them. When we did not exist, he first, by his goodness, established us in being, and ordained us to a share in his glory, which will never end. For Scripture says this of the nobility of man: Thou hast made him a little less than the angels; with glory and honor thou hast crowned him; and thou hast set him over the works of thy hands.

Do you wish to know, brothers, in what respect man is less than the angel? Attend diligently to what we say. Two intellects were created from the beginning, the angelic and the human. The angelic intellect, immediately from the beginning of its creation, was made full and perfect in the act of all knowable things, and by nature knew all things that it had to know, and

Sermon V.

...comprehends; but the human intellect at first consists only in potency toward all knowable things, knowing nothing, and in the end, through many actions, at last acquires knowledge of all things, like the angelic intellect. For the perfect consummation of nature, which is present in the angelic intellect from the beginning, will be given to the human intellect at the end. Hence it is clear that between these two created intellects there is only this difference: the angelic intellect is what it can be, while the human intellect is to receive the likeness of angelic perfection at the end, that is, after bodily death.

For when the angelic intellect was first created, without any action of its own, immovably, substantially, and by nature, it came forth full of all knowledge and perfect. And among the angels, those who adhere by love to their beginning, namely God, have been confirmed in eternal happiness; but those who, glorying in themselves, withdrew in affection from God, are forever wretched and unhappy. The human intellect, however, since it was created in the beginning in ignorance and privation of all things, must necessarily come at last, by action, motion, and art, to the knowledge of things set before it.

As long as we are in the body and are pilgrims away from the Lord, our intellect, because of its excessive commerce with the body, is confused as though placed in the darkness of ignorance, and is by no means illumined with perfect knowledge of future things. But after the soul has been separated from the body, then the intellect will rejoice in angelic perfection. Therefore we differ from the angels only insofar as we share in bodily impurity.

Fifth, God must be loved by us above all, because he first loved us and washed us from our sins in the blood of his only-begotten Son. The Creator supremely loves his creature, whom he made from nothing; it is fitting that the creature itself should supremely love its Creator, by whose goodness it was brought into being. God loves us with the greatest charity, than which no greater can be spoken or thought, and he loves us so much that he neither ought nor could love us more; for in God all things are perfect, and in the unchangeable one there is no capacity for change.

Now consider, my brothers, with what fervor of mind and with what desire of heart a man ought to love his God, by whom he is loved even without merits with the highest degree of love. Let us stretch our soul toward love of him above all things, as much as we can; for he is worthy to be loved by us with all our strength. For however much we may love God who loves us, we shall nevertheless in no way reach that measure by which he loves us. For he, as we have said, loves us supremely, and his love toward us cannot increase further, since it is certain that he loves his creature most perfectly. But however much we have loved him, we can always make further progress in loving and love more ardently until death.

O we who are weak, we who are lukewarm, we who are bound over to a muddy prison: what shall we repay to so great a lover, who surpasses us in loving by infinite degrees, since there is no comparison between the thing made and its maker?

The sixth thing, which should stir us to the love of God,

It is the regard of his supreme kindness toward us: that, after leaving so many thousands of people throughout the wide world in error, he mercifully called us in Europe, with a few others, to the knowledge of the Christian faith. Of all his benefits after the death of Christ, I think this is the chief: that he made us Christians in the faith. For outside the faith of Christ no one will be saved, whether Christ is proclaimed to him or whether he is utterly unknown to him. How many kingdoms today in Asia and Africa, how many peoples, how many islands of the sea, have no knowledge of Christ and no faith, but all their religion is in error and without any merit for salvation, even if some outside Christianity seem to adore and worship one God? For Christ is the savior of faithful souls; whoever has not believed in him is already judged, and without doubt will be condemned. Therefore we shall never be able to render to God worthy acts of thanksgiving, because he ordained that we should be born, so to speak, in the Catholic faith, and by the blood of his only-begotten Son he freed us from the destruction of death. Let us therefore be mindful of so great a benefit, and take care to live in such a way that we are not judged for ingratitude. Let us bless God the Father at all times, who has poured out the gifts of the Holy Spirit upon us and has not permitted us to be born removed from the unity of Catholic unity.

The seventh thing believed able to produce the love of God in our hearts is considered in the promise of everlasting happiness. For if we consider how great are the good things in heaven that he has promised he will give us, his love will deservedly burn sweetly in our hearts. He has promised his whole self to us as a reward: he alone is the highest and utterly unchangeable good; and although he is indivisible, he offers himself to be enjoyed by all in such a way that nevertheless he is possessed whole by each one. He loves all by whom he is loved, and he loves each one by whom he is possessed. The more, then, we love God now with a pure mind, the more reward we shall receive there.

On the Knowledge of Spiritual Grace. Sermon VI.

The holy apostle of Christ, John, teaches us that not every spirit is always to be believed, but that impulses must be carefully examined to see whether they are from God, who is the true light, lest perhaps something rise up against us from the side of darkness. For our adversary, since he is crafty, never sleeps, but devises a thousand ways by which he may catch us unawares. Yet he attacks those already making progress in one way, and deals in another way with those who are still living in the sluggishness of negligence. The more we have advanced in God’s commandments, the more necessary it is that we keep watch against the devil lying in wait for us. The demon pursues with importunity those who try to flee, and rages with envy against those who desire to please God with love. Lurking in secret under the appearance of good, he is accustomed to attack those who do not know him, whom he knows he cannot overcome in open conflict. He is accustomed to [unclear] many things.

to those who are deficient and as yet less firmly grounded in the fear of God, by which he generally tries, under the appearance of good, to overthrow unwary minds. Against his snares the best remedy is for a monk to submit all the thoughts of his heart to the examination of the elders. For demons hate the public light, and are ashamed that the thoughts of the young which they suggest should come to the knowledge of spiritual elders.

Therefore, whoever among you thinks that he stands in good, let him always be careful not to fall through the devil’s overthrowing him. There are some among you, young both in years and in conversion, who consent to their sensual inclinations more than is fitting; demons mock such men in various ways, as though under the appearance of good. They seek holiness without merit; they desire to have merit without the practice of the necessary virtues. They seem to themselves great before God in devotion, and exceptional, yet in their animal passions they have not been mortified.

You are mistaken, O wretched men, and you shamefully deceive yourselves, when you think of building the tower of holiness without the foundation of most humble subjection and obedience. First the disordered desires of sensuality must be mortified; the passions of the animal man must be restrained: anger, murmuring, the spite of indignation, and all impatience. For as long as vices rule over you, whatever gifts of private singularity you offer are not pleasing to God. All things are vain where there is not a pure conscience.

The conduct of a young monk is suspect to us, however devout it may seem to be, if the humility of voluntary subjection does not commend it. For a monk without humility and obedience cannot be good, even if he hunts for holiness every day by fasting and prayer. The devil deceives many in the hiddenness of elation and pride, whom he allows continually to keep vigil, fast, and pray. For just as no works are pleasing to God without humility and charity, so the fasting, vigils, prayers, and studies of monks without these are not fearsome to the devil.

The devil is not moved by anything that does not torment him. He does not greatly value the vigils of the self-exalted, nor does he attend to the fasting of the swollen with pride, nor does he fear the prayers of the proud. But if he finds you humble; if in all things you obey the commands of the elders cheerfully; if he sees you doing great things and thinking humble things about yourself; if he perceives the charity of God and neighbor burning in you, then surely he is stirred against you, because his envy is tormented by your virtues. He turns against you all the weapons of his cunning that he can, and with all his strength tries to overturn your purpose of holiness.

For nothing displeases demons more in a monk; nothing torments them more violently than if, for the love of God, he has truly humbled himself in all things and has always, with a cheerful spirit, kept the discipline of the monastic way of life under the guardianship of obedience. You must beware the impulses of demons, you who think yourselves to be something great without the merit of true virtues. I see you unwilling toward the commands of the elders, impatient and murmuring under correction, rather quick to rebuke another’s life, but in [unclear].

and are very slow to consider their own defects. These are very sure signs of demonic prompting, and manifest indications of contempt for necessary mortification and of self-will.

You believe yourselves to be perfect and holy cultivators of great religion and inward devotion, yet you do not regard fraternal charity or true humility as necessary in yourselves. You seek sensible devotion in prayers, and with tearful eyes you already think yourselves friends of God. But what then? Do tears in prayers make a man holy, when he prays with a certain exaltation of mind and without true humility? God gives tears; the soul, struck by adversities, gives them; the devil too, deceiver of the proud, gives them. God makes the mind humbled in true charity fruitful, like a meadow, with sweet tears; nature moves the weeping person in adversity; the devil pours streams of water upon the proud under the likeness of devotion.

Humility is the one virtue which, in the breadth of charity, makes the hearts of men truly devout. Whatever you may do in your singularity profits you nothing, O monk, if you do not have true humility with the fervor of twofold charity. For to rise before others for the night praises, to say long prayers in private beyond the custom of the order, to continue a fast beyond what the rule has established while others lawfully eat, to remain in secret while the rest go out to the common labor: two things make these meritorious, and if they are lacking, all such acts will be wholly fruitless. Indeed, whatever works of a monk charity and humble obedience have not commended will be judged empty of merit before God and will lack reward.

But you who with haughty brow despise the precepts of your elders, who do not do what they command but what pleases you by your own rashness, who prefer your own inventions to the holy common exercises of the order, are still far removed from the way of life of the saints. It is not lawful for you by your own rashness to abandon the things that belong to monastic institution, and to put new and vain things that please you before necessary things. Whatever work you do is displeasing to God if you despise that to which you are bound. The inspiration of divine grace teaches humility, persuades obedience, and follows true charity in all things; it keeps the commandment, admits no pride, despises no one, but pursues the perpetual integrity of regular discipline.

But the prompting of the devil, under the appearance of good, cunningly trips up the unwary monk and makes him subject in all things to his own judgment. For everything that pertains to preserving monastic integrity he falsely claims has been badly instituted, is contrary to him, and for that reason must be set after his own pursuits. But so that you may learn wisely to distinguish the grace of God from the promptings of the ancient enemy, mark what we say. First, then, whoever thinks himself inspired by the grace of God should carefully observe whether day by day he becomes purer in conscience as the tinder of sin decreases. For wherever the Spirit of God has poured out the gift of heavenly grace,

Sermon VI.

all inclination to sin at once withdraws. But if horror of sinning has not invaded the mind, it is certainly clear that the prompting of the devil has taken possession of the man. For as soon as the Holy Spirit has entered a man’s mind, he either lessens every blaze of vices or extinguishes it entirely. Therefore let each one of you diligently examine himself and consider by whose prompting he is moved. For the prompting of God is accustomed to lessen sin, but that of the ancient enemy to increase it. Hence, in those who are led by the Spirit of God, sin is daily diminished; but those who follow the prompting of the devil are rarely truly amended.

The second sign of the divine prompting is recognized from the evidence of virtues, because the grace of the Holy Spirit always works great virtues in a man. Therefore, when you feel yourself advancing daily in the love of God and in good works; when you experience in yourself that the habit of sinning and all vices are prevailing less from day to day, you ought humbly to acknowledge that the grace of God is present. For the love of God, which grace brings, is never idle, but is always usefully occupied in good works, because it both covers the multitude of sins and, by exercising the soul in virtues, does not permit it to sin. For the grace of God cannot stand together with sins, and it is not accustomed to be in a man without the operation of virtues.

The third sign of the Spirit of God is shown in a man when the mind does not waver in its purpose of holiness, but, growing stronger from day to day, is more firmly strengthened. For there are many who, touched by a momentary compunction, sometimes receive the first two signs, but, despising perseverance, do not reach the third. Without perseverance, however, there is no reward for a good work, as the Lord says in the holy Gospel: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

The devil knows how to feign absence for a short time, and to dissemble toward one advancing according to the two aforesaid signs of the Spirit of God, as though he did not know him or feared him. Then, bursting forth from his ambushes, he attacks the unwary devout man, and, casting the wretched man down into the former pit of negligence, wounds him more severely. O evil habits, what a heavy yoke, what unjust and dreadful dominion, and rarely to be ended before death. Let anyone whom a long habit of sin binds fear and tremble. For nothing is more difficult than to conquer an evil habit strengthened over a long time. Hence Solomon says in Proverbs: “A young man according to his way, even when he has grown old, will not depart from it.” Nevertheless, if we do not violently conquer an evil habit, we shall always find it harder and less conquerable.

The fourth sign of the presence of the Spirit of God is rightly added to perseverance in good, because, when the affection has been purified, the mind is enlightened by grace into the knowledge of the divine light. For this is the anointing of the Holy Spirit, which no one understands except the one who receives it; this is the fullness of heavenly doctrine, which excludes both vices and errors from minds. Every chaste lover of the Christian religion who [unclear] this sign of heavenly...

On the recognition of spiritual grace.

If he has received the blessing, he understands, more than before and above others, what the merits of true charity are, and likewise the exercises of piety. The state of the mind is also set in the uprightness of heavenly desire, and is enlightened toward the true knowledge of future blessedness. It has this familiar indication as a sign of attained truth: because the mind, when God enlightens it, begins to understand the loftiest things in the Holy Scriptures and beyond them; and the more it understands, the more deeply it strives to humble itself. For the Holy Spirit joins humility to his gifts; and if humility has been cast away, it is already plainly evident that the Spirit has withdrawn.

The fifth sign of God’s grace is received if the whole mind of a man is resigned to God’s will, if daily it is kindled in love for him through desire, if the conscience, so far as human weakness permits, is preserved in all purity. For the love of God, through the received grace of the Holy Spirit, is at once born in the mind, and is strengthened daily by good works and spiritual exercises; it shudders at sin, detests it, and flees from it, and admits nothing except what is pure, holy, and deifying. Wherever this sign is present, there will be no sin. If sin is present, the sign was not true.

Let those receive the sixth sign of divine prompting who are always growing stronger in soul toward what is better. For the Spirit of God makes the mind of the man whom he inhabits by his grace patient and willing to endure injuries, and renders it most ready to do good. Whoever among you thinks that he is being moved by a divine impulse, whoever thinks that he is walking in the way of uprightness, let him examine his conscience, whether for the love of Christ he becomes daily more ready to endure injuries; whether, that is, he rejoices in tribulation, and whether the devotion of his soul grows more in adversities than in prosperity. But if he finds himself unwilling and impatient in enduring injuries, he easily recognizes how far he is placed from the grace of perfection. For charity, the gift of the Holy Spirit, is patient and kind.

Those receive the seventh indication of spiritual grace who for the love of Christ despise all the consolations of the present life. The soul that has God present within itself through love despises all comforts of the flesh, and longs to come to its Lord through hard and rough ways. It does not love the riches of this world; it rejects passing honors and dignities; it strongly despises the pleasures of the flesh. It meditates always on the law of the Lord, and never forgets the most bitter passion of Jesus Christ. Which of you, brothers, does these things? Who detests all the little consolations of this age? Who thinks of nothing, seeks nothing, desires nothing except the charity of God? Whoever has obtained this sign of the presence of the Holy Spirit, if he perseveres to the end of life, will be saved.

We receive the eighth indication of a good course, and the true sign of the presence of the Holy Spirit, when in all things we humbly conform our will to the divine ordinances. This degree of spiritual progress frees the monk from all cares.

separates him from the world and calls him wholly inward. For his will is subjected to the divine will with the affection of a peaceful mind, and is set far apart from all desires that war against the spirit. Whoever has received this gift of the grace of the Holy Spirit should first give thanks with humility, and should not vainly exalt himself because of the gift; rather, the more he has advanced, the more he should learn to humble himself in all things.

Often, however, a man deserves to lose God’s grace when he neglects to preserve it in the vessel of true humility. Therefore almighty God sometimes withdraws the grace of sensible devotion for a short time from those who are advancing, so that humility may remain in the mind and the fervor of desire to seek further may burn more intensely. But since there are many causes in human beings for which the grace of God is sometimes withdrawn, it was worth the effort to state them in order.

First, then, the grace of God is withdrawn from a man because of sin, when the conscience is stained by the foulness of vices. For our God, as Scripture says, is jealous: either he alone is loved, or he is not loved together with any companion. Therefore, as often as the mind turns back, either upon itself or upon some other thing, with disordered desire, it is estranged and removed from its source, which is God. Hence it deserves to lose the grace it had, because by consenting to sin it was unwilling to keep it inviolate. For this reason the holy apostle of Christ, Paul, exhorts us not to receive the grace of God in vain; and it is indeed received uselessly and in vain when the mind of the recipient is defiled by the filth of vices.

The little vessel into which we receive God’s grace is our conscience. When it is cleansed from vices and adorned with holy virtues, it becomes a worthy dwelling place of the Holy Spirit and produces great progress in us. But if the little vessel of our conscience has been befouled by the corruption of sin, at once the Spirit of God departs with all the gifts of grace. Is not our Lord Jesus Christ the lover and faithful bridegroom of the soul, which he purchased for himself by the shedding of his own blood? With what face, with what rashness, O man, can you despise so great a lover and your savior, and love anything else in this world? God loves you supremely: he is your creator, and by his death he freed you from everlasting destruction. What will you repay him, O mortal man, from whom you have received such great benefits? He asks nothing of you, seeks nothing, demands nothing, except gratitude, love, and charity. Guard the innocence and purity of your conscience, lest you lose the prompting of grace.

The second cause for which grace is withdrawn from a man is called the pride of ingratitude. For God, as Scripture testifies, resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. By the just judgment of God, the grace of the Holy Spirit is lost whenever the one who has it is lifted up into pride. For everyone who humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled. Hence almighty God again says: Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, if not upon the humble and quiet man, and upon him who trembles at my words?

my brothers? The more each humbles himself in true purity of conscience for Christ’s love, the more fit he will be to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit. But whenever the mind is raised up in pride, the spirit of devotion is deservedly taken away, as from an unclean little vessel.

Therefore, my brothers, let no one be proud of the grace of the Holy Spirit which he has received; let no one vainly exalt himself, because, unless we are humble, we shall in no way be able to share in the mercies of the Lord. For, as the sacred lover of Christ, Paul, says: he who thinks himself to be something, when he is nothing, deceives himself.

Third, the grace of devotion is withdrawn from a man because of sloth and acedia, when the mind is little exercised in good works. For, as Scripture says, idleness is the enemy of the soul, and everyone who pursues leisure will be in want. For the wise man says: Desires kill the sluggard, for his hands have refused to work at all. Just as fire is extinguished without fuel, so the spirit of devotion, without the continual exercise of charity, fades away and grows thin.

Therefore let no one presume upon his own strength in this life; let no one trust securely in his former way of life, because, so long as someone can become better from worse, he can also become worse from better. For our whole life upon earth is a trial, in which, if we do not advance in good, we fail; and there, as holy Pope Leo says, we fall into the danger of failing where we turn back from the desire to make progress. Therefore flee acedia, and always keep watch in good works. Consider what happened to the slothful servant, who hid in a napkin his master’s money, which he had received for trading. Trade, I beg you, while there is time; as long as you live, always be occupied in good pursuits.

Fourth, the grace of devotion is very often withdrawn from those who, placed under obedience, follow their own will. For the monk who loves his own will most justly loses the grace of God. But he who, for God’s sake, humbly subjects himself in all things to the obedience of his shepherd, who despises the will of his own heart, is filled with various gifts of spiritual grace and enlightened by the light of inward fervor. We can offer nothing more precious or acceptable to God than if, for love of him, we deny our own will. Finally, the very profession of monastic discipline lays upon us, by the necessity of salvation, the duty of despising our own will and humbly submitting to him who has been set over us. Therefore the monk who follows the impulse of his own will is judged as an unclean vessel and unworthy of spiritual grace. Hence the grace of God is deservedly withdrawn from the monk of self-will, who, living otherwise than he promised, lies to the Lord.

Fifth, the grace of devotion is withdrawn from the monk who thinks that he has it by his own merits. He does not understand that sin dwells in him; if he has received anything good, he ascribes it to his own merits. Against this sluggishness of mind the holy prophet said to the Lord: Lord, by your will you gave strength to my beauty.

because it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. You turned your face away from me, and I was troubled. For no one is devout by his own merits; no one is holy by his own powers. Let us recognize that all the causes of the withdrawal of God’s grace which we have mentioned belong to our weakness.

But as regards those who are already walking in the way of perfection, another explanation is given, so long as they persevere. For God’s grace is never withdrawn from them, although the sensible fervor of compunction is sometimes taken away for a time. And let us set out in order the causes of this taking away.

First, Almighty God sometimes withdraws from his lovers for a time the grace of sensible devotion, so that, while he seems not to be present when called upon, the desire of inward love may grow. All who have felt the fire of divine love, and who are true imitators of the holy fathers, know this alternation of holy ardor. For whenever the bridegroom withdraws from the bride, the desire of the lover grows. And while she seeks in burning longing the one whom she loves, she groans from the desire of love.

Second, this grace is withdrawn from the devout for a time lest frailty be lifted up into pride. When we lose the grace of compunction even against our will, we judge, by humble examination, our weakness, which can do nothing of itself. Therefore, in order that the devout worshipers of God may remain humble in their exaltation, they must recognize their own frailty.

The third cause concerns merit: because to seek inward consolations belongs not to the strong, but to the weak. The Lord must be served freely, because he is good; but those who seek sensible sweetness in their devotion are too delicate, and seek the Lord Jesus for little consolations. The Lord must be loved manfully, and all womanish and soft affections must be driven far from the soul. Therefore, so that the Lord may increase merit for his worshipers in holy compunction, he sometimes denies them, when they ask, the grace of sensible devotion. But lest, affected by the bitterness of weariness, they grow wholly sluggish in their purpose of holiness, the consoler of the sorrowful does not withdraw far, but remains nearby. He suddenly returns to his friend; and the one whom he had seemed for a time to leave in sadness, he consoles with the sweetness of his spiritual presence.

We join to these a fourth cause, by which we are warned to walk more cautiously. For if we fear losing the grace of compunction, let us learn to guard more diligently what we have received. For a rare and precious treasure, the more it is loved, the more diligently it is guarded by its possessor. Therefore the monk who has deserved to receive from the Lord the grace of devotion must keep watch with the utmost care, lest he lose it through his own negligence.

And so that you may know how you ought to preserve the granted grace of compunction, lest it perish, the order of what is to be said makes it clear to you. First, he who does not wish to lose the grace of inward compunction granted to him strives, as far as he can, to keep himself clean and pure from every sin. Let him beware not only of mortal and dreadful crimes, but also of small sins, which are called venial, because,

222

On knowledge of spiritual grace.

He who despises the smallest things gradually falls away; and he who does not beware of many small things often, by habit, makes one great thing. The second caution necessary for the preservation of grace is said to be this: that all boasting be avoided. If you have merited to receive from the Lord the gift of compunction, strive, as far as lies in you, to hide it humbly. For the grace of the Holy Spirit flees publicity and detests every heart proud with boasting. For, as blessed Gregory says, he desires to be robbed who carries his treasure in public.

Third, if you do not wish to lose the grace of inward compunction, strive to love the quiet of solitude. For divine Scripture says: Upon whom shall my spirit rest, if not upon the humble and quiet? And again it says elsewhere: In silence and in hope shall your strength be. For the grace of inward compunction is quickly lost when the secrecy of solitude is not loved. Let the monk, therefore, learn gladly to remain with himself in his cell, if he wishes to possess the grace of God.

Fourth, one must take the greatest care not to despise in one’s heart any person, however evil; for the grace of compunction is withdrawn by the just judgment of God whenever one does not beware of rash judgment of one’s neighbor. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned.

Fifth, the monk who does not wish to lose the grace of inward devotion should strive to exercise himself in the practice of all the virtues. Let him always keep watch in the fear of the Lord, always occupy himself in the exercise of divine love; let him be constantly diligent in good works, and, as far as he is able, devoted at all times to the memory of the Lord’s Passion. For intent meditation on Christ’s Passion strengthens a person against all vices and preserves the grace of compunction.

Sixth, be constant in holy prayers, because he who interrupts the practice of prayer is not able to guard the grace of compunction. For the Savior says in the holy Gospel: Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation. The help of the Lord is near to those who call upon him; but he who neglects to pray loses grace.

But if you have lost the grace of devotion in any way, you will quickly recover it by the following six remedies. First, consider that without the grace of God you cannot make progress toward salvation, but that in all the good things you are about to do you have the greatest need of his mercy. Recognize, therefore, that you are unworthy of the grace of God for doing good; but although you know yourself unworthy because of the multitude of your sins, nevertheless call upon him, because he is near; and see that all the time granted to you as free from the common exercises of the brothers is spent usefully and fruitfully. The grace of God is necessary for you in doing good; it is acquired by the breadth of charity, guarded by humility, and recovered by the practice of saving repentance. The Lord is with you as long as you are with him in good will. But in order that you may be able to recover the lost grace of devotion, you must submit yourself to God in true humility.

Second, for the recovery of grace...

Sermon VI.

For the recovery of lost compunction it seems necessary that you in no way lift yourself up against the Lord, but conform your will in all things to the divine ordinance. “That his will be done,” we say in the Lord’s Prayer; it is fitting that in mind and in the affection of the will we should always freely agree with that very prayer.

Third, whoever desires to recover the lost grace of devotion must firmly despise every pleasure of this world for the love of God. For it cannot happen that one should receive the spirit of inward compunction while he opens the dwelling-place of his heart to earthly joys and pleasures. Therefore you must cast away every consolation of the present life, if you desire to have the spirit of divine love with its gifts.

Fourth, you are commanded to withdraw yourself perpetually from the vain cares and occupations of this world, and to occupy your mind delightfully at all times in the service of God. For, as the Lord says, no one can serve God and mammon; but whoever desires to serve the Lord in truth of heart must despise all the occupations of the world.

Fifth, we advise you to remember always to occupy your heart in meditation on the passion of Christ, since there is no shorter way to recover the grace of compunction, nor any manner of prayer more effective for obtaining from the Lord whatever we ask.

Sixth, you should strive daily to cleanse your conscience through true penitence; and whenever you have fallen into any fault, immediately come to your senses again through contrition. If you take care to observe these things with a good will, by God’s mercy you will recover the lost grace of compunction.

On the Nine Steps of Ascent. Sermon VII.

We describe for you, dearly beloved brothers, a ladder of nine steps, by which the human spirit ascends into heaven. And although one step is higher than another, nevertheless all of them, each and every one, direct us toward the kingdom of God, and they distinguish the merits of those ascending according to their merits. Therefore attend diligently to what we are about to say, and consider how much you have advanced in spiritual progress.

All, as many as have reached the kingdom of God, have ascended by the steps of this ladder. And the more anyone has advanced in the love of God, the higher he has already ascended. The first step is nearest to hell, and farther removed from the height of the heavenly fatherland. For people placed on it begin to withdraw from vices and to make progress in the fear of God; neglecting venial sins, they withdraw from mortal ones. Their minds, indeed, longing for the practice of virtues, flee the more serious sins; but, weighed down by the weakness of evil habit, they pay no heed to the smallest ones. Hence they more often fall through frailty into the pit of mortal sin, because they have not guarded against venial sins as occasions of graver ones. For no sin is so small that it does not become greater when neglected. For even if we cannot wholly guard against venial sins, nevertheless with all our strength we must strive that they not multiply in [unclear].

224

On the nine degrees of ascent.

We must attend to ourselves. But those who, by the Lord’s mercy, daily make progress toward better things in this degree fall into sin more rarely. Yet whenever they have fallen, so often do they rise again through repentance. Still, their state is close to danger, because just as a garment often torn is at last rendered useless, so a person who slips by sinning more frequently is often smothered by evil habit. Yet if any from this degree depart this life in the Lord’s mercies, they will be saved, but not without the very grievous pains of purgatory. We must therefore hasten to higher things, so that not only mortal sins but also venial sins may be avoided as far as our strength allows.

Those are believed to ascend the second degree who strive, as much as they can, to avoid venial sins as well as mortal crimes; but because of too much commerce with the body’s weakness, they do not persevere in their purpose, but frequently fall into the various negligences of this life, although they do not commit mortal sins. We, the lukewarm, trust that we have in some measure ascended this degree, who, being placed under the observance of regular discipline, guard our minds, with the Lord’s help, from the more serious sins. But because we are exceedingly lukewarm, we live very negligently and are slow to perform the exercises of holy virtues.

There are many placed in the region of this second degree whom servile fear possesses; and if this fear stands alone, it by no means draws near to the kingdom of God. For to obtain the glory of heavenly blessedness, servile fear without charity is not enough, since he is a servant who does not sin from fear of punishment, but a son does no evil from love of God. Yet it is good to begin from servile fear, so that a person may gradually be able to arrive at filial fear, which is called chaste. For even if withdrawing from evil through fear of punishments is by no means enough to obtain the kingdom of God, still it prepares the one who acts for filial fear. Hence the lowest degree of those making progress is not to offend through fear of punishment, and not to sin lest one be condemned forever.

For charity alone, discerning the merits of all, is admitted as fit to enter the kingdom of God; and whatever has been done outside it is judged unworthy of God’s kingdom. Therefore, whoever you are who have deserved to ascend to this second degree, whoever you are who have learned not to sin through fear of punishments, if you wish to reach the joy of eternal blessedness, take care to hasten as quickly as possible to higher things. But since, as the proverb bears witness, no one suddenly becomes highest, we shall indeed rightly allow you to begin from the lower things; but we judge it dangerous to stand long in the valley of darkness. Ascend, therefore, as much as you can each day, and do not persist with the beasts in the dung of stinking deeds, because if you do not advance, you fall back; if you do not ascend, you descend.

The third degree is attained by those who, persevering in a good purpose, keep themselves from every mortal sin and also withdraw from venial sins as far as their strength allows. They love purity of conscience, and in no way commit anything that could stain it. Yet in one respect they are lower than those who follow, because they do not simply act for the love of God.

Those who withdraw from evil do good, but for this reason: because they trust that they will receive the kingdom of God for their merits. Those who serve God for the sake of reward are not in the state of perfection, but, together with the weak, still stand far from the summit of holiness in lower things. Whoever truly loves God with a pure mind serves and waits upon him neither from fear of punishments nor with a view to reward, but only from love of him. And therefore all the degrees set forth above are proposed to beginners, so that, ascending gradually through them, they may at last be joined to the perfect.

It is good to withdraw from evil through fear of punishments; it is good to do good from love of reward; and although this is by no means sufficient for perfection, nevertheless it provides a beginning and a way of advancing for those who desire to make progress. For servile fear, if continued, begets filial and chaste fear; from its spring perfect charity flows forth. But after charity has once kindled the mind, it thereafter casts out every servile fear and dread.

The fourth degree strives to show the way of perfection to those ascending, and therefore it is rightly judged greater than those previously described. Whatever good is not seen in them is possessed more perfectly in this one. For those who ascend this fourth degree guard themselves with all zeal not only from mortal sins but also from venial sins, as far as is possible for them; they apply themselves most diligently to good and holy works, and above all desire to please God. In one respect they surpass those who came before: they turn aside from evil neither from fear of punishments, nor do they perform good from hope of reward, but they do all things for the love of God alone, and seek nothing other than the honor of God.

This is the way proposed to those striving toward perfection; this is the true rule of holy justice: that we love God with a pure mind above all things, and do all our works for his honor. For the true lover of God neither fears punishment nor thinks of reward, but, walking in largeness of heart, commends his will to the divine ordering. For God, because he is supremely good, is to be loved not for the reward of the heavenly kingdom, nor for anything else, but for his own sake; and in every good work he must always be held principally in one’s intention.

Hasten, my dearest brothers, to ascend this degree of the spiritual ladder as quickly as possible, so that you may one day be able to reach the summit of perfection. For if you, who have been placed under the obedience of monastic perfection, have advanced to this fourth degree, you will then ascend the fifth without difficulty. For those who are placed in the fourth degree do the good works of justice by their own will, because they have not submitted themselves by vow or profession to monastic constitutions. And in this one respect they are inferior to those who follow: because a good work is so much the more acceptable to God, the more it is commended by the merit of obedience.

Therefore those ascend the fifth degree who guard themselves with all their strength from sins and, placed under obedience, always strong and steadfast, persevere in the purpose of holiness. They love God with a pure mind above all things.

For love of him they chiefly do good works, and in their intention they neither fear punishments nor seek rewards. They humbly obey their prelates for love of God, and in no respect at all do they depart from the purity of regular observance. Among these there are some whom the weakness of the flesh sometimes makes unstable in mind, and somewhat obstinate in their opinions against obedience. They sometimes try to defend their exercises and private little observances against the determination of their prelates, and think themselves more prudent than their rulers in the examination of spiritual matters. Flee this, O monks, because the devil lies hidden in ambush; and those whom he cannot conquer by open attack he strives to overcome by hidden contrivance. For the holier and more perfect a monk is before God, the more readily will he obey his prelate without debate. But if a perfect monk disdains to obey his abbot, even an imperfect one, in lawful and honorable matters, he has certainly already lost the name of perfection. Therefore let each one take care to devote himself to the pursuit of progress in such a way that he presumes in nothing to violate obedience. For Scripture says: Obedience is better than sacrifices, and hearkening more than offering the fat of rams. Whatever you offer is something external; but the truly obedient man offers himself.

The sixth degree, then, especially befits those who, living in all purity of mind and body, love the Lord above all things; who do every good they can for the honor of God alone; and who do not depart from the commands of their prelates. Great is the virtue of obedience, which doubles a holy good work, and, increasing merit for the worker, presents him to God like trees with fruit. Let not the words of men who despise obedience move you, my dearest brothers, men who prefer freedom of will to the subjection of monks, and set a good work done from freedom above the merits of obedience. For even if a monk obeys from the necessity of his profession, nevertheless the good will by which he bound himself to obedience for love of God commends this necessity in many ways.

There is, however, a necessity by which a man is compelled to do something where the will has not consented but always resists. This necessity lessens the praise of virtue, because the good work was never in the will. There is also another necessity, arising from the inward inclination of the mind, which increases, not lessens, the praise of the good work, because it kindles the will more intensely toward that very work. There is a third necessity, which has regard to the end and does not compel the will. For if you wish to cross the Rhine by boat, a fitting necessity requires the instrument. But the necessity by which a monk is compelled to obey his shepherd is not the first, of coercion, nor the second, of inclination, but rather the third, because it is ordered to the end from a preceding will. Therefore it is necessary for a monk, on account of the end, to do what the abbot has commanded, so that he may be able to fulfill, for love of God, the vow that he has made. Since, then, this end is very much

praiseworthy, by which the creature subjects itself to its Creator out of love, the necessity of obedience in a monk does not lessen the praise of a good work, but makes it greater. O happy necessity of monks, which took its beginning from the treasure of a good will and is ordered toward the end that is God, the unchangeable good. It is of greater praise, more excellent merit, and more abundant reward to do a good work out of obedience by reason of a vow than if it were done without a vow from the freedom of one’s own will.

The monk, moreover, once offered his whole self and all his will to God, and reserved absolutely nothing for himself. Whatever good he does under obedience is referred back to the end of the religious life he has undertaken, to be preserved for the love of Christ; and no work after martyrdom is comparable to this. One who is continent from sexual activity without a vow practices one virtue, which is called chastity; but one who observes it by reason of a vow walks on a higher path, since the individual virtues are ordered toward the perfection of the whole religious life that he has professed. For the whole monastic religious life is more than one private virtue.

For one who offers God a good work that he has done without obedience gives that alone, leaving to himself what is greater: the power of acting, and at the same time his own will. But the monk who does something for God from the vow of obedience has more excellent merit, since he offers God both the act and the power of acting. For no one has offered more to God than the monk who has given himself.

Some who climb this sixth step, however, have hidden within themselves a certain defect of pride, because, while they look incautiously to themselves, they do not entrust themselves in all things to the divine will as they ought. This defect takes its beginning from a certain very subtle vanity, when the soul, trusting in its own purity, asks that something secret be revealed to it by the Lord. And in this one respect the climbers of the sixth rung differ from those of the seventh: those who are bound to God flee the signs of vanity. For signs have been given not to believers, but to unbelievers; hence the monk who asks the Lord for a sign shows that he has not yet perfectly submitted himself to the divine will.

Those ascend the seventh step who most zealously keep all that has been prescribed, and live subject to God in all things without the stain of vanity. They flee every sin, both venial and mortal, as far as they can; they perform the works of virtue for the love of God alone; they obey their pastors in all things; they seek no miracles of vanity. Whatever almighty God has ordained concerning them, they receive gladly; they do not in any respect at all depart from the observance of monastic purity. Yet in one thing they are lower than those who follow, because perhaps they suffer some defect of which they are unaware, by the impulse of which they sometimes commit something of their own sensuality.

Whoever has deserved to ascend the eighth step grants nothing further to sensuality. Here is the sweetest rest of the soul; here is perfect tranquility of mind. Nothing flawed in beauty is left in this step; nothing is here that can sadden the soul.

228

On the nine degrees of ascent.

It is found there. Here all things are clean, all things pure, all things holy, all things most sweetly burning with the fervor of charity. Oh, if only we would strive to ascend to this degree! Oh, if only we might someday deserve to reach this harbor of tranquility! The more one, standing in this holy region, has begun to taste the sweetness of inward delight, the more, hastening toward what lies ahead, he desires still further.

Oh desires of holy love, always to be proclaimed; oh exercises of venerable perfection, where the clean conscience of one who loves God shines without sins, where the wicked contests of vices have ceased, and great tranquility has succeeded them.

Those already perfected in the eighth degree ascend to the ninth, who keep all the things prescribed purely and simply for the love of God, and desire nothing other than to praise, bless, and glorify God. Whoever has ascended this degree of perfection, as though forgetful of himself, resigns himself wholly to God and humbly submits. He regards himself as unworthy of all God’s benefits; he has no care at all for himself, because he has already learned to entrust himself wholly to God and humbly to be subject in all things to his ordering. Hence he neither asks for miracles nor seeks any other consolations in this life, but with the holy Apostle of Christ truly cries out: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” “For the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

For the true monk who loves Christ has offered himself wholly to God out of charity, and has despised the world with all its riches, honors, and vanities. Hence the world is said to be crucified to him, since there is nothing in it that seems able to penetrate his mind. Happy are those monks who with pure conscience serve the Lord God in true charity; who run without offense under the rule of humility and obedience; who ascend this last degree of perfection. These are true monks, who seek nothing other than the honor of God.

Indeed, my brothers, although monks are not bound by necessity of salvation to be perfect, for otherwise very few would be saved, yet we are all bound with good will to strive toward perfection, and with all the strength we can to yearn for this ninth degree. For it is very contrary to the monastic profession to be unwilling to make progress; it is a kind of apostasy, after a vow of perfection, to wish to remain in imperfection. For the vices that attack us are enemies of our salvation, and until they either conquer or are conquered, they do not cease to persecute us. Let us imitate the history of the ancient battle, when the children of promise destroyed their enemies not in one day, but successively. For it is difficult to conquer all things at once, unless the charity of God has suddenly overshadowed the mind. Against all the vices that in any way attack us, let us wage war. Let us conquer gluttony today; when it has been duly laid low, let us overcome sloth; and let us deal so with the rest, that at last we may come forth victors over them all. The Lord will be with us as we fight, and God will give victory to those who love him. Amen.

THE END.

JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, ABBOT OF SPONHEIM, OF THE ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT OF THE BURSZFELD OBSERVANCE

A MOURNFUL BOOK ON THE STATE AND RUIN OF THE MONASTIC ORDER IN THE PARTS OF GERMANY, NO LESS USEFUL THAN PLEASING TO ALL RELIGIOUS AND DEVOUT MEN

To the venerable and most beloved Father and Lord Blasius, Abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, Brother Johannes, called Abbot of Sponheim, sends greeting and charity.

Although your request far exceeds the powers of my talent, and that of your brothers, most beloved Father, I have nevertheless preferred to undertake the arduous burden rather than fail to satisfy your charity as far as I can. For the love of God, zeal for the Order, and fervor for discipline make you worthy that I should deny you nothing when you ask for the honor of God. You asked me when I was present by word of mouth, and more often when I was absent by letters, and in a certain manner you compelled me by the authority of your presidency, to write you something concerning the calamity of our Order, so that you might stir up the fathers to be assembled with you in chapter to have compassion on it. The request is holy, but the difficulty of obeying is great.

I shall be torn by the teeth of the envious. I know that some will judge me either presumptuous or excessive; but with my ears stopped I shall pass securely by their reproaches, provided that the burden I bear is pleasing to holy and learned men. I do not remember having written anything that rivals can justly tear apart, but things true, manifest, and open to the eyes of all; and if they do not wish these things to be written, let them also grieve that they have been done. In this publication alone charm of speech will be lacking; on that point I do not fear being reproved among religious men. For what? Is truth therefore despised because it is not clothed with the ornament of eloquence? Far be it. For plain and true speech is better than adorned and false speech. But these things are nothing to the point.

I therefore submit this little treatise to your examination, so that, if you judge it worthy, it may be read to the brothers; but if unworthy, it may escape the eyes of the lords. Farewell. In the year of the Lord 1493, on the Kalends of May.

The Pentichus Book of Lord Johannes of Spanheim, Abbot

On the ruin of the Order of our most holy father Benedict in the regions of Germany.

Chapter 1

When I recall to mind the former beauty of our Order, I grieve deeply over the deformity that we now endure, so that I would rather shed tears than compose a lamenting discourse. For who would not weep over its ruin, if he weighed its ancient glory? O, if we were ever to call back to memory the golden ages once possessed by this most sacred Order, when like a river of paradise it watered the whole Church throughout the world with doctrine and holiness, we would easily perceive how little its present state is.

Indeed our observance, which we call regular, when compared with the institutions of the ancients, is found not only lesser, but also in many respects more lax. How has the gold been darkened, the finest color changed? The splendor of surpassing holiness, once shining bright, has been obscured by desire for earthly things. The rule of honor has yielded to the enticements of pleasures. Therefore let my eyes pour forth tears day and night, and let them not be silent, because the religion of my people has been crushed with a great crushing, with a very grievous wound. If I go out into the fields, behold the idle and vain; if I enter the monasteries, behold those thinned and weakened by pleasures. For I find many professing the rule of Father Benedict; I see few walking according to his tradition.

“You have multiplied the nation,” says the prophet to the Lord, “but you have not increased the joy”; because, while the holy exercises of monks fail in many, corrupt hearts do not admit the true joy that is born of virtue. Would that we might awake, even late at last, after the destruction of so many souls, which, having despised the yoke of regular observance, have descended into the abyss of damnation. Would that we might fear the sentence of Benedict our lawgiver, who so often strikes the madness of a harsh abbot by summoning him to render account to God.

To you now, therefore, most reverend Fathers, my speech must be directed, you who receive the power to compel rebellious men to discipline, you who have zeal for our Order according to knowledge. Thus I address you; to you I shall try, according to my strength, to persuade that you come to the aid of an Order close to falling.
