When he had taken the monastery of Saint Andrew as a dwelling from Pope Adrian in the city of Rome, and had been warned in a third vision by the same Apostle and by Saint Gregory not to occupy the dwellings of monks any longer, and, though ordered to depart from there, pretended not to notice, he perished with all his people by a harsh death. Whether those who occupy the monasteries of monks are secure before God, we leave to their own consciences. A man who possesses another man’s goods without his will is bound to restitution. Let him who occupies the goods of any saint against that saint’s will consider what he deserves. We have now used a long enough discourse against the transgressors of our order; let us now come to what remains.

How these dismemberments by apostate monks are to be opposed. Chapter VII.

Although both my spirit and necessity itself offer abundant matter for inveighing against the destroyers of our order, nevertheless, since those are not present who might be called back to repentance by exhortations, I think enough has been said against them. For all who so wickedly oppress the honor of their own order are senseless; and I judge that they must be resisted not only with words, but with deeds [unclear].

For those who do not fear God will by no means acquiesce in our exhortations. Come now, most reverend Fathers, you who have assembled in chapter for the honor of our order, you who labor for its restoration: recall to mind its former state, and consider into how great a calamity it has fallen in this time. Behold, monasteries are being snatched from the hands of Saint Benedict; our order is being destroyed all around by the enemies of God; monks are returning to the world; the impious tear apart our religious life; strangers are endowed with our goods. What shall I say of internal wars? What shall I report of civil evils? It is no wonder, Fathers, take heed, if we are put to shame from without, since we are torn apart by our own people within.

Our abbots kick against discipline, tear apart the unity of the order, neglect the statutes of chapters. They spurn visitations; they despise your censures, O Fathers. Unless you strive very quickly to bring them back to regular observance, you will not be able to keep them long under the order. Why then do you dissemble? How long will you sleep? When will you awaken? When will you fight for the inheritance of Saint Benedict? O Fathers, Fathers, arm yourselves with zeal for God, for the order, and for discipline, because it is time. Fight for your lawful rights. Defend the rights of holiness; stand manfully against transfers of the order.

Behold, already in our own times, in the province of Mainz alone, six monasteries have been transferred from our order; and unless we watch more carefully, we shall suffer graver losses day by day. Thus, while we dissemble, not to say grow sluggish, the order is gradually diminished, until at last it is entirely scattered. Why do we not meet such great dangers? Or, while the others perish, do we wisely trust in our own security? Did not the poet truly say: “Your own affair is at stake when the neighboring wall is burning”? Yesterday the danger was theirs; tomorrow a like danger will hang over us.

Each one of you, I do not doubt, loves his own monastery, and would by no means consent that it be transferred from the order, so that he desires not only its present happiness but also its future happiness to be prolonged for eternal years. Why then do you not defend in common what each of you fears to lose individually? I fear, Fathers, that in this dissembling our very wicked tenacity is being exposed. We love, and yet we lose, a monastery; we fear a few expenses, and lose spacious dwellings. We are unwilling to lay out a small sum of money, and we allow most abundant monasteries to pass from the order to outsiders. We put private advantages before the common good, and we do not care to preserve the honor of the order. We say many things, we determine many things for the useful defense of the order; but all of us are afraid to spend coins. O feeble zeal, which stinginess renders useless. If we do not give money for our brothers, when shall we lay down our life? If we do not contribute a few expenses for the preservation of the order, when shall we give our bodies? He who is grasping in a small matter: when will he be generous in a great one?

Now I shall speak to you, Fathers, who dissemble while the order has been placed amid such great dangers and needs aid. Blessed Benedict made you rich from poverty.

has made, now asks alms from you and, shameful to say, does not receive them. Behold how many are found among us, if I may say so with your pardon, who distribute the substance of the monastery to frivolous persons, prepare banquets for birds and dogs, enrich parents and kinsmen from the monastery’s goods, and squander the rest in vain and voluptuous feasts.

Few there are who grieve over the desolation of our order; fewer think about a remedy; very few supply help. Is this how the holy order of Benedict, once most excellent among all, is defended from the enemy’s assault? Wake up, Fathers, while watchfulness is useful, lest too late you repent of having slept. Look at the professors of other orders, how carefully, how zealously, how steadfastly they defend the rights, privileges, and monasteries of their religion, sparing neither expenses nor labors nor contributions, so that they may preserve their orders in their strength.

Are you inferior to them? Are you poorer than the mendicants? If one chooses to consider the number of monasteries of the order, we are more numerous; if the substance of temporal goods, richer; if power and authority, undoubtedly superior. What do we lack, except zeal and constancy, that they possess? Why then do we hesitate? Why do we grow feeble in idle inactivity? Why do we not keep watch for the defense of our order?

Do you not know, O Fathers, that the laws aid those who are watchful? That is not good patience by which God’s honor is neglected, the worship due to him is diminished, and the integrity of the holy order is violated. What shall I say? You grieve over monasteries already transferred, and yet you do not undertake to preserve those that are to be transferred. You put private interests before common ones; therefore your zeal bears little fruit. Each of us, as I see, thinks himself safe if, when his neighbor’s house is burning, his own wall does not at once grow hot. But O folly, O stupidity deservedly to be blamed: he who, wrapped in so many dangers, now raises himself up in confidence of his own security will shortly, once fallen, be compelled to lament.

Therefore, Fathers, if we desire to preserve our houses unharmed from fire, let us meet the fire with water while it is still far away. For if the flame is allowed to pass as far as the neighboring houses, thought is taken for a remedy too late. Hence the poet says: “Resist beginnings; too late is medicine prepared when evils have grown strong through long delays.” Dangers that are ignored gain strength with time, and what at the beginning easily admits a cure gradually becomes an incurable wound.

At the same time take care that an error now neglected does not, in the course of time, grow without measure, when no one will be found who will steadfastly oppose himself for the order. But if you say that litigation was always brought against the authors of the dismemberment, and that they nevertheless prevailed, I answer with that Virgilian saying: “Because the herdsmen came too late.” After the confirmation of letters, a sentence once issued is not easily revoked. For if Pilate was unwilling to change what he had once written, how will the supreme Pontiff, the Vicar of Christ, revoke what has once been decreed? A sentence is more easily prevented than revoked. But he who neglects his own right concedes it to his adversary. All must keep watch in a cause which

It touches all, because what is snatched from one is judged to have been taken from all. Whenever a monastery is seized from our order, our common inheritance is in part wasted. If anyone has attempted to occupy your house or field, you immediately accuse him before the judge, immediately ask for an injunction, and until you conquer your adversary you do not cease from the lawsuit. Why, then, do we all not do in public causes of the order what each person does in private ones? Will what one man does be impossible for many, unless perhaps where there is a multitude there is also confusion, so that what is entrusted to several is preserved more negligently? For we gladly embrace the command that each man be nearest to himself. But while, with our body drawn in on every side, like a hedgehog, we roll our own affairs about within ourselves and cast aside care for the order, at last, caught by the snares of hunters, we think too late about the remedy of flight.

Therefore now, reverend Fathers, with the goodwill that befits a monk and with all the attention I can, I beg you: come to the aid of your order, which is nearly falling, and oppose these dismemberments as quickly as possible. Do not put money before such necessities; do not love coins more than the order. Shameful is the keeping of riches by which the commonwealth is not helped in necessity. What will an insatiable desire for gold profit you, if the desolation of your order, so holy, so venerable, so glorious, should prevail? If our predecessors had watched over the order with no greater care than we do, long ago in many monasteries the name of our religion would have perished. Let us therefore imitate the constancy of those whose inheritance we have received. If we love God, if we love the honor of the order, if we desire to preserve it, let us think in time about a remedy. Let us contribute a little to the preservation of the order, that we may deserve to receive much; let us spend a part, that we may be able to preserve the whole; let us offer worthless things, that we may be able to acquire precious ones; let us give earthly things, that we may be able to possess heavenly ones. Let us spend money and also prayer, since by the former man is appeased, by the latter God.

Whatever we have belongs to the right of our holy father Benedict; when we spend anything for the preservation of the order, we do not give him what is ours, but restore to him what is his. Indeed, we are bound to him not only for the souls entrusted to us, but are also obliged to give an account for the substance of the monastery. Yet an account of revenue is never rendered more safely than when money is opportunely expended in the causes of the Lord. But if money is spared in the Lord’s necessity, suspicion is generated of the servant’s unfaithfulness.

At the beginning of this chapter we set down the title concerning the manner of resisting the dismemberments of the wicked; lest we seem to have passed over these matters untouched, let us briefly explain them. And although this treatment does not pertain to me, nevertheless, since I am a foster-son of your same order and a lover of the chapter, the admonition of a disciple will not, as I think, be burdensome to you. It is yours, O Fathers, to distinguish the true from the false; let it suffice for me to have explained what I think. The manner of opposing these presumptions of monks is easily learned, if from the example

Let it be put into practice: look at the other orders, and from their diligence you will recognize what you must do. They appoint procurators from among their own men in the city of Rome, who vigorously resist the beginnings of evils and allow nothing to gain strength against their order. And you, Fathers, unless you do the same, will suffer serious losses in the future. Therefore, if it can be done, if it is pleasing, let someone be chosen from the order: a zealous, devout, learned, and experienced man, who will fight no less by influence than by zeal, who will not prefer his own interests to the common good, who will not flee labors, who will attempt nothing rashly beyond the commission to be entrusted to him, and who, once appointed procurator of the order in the city, will always keep careful watch on its behalf. I believe that, if such a man were available, he would forestall many dangers to the order.

For it is the greatest foresight if the procurator in the city can denounce before the Pope the false and fictitious allegations which perverse monks falsely present as true for the sake of their own dismemberment. And this is not a work of great difficulty, for all the causes they allege are full of fear and falsehood. But the Vicar of Christ, who grants transfers of monks more because of importunity than out of favor, when he has seen their allegations refuted by the diligence of our procurator, will rejoice that he has found an occasion for denying what he was unwillingly granting. For he too fears the judgment of his Lord. Therefore, if we were watchful, we would have him as defender and advocate of our order. Our negligence alone is accused. Our stinginess alone is condemned.

Against those who uselessly consume the goods of monasteries and disdain to assist the order even in any measure. Chapter VIII.

But now I am pleased to turn the force of my words against those who, amid such great necessities, do not deign to assist the holy order even in any measure. These are worldly abbots, useless men, given over to pleasures, who, to use the words of Mantuan, neglecting the worship of those above and despising the command of the Thunderer, indulge Bacchus and serve Venus. They carry sacred things with gold, build altars with coins; with gold they pour libations of wine, with gold their paneled ceilings gleam. They cover whores with jewels, set banquets before dogs; adorned with the spoils of the poor and enriched by plunder, puffed up by success, they laugh at heaven and Acheron alike.

They have no care at all for the salvation of souls, no love of God, no reverence for the saints, no practice of the virtues. These are the abbots rebellious against your chapter, who neglect the statutes, spurn the sanctions, and despise the Rule. From the rejected they have been raised to greatness, but they impiously despise the order that honored them. Saint Benedict exalted you, ungrateful abbot; he made you rich, received you as a monk, and appointed you shepherd of his brothers. Why, then, do you not acknowledge the generosity of your lawgiver? Why do you not repay his benefits in return?

What do you have that you did not receive from his Rule? Who endowed the monastery entrusted to you? Was it not the devotion of princes and the alms of faithful peoples? Why, then, are you ungrateful for such great benefits? See, you think of nothing less than regular observance: you reject discipline; you spurn God, despise his precepts, and presume upon security. See, with the birds of the sky you sport against the Rule; see, with unclean dogs you hunt against the law of clerics; see, in the pleasures of the flesh you delight against decency; see, what is most shameful, despising your oath of chastity, you consume the property of Saint Benedict with prostitutes and pimps. You are not afraid to spend thirty or forty gold coins at the baths, and yet you refuse to offer even one to Saint Benedict? I lie if I have not known abbots who spent more than fifty florins at the hot springs, some of whom are foremost among those who resist the subsidies of the chapter. Others also among those who wish to be called Observant, unable to endure seclusion and quiet, and unable to remain long in the monastery, judge every occasion suitable by which they can migrate here and there at great expense.

What shall I say about buildings, both curious and superfluous, which are liable to blame no less than to expense? Walls are adorned with paintings, pinnacles gleam with gold, windows are marked with monuments; the poor cry out at the door, the sacred order, being in straits, asks for help, and no one deigns to assist. O abbot, servant of pleasure, cultivator of vanity, enemy of piety, you who shamefully pour out the substance of the monastery, you who drink wines from gold, you who deny aid to your order, how will you render an account of your stewardship to Saint Benedict? If the rich glutton was buried in hell because he did not give Lazarus help from his own goods for God’s sake, where will the abbot be buried who denied to his lord what belonged to another? If he who did not give alms from his own goods will burn forever, what does the abbot deserve who has committed robbery?

What do you have, O abbot, that you did not receive? For everything you possess belongs to the right of Saint Benedict. It is a moral principle for all that he who lives by the support of justice should dare to deny no one what is just. The definition of justice is to render to each what is owed to him by right. But we who are established in monasteries have nothing of our own, but possess another’s goods in good faith. What belongs to another is judged liable to restitution. For all things that princes and faithful peoples bestowed on monasteries for the sustenance of monks are remembered as having been handed over to Saint Benedict. If, then, you have squandered his substance, if you have despised rendering to him what is his, you will be subject to a twofold condemnation, since from your unfaithfulness you will be judged sacrilegious, and from your denial of trust, criminal.

Render therefore to each what is his, and do not usurp for yourself what is not yours. Give to your lawgiver what he rightly demands; give aid to his order, that it may subsist. Why do you not spend the subsidies owed to your religion? Why do you not render a part to him who bestowed the whole on you? Why do you deny a little to him from whom you have received much? Surely...

Will you be able to plead the poverty of your monastery, you who so shamefully squander so much? I am ashamed to say what many abbots are not ashamed to do: sunk, or rather maddened, in the pleasures of the flesh, they preserve nothing of monastic honor and omit nothing of worldly baseness. They think everything is permitted to them, since they consider not what is fitting, but what pleases them.

See: one, abhorring monastic quiet, seeks comfort in the world by wandering about; another, impatient of the seclusion required by the rule, goes out pompously in public; another, despising honorable discipline, sits all day as a drunken dinner-companion among frivolous people; this one, scorning the meekness of the saints, entangles himself in the lawsuits of litigants; another sits playing at the gaming-board; another foolishly dances to the drum.

What do ambitious abbots not presume to do? What do they leave untried in their pleasures? When they dine, the knees of servants are bent before them; when they pass through churches, carpets are spread beneath them; when they go forward in public, a huge crowd of servants follows. You will find, I am not lying, an abbot among them, even among those who boast in the name of reform, whose ambition is so great that he does not wish to be called inferior to a bishop; who sits at table with such display that the abundance of vessels, the variety of food and drink, and the multitude of attendants would suffice for any prince. In short, if you met him as he proceeded through a city, you would see him surrounded by such a crowd of servants that you would think not an abbot but an archbishop was passing by. If they did not pretend to be poor, but were poor, vanity would by no means pour itself out in such great solemnity. For I am certain that this crowd follows prey, not a man. Who could find prey among the poor, or would wish to?

O abbot, fugitive shepherd, ungrateful and faithless steward of the goods of your Lord, who spend the substance of the monastery so uselessly, who live voluptuously and shamefully: who will help you at the final examination? Whom will you appoint as advocate when you must render your account? Behold, you consume the goods of Saint Benedict in pleasure; from them you aid your relatives; you lavish gifts on base men; you distribute presents to your flatterers; day and night you serve gluttony and drunkenness. You eat the richest things of the earth and drink the best wines; poor monks live in want, humble brothers eat the bread of sorrow; the sheep entrusted to you are fed on worthless fare.

O vain shepherd, who neglect the Lord’s flock, who despise the necessities of your brothers, remember to whom you are going to render an account; call to mind how dreadful it is to fall into the hands of the living God, who does not regard the person of any man, who repays each one according to his works. But hear my counsel: do penance, redeem your sins with alms, indeed discharge the repayment of what is owed, so that before the eternal judge you may deserve to find mercy. Lay aside your arrogance; cast off pride; abandon vanity. Be the abbot of your brothers according to the rule; be a shepherd in solicitude, a father in charity. Feed them by word, feed them by example, feed them...

with nourishment; if you omit either of these, you will be a useless shepherd. For without spiritual things, temporal things do nothing toward eternal salvation; without the aid of temporal things, spiritual things do not long subsist in this life. Therefore, if you wish to be a good shepherd, know that the care of both kinds of feeding has been laid upon you, namely spiritual and bodily.

I had said that your sins must be discharged by repayment of a debt. Of what debt? Of that, namely, by which you are deemed bound to St. Benedict. What is that debt? Everything that you have. For from him you have it that you are a monk; from him, that you are wealthy. And now he from whom you have all these things knocks at your door; for the necessity of his order he asks help; he desires to receive back the least part of the very great things he has entrusted to you. Why do you deny him his own goods? Why, when they are demanded of you, do you not at once restore what was entrusted to you?

Divine Scripture commands and says: If you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh. Behold, your order stands naked; behold, your torn religion cries out, begs alms, asks back what is its own, seeks help. If there are in you any bowels of pity, any heart of sweetness, any love for your order, any love of God, do not despise your own flesh; do not scorn so great a public kinship. Honor him who first honored you; give alms to him who raised you up; bestow a little on him who made you rich in many things. However much you give him, nothing at all is diminished for you, if only you apply a good will: you will give a little and receive much; you will generously bestow earthly things and hope for heavenly things.

Nor should it escape you, since, as is commonly said, whatever is withdrawn from honor is reserved for shame. For the legal maxim says: The treasury takes what Christ does not receive. He is not free from the guilt of crime who sets greed before the order of piety.

But why do we strive in vain? The word of piety has no place in wicked hearts. If they despise the words of God, what wonder if they scorn ours? Though I may speak many things, say many things, urge excellent things with words for contributing to the order, I shall never bend the rebellious man. Indeed, unless your authority, lord presidents, intervenes, the speech of one who admonishes labors in vain. It therefore belongs to your office to bend the rebellious; to you is committed the humbling of the disobedient; ours is humbly to obey your decrees. Therefore, if you desire to defend our order from the assault of the wicked, take care first of all to recall rebellious abbots to obedience, because unless the unity of the order is restored, the impiety of its adversaries will easily prevail. For the Lord says in the Gospel: Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and house will fall upon house. Division alone confounds the order.

The Pentichus of Johannes Trithemius.

How disobedient and rebellious abbots are to be compelled to come to the aid of the order. Chapter IX.

If judges lack authority to restrain the rebellious, legislation is made in vain. For we always strive after what is forbidden, and unless compelled we resist commands. For where there is no fear of power, the condition of law is quickly despised. The preservation of law, therefore, is fear of power. But where the relaxation of power looks the other way, the vigor of law totters; for a constitution, however holy or necessary, is quickly snatched into oblivion if authority is lacking by which contempt may be punished.

Take away power, and the commonwealth will be nothing other than a confusion full of sedition. For rustic savagery is not led by reason, nor quieted by gentleness. Among our own people too, God amend it, there are many abbots and monks coarser than peasants, more savage than beasts, who are not bent by gentleness to the observance of God’s commandments and the Rule, nor are ever persuaded by exhortations, however holy. If the authority of those who preside does not oppose such men, they will never be led by any obedience to their head.

For this reason the supreme pontiffs, founders of this most sacred provincial chapter, established for us many useful remedies, by which we may compel the abbots subject to the chapter to contribute to the support of the order. We have authority; do we hesitate about power? And what is authority worth without power? If you wish, most honored Fathers, that I speak more openly about what I have meant by the power of authority, you will pardon me if I mark your timidity, not to say negligence.

Behold, we have learned that one hundred twenty-seven abbeys are established under our provincial chapter, yet we do not receive from all of them the subsidies of the contribution due. Why is this? We receive the authority to demand it, but we do not exercise the power. We receive what is offered willingly; we are afraid to compel the disobedient. For I am certain that many abbots of our province contribute nothing to the support of the order; indeed, if they are asked, they object as though by prescriptive right.

What are we doing? Why do we dissemble so long? We apply spurs to the one who runs willingly; to the one lying down, indeed kicking back, we do not even apply words. From this arises contempt for our statutes; the authority of the chapter is despised; the inheritance of the order is laid waste on every side. These things must be referred to you, O Fathers, who neglect to tame the rebellious at the beginning.

Consider what this dissembling will finally bring forth; and if you love your order, think as quickly as possible about a remedy. A body is weak and close to dissolution when it is deprived of the support of its members. Behold, out of one hundred twenty-seven abbots, how few you see in the present chapter, though all were bound to attend by statute. Where are the rest? Where are the procurators of all the absent? Few for the necessity of the or[unclear].

The preservation of law is fear of power.

Authority without power is worth nothing.

How many abbeys the Bursfeld congregation once had in the author’s time.

The rebellious must be tamed at the beginning.

fewer observe the statutes of the order; very few have assembled at the chapter. Where are the letters of excuse of those who did not send procurators? Where are the double expenses of the rebels? Who among the absent and rebellious, in all these many years, has ever been compelled to pay the double penalty? What use are statutes to us, what use are laws, what help are the privileges of the supreme pontiffs, if in a time of necessity they are not put into practice? Behold, Pope Benedict XII provided for us fittingly in all things, when he promulgated that the restraints of censures should be imposed against the contumacious and rebellious. Why then do we delay? Why do we not put into practice against the disobedient the remedies granted to us?

Truly, fathers, this dissimulation of ours which we practice is not praiseworthy. For the rebellion of a few, if passed over in silence, will be an occasion for many to resist. But if a small number is compelled to obedience by discipline, the boldness of the multitude is restrained by fear. Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and every religious order at variance with itself is gradually scattered. It is no fair appearance of order where confusion troubles unity; for in every commonwealth the first road to desolation is the disobedience of subjects.

Therefore, venerable fathers, if you desire to continue the provincial chapter, if you wish to oppose the dismembering of the monks, if finally you wish to defend your order from the hands of enemies, take care first of all to recall the contumacious to obedience, lest what you acquire outwardly by diligence you lose inwardly through the division of your subjects. This indeed must first be attempted by the gentlest exhortations. But if they contemn these with hardened neck, they must be struck with harsher rebukes. If, however, they care neither for gentle words nor harsh ones, then ecclesiastical censure should be promulgated against them. For fools are not corrected by exhortations, but become proud.

In these matters, however, moderation must be observed, and necessary discretion, without which no rebellion is ever softened. For it is better to have weak sheep than none. But who is so fit that he can preserve discretion everywhere? It is difficult to apply moderation to all deeds. He who wishes to heal infirm souls must be both severe and compassionate, and tempered as though from a certain mean between the two, so that severity is not excessive nor compassion lax. For the one breaks, the other loosens. But the fairest manner of coercing the rebellious and contumacious is that which the long experience of elders commends.

On holding the provincial chapter. Chapter X.

When you come together as one, most excellent fathers, let us diligently investigate what the celebration of the provincial chapter requires. For the greatest strength of our stability is placed in it, if it is celebrated rightly. For it is the one fortress of our order, without which our whole religious life would be thrown into confusion.

For a chapter is the preservation of order, the increase of regular discipline, the uniting of unity. In it, indeed, integrity is given to morals, purity is increased in minds, and the equality of regular life is restored. But hear what is required for it to be celebrated rightly; hear what its sincere celebration demands. It requires zeal, it requires knowledge, it requires piety: without these three the celebration of a chapter is worth nothing. For if zeal is lacking, who will correct offenders? If knowledge is lacking, what fruit will excessive piety bring forth? Again, if piety is lacking, neither does zeal receive love, nor knowledge discipline. For piety avails for all things: zeal sharpens, knowledge directs, piety produces fruit. Without zeal, knowledge remains cold; without piety, fruitless. Likewise zeal without knowledge will be excessive and undiscerning; without piety, hateful. But piety avails for all things, although without zeal and knowledge it is not sufficient for the governance of souls. For it pleases all, and benefits only the humble when set apart.

Therefore the whole matter of celebrating a chapter consists in the disposition of the presiding officers, which requires men who are zealous, learned, and gentle. For if they are lax, inexperienced, cruel, and impious, how then will they reform others to piety? If the man who sits to punish crimes admits them himself, whom like himself will he amend? Therefore this fault must be referred to you, Fathers, if you choose deformed and vicious abbots for the presidency. With the greatest care, then, see that you appoint as presiding officers over the chapter such men as an irreproachable life commends. Let zeal for holy religion sharpen them; let instruction in saving knowledge temper them. For one who presides over others must be a man upright in morals, mature in conduct, fervent in zeal, instructed in knowledge of the Scriptures, adorned with gentleness. Such a man, O Fathers, is rightly to be preferred over us, whose life offers an example and whose teaching gives an increase of virtue. If the presiding officers of the chapter are such, those subject to it will easily be brought back to obedience. For those will be fit to preside who can instruct the teachable by word, the rude by example, and the obstinate by authority. In these ways, indeed, the chapter will be rightly celebrated, and the souls of the subjects will be built up.

The other things that make presiding officers suitable I am not permitted to describe on this occasion, since I believe none of them is ignorant of what sort of men they ought to be. Therefore I turn again to you, O Fathers, who have gathered in this place for the celebration of the chapter. I address you; I exhort you to direct your intention to the restoration of the order, and to consider with careful mind why the chapter was instituted. Do you wish to know why chapters were instituted? Seek out the decrees of the supreme pontiffs, and you will know the cause of their institution. But lest either laziness or occupation hinder the understanding of this matter, I shall briefly explain the cause for the establishment of the chapter. The purpose, then, of a provincial chapter is the preservation of regular observance. For the Roman pontiffs and the general councils, seeing...

On the State and Ruin of the Monastic Order.

The presidents, judging that our order could not long subsist in observance without a special remedy, determined through the provincial chapter to come to its aid; in which, through the diligence of the presidents, all would be instructed to live according to the Rule, and no one could deviate from the reform once begun. For in the chapter of abbots vices are to be corrected, exhortations to virtues are to be made, so that the bad may find something to fear, and the good may hear something by which they may become better. Therefore various things are read for edification, so that increases may always be present to good minds. There the abbot is instructed concerning his governance; there he is admonished concerning the danger of pastoral care; there what he is to do is prescribed, and what he is to avoid for the love of God is forbidden. Finally, when we gather thus for chapter, many useful things come about for us, which, if we seek the salvation of souls, are very necessary. For, to pass over the rest, mutual acquaintance in charity is there conceived, and experience shows how greatly this conduces to love of regular observance. There, from acquaintance, brotherly charity is both preserved and increased; otherwise it would quickly grow lukewarm if it did not have the nourishment of mutual recognition. Here an easy access to uniformity lies open, where, from the conference of the fathers, a mutual fire is prepared for honorable conduct, and from the fellowship of holiness an example is offered.

These are the camps of God, O Fathers, and the defenses of our order, by which all the devices of our adversaries may be reduced to nothing. But there is not one sincerity in all, nor does equality of manners appear among you. Whence could such a disparity of manners arise in one order, where capitular unity is seen? Who has divided between you and the Rule of Saint Benedict, O Fathers, long-haired with matted hair? Why do you not look to uniformity, you who celebrate assemblies of unity? If you love the holy order which you profess, why do you not love uniformity in it? What is the shadow of a long-haired head to you? What ornament do you think the summit of a curled crown bears? Believe me, Fathers: a face covered with hair is reckoned a disgrace in a monk, not an honor. O how beautiful this assembly would be if, as it ought, it came together into one discipline of regular observance. What shall I say? I praise the assembly, but I rebuke the deformity among its members. For because of the disorder of the order, the present unity grows cheap. The outward habit indicates what the inward garment reproves in the life of many. Truly, Fathers, this disparity of manners and habits offends the provincial chapter no little, since it is known to have been instituted for this reason, that equality of life might be preserved above all things. For outward discord is the sign of inward discord. Therefore, that we may be of one mind in the observance of regular discipline, let us strive first of all to be conformable in habit and tonsure.

The Pentichus Book of Johannes Trithemius

How necessary a diligent reform of the monasteries in our Province would be. Chapter XI.

How necessary a diligent reform of the monasteries in our Province is, you yourselves, O Fathers, know, for you are not ignorant of the condition of the monks of this time. I know it is known to you with what labors, expenses, and sweats the Fathers once reformed our order; concerning these things we find records in our age both few and weak. Among all the reforms of our order in our province, however, three have lately shone forth above the rest, namely the Castellan, from Castellum; the Melk, from Melk; and the Bursfeld, from Bursfeld, having taken their names from them. All these, just as they were fervent in the beginning, so, gradually growing lukewarm, are approaching their end. For the first two, as though worn out with age, have been reduced to a small number; but the last, which is also the later one, because it is still younger, seems also to be more steadfast. Nevertheless even this itself now seems in certain of its members to be growing lukewarm and again declining toward the laxity of its former life. Thus once the Cluniac reform, known throughout the whole world, when it spread itself far and wide, gradually failed, as though its strength had been lost through expansion. For it is said in the proverb: everything that grows old is near destruction. For any reform, however celebrated or holy it may have been, unless it is often renewed through the diligence of prelates, gradually vanishes. For as much as it grows with time, so much is it diminished in fervor. For when those who had shown zeal for the order in deed passed away, new abbots arose after them who, neglecting the holy fervor of reform, relapsed into their former deformities. And, to touch on matters nearer at hand, where is that reform which Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa, as legate, began with incredible zeal? Where are those terrible oaths of all the abbots of our province, by which they bound themselves to regular observance in the hands of the same Cardinal before the altar of Saint Stephen at Würzburg? Where is the regular observance that was promised? Behold, Fathers, you have under your chapter one hundred twenty-seven abbeys; of these, from the three observances already mentioned, scarcely seventy have remained under reform. Yet there are, I do not doubt, some who think themselves excellently reformed, but their conduct denies it. Would that the abbots would heed the threat of our holy lawgiver, often repeated, by which he says that the governance of souls is subject to the strictest accounting. Would that they would drive the sheep entrusted to them to the pastures of heavenly life, lest they themselves perish eternally together with the sheep. Consider the conduct, both of abbots and of monks, without the law of monastic honor, smoking all around; when it is known, it is a shame for me to speak of it, and a horror for you, O most revered Fathers, to hear it. For the three vows of religion, which because of their excellence are called substantial, not

On the state and ruin of the monastic order.

Why the Canonical Hours are performed by some without devotion.

they care less than if they had never promised to observe them. They confound everything, profane everything, presume everything. If we look to divine worship, they perform it so confusedly, so disorderly, so laxly, that neither do the words convey sense, nor does the melody sound the proper tone. For they are devoid of all instruction in the good arts, so that they understand absolutely nothing of what they sing. Hence it comes about that, without feeling, without devotion, without any savor of inward sweetness, they do not so much discharge the canonical hours as confound them. In their hands the book of divine Scripture is never seen; no practice of edifying discourse is ever taken up; no account is ever taken of the formation of morals. The whole day is consumed in obscene gossip; all time is enslaved to games and feasting. There is never any mention of reform. The madness of men at odds with one another rages mutually, and among the cowls, peace broken, the monastery, with law despised, [unclear] insane with lawsuits. Spear there, and sword, and bow are at hand, so that you would think what you see is not a monastery but a stronghold of men at war. As witnesses of their private ownership, contrary to the statutes, contrary to the laws, contrary to the rule, they each inhabit separate houses, in which they pursue not the studies of monks but those of clerics. They neither fear nor love God; they think nothing of the life to come, since they put the concerns of the soul after the pleasures of the flesh. They do not read the rule of monks; they do not heed the statutes; they despise the decrees of the Fathers. They scorn the vow of poverty, know nothing of chastity, and hold obedience cheap. And would that, since they refuse to be chaste, they would at least deign to be continent. The filth of vices smokes all around, and what everyone knows, we alone, who are ordered to amend it, do not know. Why should I say much? So many, so great, so varied are the unlawful things they commit there against the Rule of Saint Benedict, that I would more readily think a monk could be formed anew than that the life of these men could be amended. For nothing of monastic honor remains inviolate among them; rather everything lies neglected, spurned, despised, and torn apart. Anger, quarrels, dissensions, envy, detractions, curses, oaths, insults, and things like these are not judged among them to be sins, because what is public has begun to be lawful. A place lies open for vices and crimes; virtue alone does not deserve entry. They laugh if anyone begins to speak before them about penance, and, as Mantuan says, they despise the gods above and Acheron. There is no fear of punishment, no dread of the Judge. Among them you would see, as in a spring of all vices, pride, greed, lust, gluttony, sloth, anger, hatred, and every pleasure of the flesh abounding; if they can grasp it, they rejoice; if they cannot, still they eagerly desire it. The beasts have rotted in their own dung, and, as if reason had been lost, they do not wish to be recalled to penance. O good God, to what great calamity has the order been brought down, once so lofty, which could deservedly be preferred to all orders. O holy Father Benedict, who once

The Pentichus Book of Johannes Trithemius.

You were so solicitous for your religion; why do you abandon us at the end? Why do you not look to your inheritance? Why do you not now, even now, come to the aid of your order as it totters? Have you cast off care for it? Or has your soul abhorred your sons? Come to our aid, help us, bring assistance, because your religion has never been surrounded by such grievous evils. Behold, it is being destroyed from without by lovers of the world; behold, it is being torn apart within by perverse monks, so that no one can easily discern which is the greater crime: for monasteries to be transferred into the hands of secular clerics, or to be kept longer under the hands of such criminal monks.

Alas, holy Father, what shall I say? You, once instructing abbots, commanded them to be solicitous concerning weak monks. Now shepherds have no care for the sheep, no diligence for the salvation of souls: all seek the things that are their own, not the things of Jesus Christ. Behold, your sons, Father, having zeal, desire to come to the rescue, but they accomplish nothing, hindered by the rashness of the wicked. Who, amid these things, will truly come to our aid? The bishop? But he cares for his own affairs, seeks his own, despises ours. Princes? But they sell favor, reject discipline, seek temporal things. There is no one who grieves over the crushing of your order; no one who comes to its aid; no one who provides help. All who can restore it neglect it; others, who seem to have zeal for discipline, try to help, but cannot.

O abbots, abbots, you who are the occasion of all evils in your monasteries. You who, given over to vanities, do not at once correct monks who do wrong: what a harsh sentence of condemnation you will receive. To you, believe me, to you will be imputed the damnation of your monks. You, placed as their rulers, have neglected to instruct their morals. Woe to you. It would be better if you had never been abbots. You, devoting yourselves to avarice and lust, neglect the work of the Lord, despise the care of souls, think nothing of the path of observance. You who ought to correct the vices of monks commit vices, and, lest your own be reproved, you conceal those of others.

You see, most adorned Fathers, what the condition of your order is, what the abbots are, what the monks are, since those who [unclear] the wicked are lacking; among them only those who [unclear] occur. Why, then, do you delay? Why do you not think about the reformation of such men? Why do you not restrain the wicked pursuits of the monks? Their ill repute confounds us; their examples scandalize us, because the greater they are in number, the better in conduct they are believed to be by those who do not know.

Rise up, Fathers, because the days are both short and evil; reform, according to your powers, the deformed order; raise up what has been cast down; restore what has collapsed. For unless you apply a remedy quickly, you will shortly suffer grave loss. For dissolute monks, enemies of regular discipline, always aspire to worse things, and, lest they be saved in the order, they strive to abandon it. You have the aids of law for beginning reformation; you have the Rule; you have statutes. This alone is required of you: that you put them into practice. Therefore, if you love your order, indeed because you love it: do not neglect, do not delay,

On the Condition and Ruin of the Monastic Order.

because the greatest necessity presses upon us, since the impiety of perverse monks everywhere grows bold. Behold, the rich men of the world violently seize the goods of monasteries; behold, the worshippers of avarice invade the possessions of the order; behold, secular clerics receive the abbeys of St. Benedict in commendam. None of these things would happen if abbots and monks had persevered in regular observance. Let us therefore impute to ourselves what we suffer, since we did not resist the rashness of the wicked from the beginning. To us, I say, this fault is justly ascribed, since, intent on our own advantages, we do not care for the losses of the order, as though they were someone else’s. Let us rise up, I pray, Fathers; let us rise up, even at last, though late, after so many losses, so many dangers, so much destruction of souls, and let us do what lies in us, beseeching God’s mercy for the rest, that he may supply our deficiency, direct our zeal, and bring our holy efforts to completion. And if we cannot bring the whole order back to the unity of good conduct, let us at least strive, as far as possible, to reform those monks who are in our province. But if complete conformity cannot be had in all things, let it at least be reformed in the three substantial things, without which the life of monks must be judged nothing other than the foul brothel of an unbelieving soul. Reform, moreover, must begin with the abbots, and thereafter be continued among the monks. For unless the shepherd has been brought back to sincerity, the health of the sheep will not long endure. For it is commonly said: When the head is sick, the other members suffer. Therefore every adornment of the body must begin from the head. There are certain deformed abbots who wish to compel their monks to reform, but they themselves do not wish to submit to regular observance, not even in the least; hating in themselves the good that they love in others, and not blushing to do themselves what they forbid their subjects. Do not trust such men, O Fathers, for they are the very ones who confound us: they spurn visitations, they despise the decrees of chapters. Let experience make us cautious, whom zeal at another time, without knowledge, made penitent.

That visitors ought to be solicitous for the reform of our order.

Chapter XII.

The chief force of reform, however, is placed in the diligence of the visitors. Therefore it is said in the constitutions of the Fathers that suitable men should be appointed to the office of visitation: men who, by word and example, can effectively instruct those to be visited in uprightness of conduct. For a Visitor must be learned in divine law. He must be holy and irreproachable in life, so that by word he may teach the teachable, and by example instruct the stubborn. For one without the other is not sufficient in a ruler of souls. For if he is unlearned, how will he instruct others? If his conduct does not provide those to be visited with an example of good action, how will he exhort them to reform? He will indeed hear the reproach of the proverb, in which it is said: Physician, heal thyself.

The Pentichus Book of Johannes Trithemius

Nor undeservedly. For indeed, by what presumption are you led, O Polylogue the Visitor, to try to reform others, when you still lie in your own deformity? You are polluted with the filth of vices, and will you be able to cleanse others? Believe me, the Holy Spirit will not give power to your words, when by a contrary life you offend against his grace. A sermon lacks efficacy in the heart of the hearer when the preacher’s conduct reproves it.

What shall I say? I lie if the stubborn man does not often rebuke the stubborn, the foul man defame the foul; and he thinks that he has escaped being conscious of himself, as though conscience were not enough. There are, I say, among them those who, vicious in life, accuse others: in public accusers, in secret guilty parties, at once judges against themselves and offenders. Outwardly they condemn what inwardly they do; they willingly admit what, when they have observed it, they charge as a crime. A boldness wholly suited to the abusive, and an impudence fitting for the impudent.

Often the miser rebukes the covetous man; the lustful man, the unchaste; the proud man, the arrogant; the criminal, the foul. What, Fathers, what do you think? Can deceivers of this sort be found among the visitors themselves? I do not dare to say it; yet I experience it. Many say many things; few show by deeds what they speak. They cannot reform themselves and their own, and they strive to compel others to observance. They say great things, they do the least things: foolish presumption, which, neglecting its own affairs, is carried off to those of others. He who is not sufficient for himself, for whom will he abound? He who cannot bring himself and his own to amendment of life, when will he be able to amend others?

I have said these things against those who are such, who condemn in others what they scorn to amend in themselves. For the rest, I would not wish anything to have been said as an injury to zealous, good, and suitable visitors, of whom I have known several. But you, most excellent Fathers, who have to choose visitors, take care to appoint the better men to that office, if you desire to bring monks to regular observance. For the highest point of regular discipline lies with the visitors: when continued it grows, when neglected it fails.

Indeed, if the visitors diligently fulfill their office, they will preserve reformed monasteries in regular observance, and will easily restore deformed ones to a better state. But if they are negligent, they quickly destroy even those things which have been well begun by others. For nothing so confounds unity; nothing so disturbs peace; nothing so harms charity as the ignorance of visitors, which grows hot not with reason but with undiscerning will. Experience has very often taught us how great disturbances, dissensions, angers, quarrels, slanders, and hatreds unskilled visitors have stirred up in congregations of monks, visitors for whom everything rests on command, and nothing on knowledge and charity. But I have said enough about this, lest I seem to accuse those whom, because of the dignity of their office, we are commanded to treat with honor.

On the State and Ruin of the Monastic Order

How dangerous the governance of souls is. Chapter XIII.

If we consider how perilous a thing is the rule of souls, how heavy a burden is pastoral care, and to how strict an examination it is liable, it would be a wonder if ever in this life our heart presumed upon security. For Scripture says: “A most severe judgment shall be made upon those who are in authority.” For, as blessed Benedict declares in the Rule, the abbot will have to render account to God for the souls of all the monks committed to him. Therefore he says: “Let the abbot who has been ordained always consider what a burden he has taken up, and to whom he will render account of his stewardship.” It is certainly a heavy and dangerous burden to render account for the souls of many, when scarcely anyone is able to answer for himself. O what will abbots devoted to earthly things have to answer to the supreme Shepherd, who destroy the souls of their brothers by evil example and feed them neither by word nor by deed? What shall I say about certain abbots of our order, who neither read the Rule of Saint Benedict, which they profess, nor, if they read it, understand it? I lie if I have not known abbots established under our chapter who are wrapped in such great darkness of ignorance that they do not understand the smallest sentence from the Rule. They neither know nor love the divine Scriptures. Submerged in the vanities of the world, they vanish away. They serve the desires of the flesh, not the Spirit. According to the command of our lawgiver, the abbot must be learned in divine law, so that he may know whence to bring forth new things and old; chaste, sober, merciful, etc. What will those men say, what will they teach, what will they exhort, who understand nothing of the holy Scriptures, nothing of regular discipline? O good God, to what misery our order has come, which once was most learned and full of most holy men. Where now is the lover of regular observance? Where is the study of the Scriptures? Where is the preservation of holiness? All have perished together, and in only a few do we find traces of former honor. Our abbots, except for a few, either given over to avarice or carried away by the vanities of the world, think of nothing less than knowledge of the Scriptures, although many consider themselves learned; but from their works the character of their erudition is known. Now the avaricious man is thought learned. Now he is called religious who joins field to field, who keeps watch over earthly profits, who gives free rein to his appetite for gathering riches. But believe me, fathers, because I am about to speak the truth: temporal riches do not make discipline stable in the order. O how terrible a sentence those abbots will undergo who neglect the Rule, who do not go before their monks by word and by example of holiness; who despise spiritual exercises; who devote themselves to earthly gains; who contemn the discipline of monastic honor. Would that they were wise and understood, and foresaw their last things, and either governed the burden of so great a rule with solicitude, or, if they could not, humbly laid it down.

The Pentichus Book of Johannes Trithemius. 273 Happy is he who stands solicitously upon his watch; who always does the will of the Lord; who, without pretense, lives according to the purity of the Rule.

But for the present these things which we have said concerning the state and reformation of our order will, as I believe, suffice; and let their reading, with the end of the chapter, also come to its close. Moreover, all and singular things which either in this treatise or in others I have written or shall write, I submit to the examination of the sacrosanct Roman Church, whose faith, doctrine, and definition I wish always and everywhere to preserve, teach, believe, and defend as long as I live. But if anything, which God forbid, has been said by me otherwise than she holds, teaches, and believes, I now by these presents simply revoke it and wish it to be held as not said. By this my declaration I wish and judge the supreme pontiff, the vicar of Christ, to be in all things the judge and moderator of my faith and doctrine.

The present treatise was read at table in the provincial chapter of the Order of Saint Benedict of the Province of Mainz, celebrated at Hirsau, in the year of the Lord 1493, on Jubilate Sunday and on the following days until the end. Moreover, with all the abbots gathered there willing and consenting, it was decreed that it should be printed, and that in future provincial chapters it should always be read publicly at table, as is clear in the statutes.

End.
